title: China's rival reveals hypersonic interceptor specs in funding push
content: Taiwan has revealed new details about its homegrown Strong Bow anti-ballistic missile system as the government seeks funding to move the weapon into mass production. The disclosure came earlier this month, as Taipei works to strengthen its air defenses amid growing military pressure from Beijing.The National Chung-Shan Institute of Science and Technology (NCSIST), Taiwan’s main weapons developer, released specifications covering the missile’s propulsion, guidance and radar systems. The government is seeking NT$36.1 billion (about US$1.13 billion), to produce two Strong Bow systems and 128 interceptor missiles.A high-altitude missile shieldStrong Bow, also known as Tien Kung IV, is designed to intercept tactical ballistic missiles at altitudes of at least 70 kilometers (43 miles). That puts its intended interception zone above Taiwan’s existing Patriot and Tien Kung III systems.The interceptor launches vertically and uses a two-stage solid-fuel rocket motor, allowing it to reach hypersonic speeds. During its flight, it relies on inertial guidance and gets updates through radar uplinks.An active seeker guides the missile in the final phase. Thrust-vector control helps the missile maneuver at high altitudes, where the air is thin. The interceptor is equipped with a high-explosive fragmentation warhead.Mobile launchers and advanced radarThe Strong Bow system uses mobile launchers, and each one holds four missile canisters. Tactical command vehicles support the launchers, and an advanced radar system helps with detection and tracking.The radar is designed to identify several threats at once and continue operating against electronic countermeasures. Taiwan’s defense ministry said it can detect threats at greater ranges and altitudes than the radars used with the Patriot PAC-3 and Tien Kung III.Taiwan plans to use Strong Bow as the outer layer of its planned multilayered missile defense network, known as T-Dome. Lu Chien-sheng, deputy director of the institute’s Tien Kung program, said the system was developed specifically for tactical ballistic missiles and could work with other air defense units.Funding remains a major hurdleStrong Bow had initially been included in a proposed NT$1.25 trillion special defense package. The plan called for production to begin this year, with the first integrated locally developed regional air defense system targeted for completion in 2027.However, the opposition-controlled legislature approved only about two-thirds of the requested package in May, leaving Strong Bow outside the final allocation. Attempts to move the program into the regular 2027 defense budget have also faced pressure from other weapons commitments and payments for U.S. arms.The government is now preparing a supplementary budget. The defense ministry has confirmed that additional funding is being considered for missile and drone programs that failed to secure approval.Analysts warn against further delaysSu Tzu-yun, a senior analyst at the Institute for National Defense and Security Research, described Strong Bow as essentially a new missile despite its Tien Kung IV designation.“The tactical advantage is that the higher it can fly, the larger the area it can protect,” he said, estimating that a battery could provide 100 to 150 kilometers (62 to 93 miles) of coverage.Su said Strong Bow had been described as “Taiwan’s version of THAAD,” referring to the U.S. Terminal High Altitude Area Defense system, and estimated its radar detection range was almost 1,000 kilometers (621 miles).Chi Tung-yun, president of the Taiwan Security and Development Association, said combining Strong Bow with Patriot PAC-3 Missile Segment Enhancement interceptors could provide defenders with additional opportunities to engage incoming ballistic missiles.He urged lawmakers “to fund production as soon as possible”, warning that postponing it until 2028 would be “bad news for Taiwan’s missile defense capability” as the PLA continued expanding its ballistic missile forces.Beijing claims Taiwan as part of China and has not ruled out using force. Washington opposes a forced takeover and continues to supply Taiwan with weapons.

title: First full-stack neutral-atom quantum computer debuts with 50 qubits
content: Japan’s first operational full-stack neutral-atom quantum computer, which packs approximately 50 qubits at launch and could eventually reach 500, has just been switched on.Called Shunkai, the system was designed by a research team led by Kenji Ohmori, PhD, a chemist and a renowned Japanese professor at the Institute for Molecular Science (IMS), part of Japan’s National Institutes of Natural Sciences. The machine officially went live on August 24.Shunkai is powered by a quantum processing unit (QPU) supplied by Colorado-based quantum technology company Infleqtion. The company was also the only foreign quantum partner selected by the Japan Science and Technology Agency (JST) for its Quantum Moonshot program.The program is a Japanese government effort aimed at developing fault-tolerant universal quantum computers by the year 2050. “This milestone marks a pivotal moment for Japan’s quantum ambitions as well as Infleqtion’s role in advancing production-ready quantum platforms at scale,” Pranav Gokhale, Infleqtion CTO, pointed out. Japan’s quantum ambitionsAccording to Infleqtion, Shunkai will initially run with 50 qubits before expanding to around 500 as development progresses. Neutral-atom quantum computers use individual atoms as qubits, the basic units of quantum information. They can run at room temperature without large refrigeration systems. Also, the atoms can be trapped and manipulated with precisely controlled laser light. This allows scientists to connect different qubits and also tailor their layout to specific algorithms. Because neutral atoms can be arranged in large arrays while maintaining precise control over their quantum states, the technology is considered a promising route toward much larger quantum computers. It could make it easier for engineers to build computers with more qubits while preserving quantum information. Infleqtion shared that its QPU helped the Japanese team move from research and development toward an operational full-stack computing platform. “Our quantum processing unit delivers the programmability, scalability and fidelity control that next-generation systems demand,” Gokhale explained. Reaching fault toleranceMeanwhile, the current launch is not Shunkai’s end. A new phase of the Ohmori Moonshot project began in April 2026. It will focus on improving the computer’s integration, stability and scalability.The researchers aim to develop a high-performance, fault-tolerant neutral-atom quantum computer with as many as 10,000 physical qubits. “Bringing a full-stack quantum system into production operation is a meaningful step toward fault-tolerant quantum computing that also serves as strong validation of neutral-atom architecture,” Gokhale reported in a press release. Still, reaching that size alone will not make Shunkai fault-tolerant. The researchers also plan to develop ways to detect and correct errors caused by noise and other disturbances during quantum calculations. Quantum systems are particularly sensitive to their environments. This means that errors can accumulate during calculations. Error correction seeks to overcome this by using multiple physical qubits to protect the quantum information needed for computation.The scientists also expect the technology from the project to eventually become available to other external users. This could allow researchers in both, academia and industry, to come up with applications and provide a platform for further work on quantum error correction.Ohmori said opening Shunkai to outside researchers and companies could help advance error-correction technologies and practical quantum applications while creating wider benefits across industry, academia and government worldwide. “I think it is extremely significant that now we have developed Japan’s first full-stack quantum computer in this cutting-edge modality and started its operation,” he concluded in a statement. The team plans to integrate Shunkai with IMS’s existing shared supercomputer facility to create a hybrid quantum-GPU computing center.

title: Higher illness rates found near US nuclear meltdown site: Study
content: A new study has found that people living closer to the Santa Susana Field Laboratory (SSFL) in Ventura County, California, reported higher rates of autoimmune, endocrine, and metabolic disorders. The findings expand earlier research that mainly examined cancer among residents within 5 miles (8 kilometers) of the site.The SSFL operated for nearly six decades as a nuclear reactor and rocket testing site. There were several accidents, including a partial nuclear meltdown in 1959. Radioactive and chemical waste from the facility contaminated the nearby soil and groundwater.The site was named a Superfund site in 1989. Since then, researchers have studied its possible effects on nearby residents. The latest study, published in Risk Analysis, surveyed residents up to 15 miles (24 kilometers) from SSFL and looked at chronic illnesses other than cancer.A wider look at health effectsA team led by Jenna Blyler from the University of California’s Wrigley Institute for Environment and Sustainability surveyed 475 people living within 15 miles (24 km) of SSFL.The researchers wanted to find out whether health effects went beyond the diseases studied before and whether living closer to the site was linked to illness. They also looked at how residents understood environmental risks and if those views affected what precautions they took.The survey population was relatively affluent. About 56 percent of participants reported annual household incomes of $100,000 or more. More than one-third said they had received at least one diagnosis since moving into their current home.Illness rates rise closer to SSFLThe biggest differences appeared among residents living within 5 miles (8 km) of the facility. About 18 percent reported an autoimmune diagnosis, compared with 4 percent among people living 11 to 15 miles (18 to 24 km) away.A similar pattern appeared for metabolic and endocrine disorders. Around 15 percent of residents within 5 miles reported one of these diagnoses, while the figure fell to 2 percent among those living 11 to 15 miles away.The researchers warned that these results do not prove SSFL contamination caused the illnesses. Participants reported their own diagnoses, and researchers did not check them against medical records. The survey also did not track how often each condition occurred or recurred. However, more research is needed to confirm the findings.Residents respond to environmental risksThe study also found unexpected patterns in how residents responded to contamination concerns. People who felt more threatened by the pollution were more likely to say they had taken precautions.Residents who thought protective measures were more expensive also said they took precautions more often. How far they lived from SSFL did not seem to affect their behavior, but having personal experience with illness did.The findings could become more important as climate change increases conditions that can help spread contaminants. Previous research has linked drought and wildfires with greater movement of pollution from the SSFL area.Blyler’s next study will examine how perceived distance from environmental hazards affects protective actions at both individual and community levels.“It may be that people in wealthier and more influential communities have the resources, access, or preference to advocate for protection at a broader level of society, rather than acting only to protect themselves individually,” she added.

title: Las Vegas home conceals a 16,000-square-foot underground world
content:
According to
8 News Now
, Henderson believed nuclear war was a serious possibility and set out to create a protected home without abandoning the lifestyle his family enjoyed. The result became known as the Underground House.
A Cold War home built beneath the desert
Henderson’s interest in underground living began years before the Las Vegas project. The University of Nevada, Las Vegas’ Special Collections documents Henderson’s involvement with the World Underground Homes Corporation, a company associated with underground-living pioneer Jay Swayze. Henderson had also previously commissioned an underground residence near Boulder, Colorado.
He commissioned the Las Vegas project in 1971, with planning beginning in 1973. The underground residence was completed in 1978, according to
UNLV’s archival records
. Henderson and his wife, Mary, lived in the underground home full-time until his death in 1983. Mary later had a conventional residence built above the underground complex and remained on the property for several more years. What Henderson created was effectively a full-scale home placed inside a much larger underground enclosure.

title: MIT startup to build 1,200-mile range hybrid-electric aircraft
content: In 1903, two brothers from Dayton, Ohio, proved the idea of flying planes. More than a century later, a quiet revolution in regional transit is returning to the exact same soil.Electra, an aerospace startup born out of a 2017 MIT classroom project, is preparing to manufacture a new kind of hybrid-electric aircraft in Springfield, Ohio. Supported by a massive $850 million investment, the company’s new 96-acre production facility is projected to create nearly 2,000 local jobs.The hybrid aircraft is being designed for short-runway takeoffs and landings. It is powered by eight electric wing motors and a small, highly efficient gas-powered generator. The fixed-wing plane offers a 1,200-mile range and a cruising speed of roughly 200 mph. Its minimal runway requirements allow it to operate from nontraditional locations like soccer fields, parking lots, and barges. The idea is to offer cleaner, more direct regional transit for communities outside major airport hubs.“Helping people travel between 50 and 250 miles is the sweet spot for this technology,” said Chris Courtin, Electra Director of Technology Development.“This can be a better option than driving or commercial airlines for many kinds of trips. There’s a lot of people traveling in that range and a huge amount of friction in existing ground and air transport systems. This could be a big benefit to those people,” Courtin added.The eight motors allow the aircraft to take off and land in areas about the length of a soccer field. Credit: ElectraHybrid design The firm aimed to rethink regional air transit by choosing ultra-short takeoff and landing (eSTOL) design over eVTOL concepts.Driving 150 miles often means battling hours of traffic, while taking a commercial flight for the same distance requires driving to a major airport, waiting through security, and dealing with flight delays. Electra overcomes both hurdles. The firm’s hybrid design combines a small, efficient gas generator in the nose with batteries under the floor to power eight electric motors on the wings. This setup creates extra airflow over the wings, a phenomenon called “blown lift.” It enables the plane to take off and land in extremely tight spaces like a soccer field. As the batteries provide the extra boost needed for takeoff, the main engine only needs to handle steady flying, which saves fuel and gives the aircraft much longer range than fully electric planes.Set to reshape regional travelFollowing subscale testing at MIT and the company’s official founding in 2019, Electra validated the concept with its EL2 two-seat demonstrator, which has logged over 200 flight tests since 2023. And it is now leveraging new investment to scale manufacturing for its nine-passenger commercial aircraft in Springfield and Clark County.Electra will offer travelers substantial time savings by skipping traditional airports and train stations. It can also connect remote rural communities directly to major hubs by landing in compact spaces without adding to runway traffic.Interestingly, the aircraft operates far more quietly than other planes or helicopters because its power is distributed across eight smaller propellers. This quiet operation makes it both more affordable to run and suitable for noise-sensitive urban and suburban areas.Electra will break ground next year on a 96-acre manufacturing facility. The aim is for an initial annual capacity of 400 nine-seat aircraft, with plans to scale to 800 per year.In addition to shuttle flights to major hubs, the company envisions replacing conventional airports altogether by utilizing existing soccer-field-sized spaces for low-cost passenger transit, cargo delivery, military logistics, and humanitarian aid.

title: New battery design could help EVs keep more power in freezing weather
content: Cold weather remains one of the most persistent challenges for lithium-ion batteries. As temperatures fall, batteries can lose usable energy, deliver less power, and charge more slowly, creating problems for everything from electric cars and heavy trucks to drones and spacecraft.Israeli battery technology company Addionics says it has developed a new battery architecture designed to address that problem from inside the cell itself.The company has introduced a low-temperature battery architecture based on its Smart 3D Porous Current Collectors, which replace the flat metal foils found in conventional battery designs with an engineered three-dimensional porous structure.According to Addionics, the architecture is designed to improve the movement of lithium ions and electrons within the battery, helping cells retain more of their intended performance as temperatures drop.Why cold weather is so hard on batteriesLow temperatures can create a double challenge for electric vehicles. Batteries provide less usable energy and power, while the vehicle may simultaneously need additional energy for cabin heating, battery heating, and thermal preparation before charging. Addionics says an electric vehicle can lose up to an estimated 40% of its range in severe winter conditions.The problem becomes even more significant for applications where power availability is directly tied to operational capability. A heavily loaded electric truck may face reduced power output in freezing conditions, potentially affecting payload or route planning. Defense drones can experience shorter mission durations and reduced operational range. Spacecraft, meanwhile, require energy-consuming heaters and additional thermal hardware to keep batteries within their preferred operating temperatures. The challenge, therefore, is not simply storing more energy; it is ensuring that the energy already stored remains accessible when conditions become hostile.A different approach inside the batteryTraditional lithium-ion batteries typically use flat metal current collectors to support the movement of electrons through the electrode. Addionics is attempting to change that geometry.Its porous three-dimensional current collectors are designed to allow electrolyte and lithium ions to move through the structure, creating additional pathways within the electrode. According to the company, this reduces effective transport distances, improves access to active materials, and distributes electrochemical activity across a larger volume.The underlying idea is straightforward: rather than relying on improvements to a single battery material, the company is redesigning the internal architecture through which ions and electrons move. That could be particularly important in cold conditions, where electrochemical processes become more sluggish and moving lithium ions through the battery becomes increasingly difficult.“By transforming the architecture of the battery cell, Addionics is removing some of the largest limitations that electrified systems have faced,” said Dr. Moshiel Biton, Addionics’ CEO and founder.Potential applications go far beyond EVsWhile cold-weather EV performance is an obvious application, Addionics is positioning the technology for a much wider range of electrified systems. For electric trucks, improved low-temperature performance could help preserve power availability during long-distance winter operations. For drones, it could translate into longer missions and greater operational flexibility.Space applications could also benefit if batteries require less heating. Reducing thermal-management demands could have knock-on effects across the entire spacecraft power system, potentially lowering requirements for stored energy, solar arrays, thermal hardware, and even launch mass.Addionics says it is working with companies across sectors including automotive, defense, space, robotics, energy storage, and other industrial applications. The company’s announcement is based on its own technology claims, and the press release does not include detailed independent performance data for the newly introduced low-temperature architecture. Still, the concept highlights an increasingly important direction in battery development. Rather than focusing solely on discovering entirely new chemistries, engineers are also looking at how the physical architecture inside the cell can be redesigned to improve performance.

title: New nuclear tool speeds reactor development, cuts search time 80%
content: US nuclear technology firm NuScale Power is deploying nuclear-specific AI tools to help engineers find and use technical information faster as it moves its small modular reactor technology toward deployment.The initiative brings together NuScale’s nuclear engineering expertise with Nuclearn’s AtomAssist platform and NPX’s experience in nuclear projects and technology implementation. The tools are designed to search through engineering information, licensing evidence, technical standards and other controlled material.NuScale said an initial proof of concept showed the tools could reduce the time needed to find relevant information by as much as 80%. The system is also designed to surface engineering methods and standards relevant to a particular task.The goal is not simply to speed up document searches. In a heavily regulated industry, engineers need to know where information comes from and whether it can be trusted before using it in design, licensing, or project decisions.Nuclear data gets faster access“NuScale is building a transformative deployment model to integrate NuScale Power Modules™ (NPMs) into nuclear power plants in the near-term, which requires executing with speed, precision, and confidence,” said Dr. José Reyes, Chief Technology Officer of NuScale Power. “This partnership with Nuclearn and NPX will equip our teams with the right purpose-built AI tools – grounded in our extensive proprietary knowledge –to work more efficiently while maintaining the highest safety and quality standards.”The tools are being built around nuclear-specific terminology and workflows rather than treating nuclear engineering like a general information-search problem. That distinction matters because technical documents can contain information tied to specific designs, regulations and safety requirements.Nuclearn said its platform can connect answers to the original controlled sources, allowing engineers to trace information back to the material used to generate it.“AI is only as valuable as the knowledge it can be trusted to deliver,” said Jerrold Vincent, CFO and Co-Founder of Nuclearn. “In a highly regulated, safety-critical industry like nuclear, every answer must be grounded in controlled engineering and licensing information.”The partnership comes as NuScale works to advance its small modular reactor technology from design toward deployment. Its NuScale Power Module is a pressurized water reactor designed to generate 77 megawatts of electricity per module.Smaller reactors need smarter workflowsNuScale says its modules can be combined in different configurations, with an array of up to 12 modules capable of producing as much as 924 MW of electricity.Managing the engineering and regulatory information behind such projects can become increasingly difficult as designs progress. The company is therefore using the new tools to reduce the time engineers spend locating information and increase the speed at which they can apply it.“Across Canada, the United States, and the global nuclear market, new nuclear projects face the same challenge: how to move faster without compromising quality, safety, or regulatory discipline,” said Joshua Bell, Director, NPX US. “NuScale is taking a practical step the rest of the industry can learn from.”For NuScale, the technology is being positioned as an engineering and knowledge-management tool rather than a replacement for nuclear professionals. The company says the system is intended to help teams work with existing technical knowledge while maintaining traceability and regulatory discipline.The approach could become increasingly important as nuclear developers handle larger volumes of engineering, licensing and project information while attempting to shorten development timelines.

title: OpenAI chip beats Nvidia systems with 1.9x more work per watt
content: OpenAI says its first custom inference chip, Jalapeño, can deliver more AI work per watt while also reducing response times, pointing to a hardware design aimed at handling increasingly demanding model workloads more efficiently.The company tested Jalapeño across three public models: GPT-OSS 120B, DeepSeek R1 670B, and Kimi K2.5 1T. Across the tests, the chip delivered 1.5 to 1.9 times more AI work per watt at peak throughput and 1.7 to 3.6 times lower end-to-end latency than the comparison systems.For highly interactive workloads, OpenAI said Jalapeño achieved 2.1 to 4.1 times higher performance. The company argues that combining throughput and low latency in one architecture could help reduce the hardware and power needed to serve AI models.The chip is rated at 700 watts, although OpenAI said its measured sustained power remained at or below 550 watts during the tested workloads. The company compared Jalapeño with commercially available accelerator systems using the public InferenceX benchmark from SemiAnalysis.One chip tackles both bottlenecksA major focus of the design is avoiding the usual tradeoff between throughput and latency. AI inference has different demands depending on what the system is doing. Processing a user’s prompt, known as prefill, is generally compute-intensive, while generating the response token by token, known as decode, depends more heavily on memory bandwidth.Jalapeño was designed to handle both phases within the same architecture. OpenAI said the chip keeps model state, including the key-value cache used during generation, closer to the processing resources that need it.Its networking system is also integrated into the architecture to reduce the amount of data that needs to move between chips. That is intended to limit communication delays that can leave computing resources waiting for data.The approach becomes particularly relevant for AI agents, which may perform many inference steps in sequence. A small delay in each step can add up to a much longer overall task.AI helped build JalapeñoOpenAI also used its own models during the chip’s development. The company said AI helped engineers explore implementations, shorten design and verification cycles, and optimize arithmetic circuits.The team moved from initial design to tapeout in nine months. OpenAI then used Codex with GPT-Astra to bring three open-weight models that were not part of the original production plan to high performance on Jalapeño within two months.For selected GPT-OSS attention and mixture-of-experts blocks, AI-generated implementations ran 1.5 to 1.8 times faster than existing implementations written by human experts. OpenAI stressed that these results applied to individual blocks rather than the complete models.The company also tested Jalapeño against large models including Kimi K2.5 1T. On that model, it reported about 1.5 times higher peak performance per watt and 3.4 times lower end-to-end latency than the comparison system.OpenAI plans to begin deploying Jalapeño in its compute infrastructure by the end of 2026. The company said the chip is the first generation of a multigenerational roadmap, with second- and third-generation designs already in development.The broader goal is to make inference faster and more power-efficient as OpenAI expands its computing infrastructure and serves increasingly capable models.

title: Phased array antennas steer space beams without moving for satellites
content: Redwire is expanding its investment in phased array antennas as demand grows for faster military communications from space.The aerospace and defense technology company plans to accelerate development of adaptable antenna systems for satellites across multiple orbits. The systems could support U.S. military networks that need stronger connections and lower communication delays.Redwire has already supplied antennas for the Pentagon’s Proliferated Warfighter Space Architecture, or PWSA. In 2023, those antennas helped enable the first U.S. military Link-16 communications from space.The new investment pushes deeper into a technology that could shape how future satellite constellations handle data.Antennas that steer electronicallyTraditional antennas often require physical movement to point signals toward a target. Phased array antennas take a different approach.They use many small antenna elements and electronically direct a beam without moving the entire structure. That allows systems to respond faster and maintain connections with changing targets.Redwire wants to apply that capability across low Earth orbit, medium Earth orbit, and geostationary orbit. Future satellite networks will likely rely on large groups of spacecraft instead of a handful of major satellites. Those distributed networks need antennas that can rapidly switch connections and manage heavy data traffic.Mike Sharkey, senior vice president at Redwire Defense Tech’s RF Systems group, said phased arrays will play a central role in that transition. “Space data networks are evolving at an unprecedented pace,” Sharkey said. “Phased arrays are a foundational technology enabling that transformation.” Redwire expects its expanded investment to produce communications hardware with greater flexibility and stronger link performance.Supporting proliferated constellationsThe Pentagon has increasingly focused on proliferated satellite architectures, especially for military communications and data transport.Instead of concentrating critical capabilities in a few large spacecraft, such networks spread them across many satellites. That approach could make the overall system harder to disrupt.Reliable connections become especially important in that environment. Satellites must communicate across rapidly changing orbital positions and potentially contested regions.Redwire says its phased array technology will support dynamic beam steering and higher data throughput. The systems will also target improved connection reliability.Those capabilities could help military users maintain communications across increasingly complex satellite networks. The investment also extends beyond defense missions. Redwire sees applications in civil and commercial space operations as demand rises for high-capacity satellite communications.More production behind technologyRedwire enters the expansion with an established portfolio of radio-frequency hardware. Its RF Systems group operates from Longmont, Colorado, where it supplies tactical communications and sensing payloads to major aerospace and defense contractors.The company says it has delivered more than 200 flight antennas. Its portfolio also includes complex RF payloads, including systems now under production for a European defense contractor.A recent capital upgrade at Redwire’s RF flight electronics assembly facilities will support the broader technology push. The investment reflects a larger shift in satellite communications. Future networks will need to move more data and adapt quickly when conditions change.

title: Scientists make graphene using a kitchen blender and old newspapers
content: Graphene is often described as a “wonder material,” associated with futuristic electronics, advanced batteries, sensors, and ultra-strong composites. But a new study suggests that producing useful forms of the material may not always require expensive equipment or exotic chemicals.Researchers have demonstrated a surprisingly low-tech approach using a kitchen blender, tap water, old newspaper, and graphite recovered from electronic waste.The work, published in ACS Sustainable Resource Management, explored whether graphene could be produced through a simplified version of a process known as liquid-phase exfoliation, while replacing specialized laboratory materials with common household items and waste products.Turning electronic waste into grapheneThe starting material is graphite, a form of carbon made up of countless stacked layers. A single layer of this carbon structure is graphene. Graphite is commonly found in electronic devices, where thin sheets can act as heat spreaders, moving heat away from sensitive components. Once a phone or laptop reaches the end of its life, however, these materials typically become part of the growing electronic waste stream.Conor Boland, assistant professor of materials science at Dublin City University, writes in an article in The Conversation that the researchers investigated whether this discarded graphite could be given a second life. Using liquid-phase exfoliation, they placed graphite in a liquid and applied mechanical energy to separate its stacked carbon layers. Instead of relying on specialized processing equipment, however, they used an ordinary kitchen blender. They then used a simple kitchen sieve to remove larger pieces that had not broken down properly.Why old newspapers proved usefulNewspaper contains cellulose, a structural material found in plant fibers. The researchers washed and softened discarded newspaper in tap water before blending it into a fiber-rich mixture. When graphite was processed in this solution, the cellulose-derived material helped keep the separated graphene sheets apart.Separating graphite into thinner carbon sheets is only part of the challenge. Once separated, the sheets can begin sticking back together. Researchers normally use carefully selected solvents or chemical stabilizers to prevent this. In this experiment, the team tested a much simpler alternative: fibers from old newspapers.The approach was not perfect, but it significantly improved the stability of the mixture. Without the newspaper-derived material, the processed carbon settled from the water within minutes. With it, the solution remained usable for several hours and could be mixed again with a simple shake. Sophisticated laboratory equipment was still required to verify that graphene had actually been produced, but the production process itself relied on remarkably accessible materials.Making nanoscience more accessibleThe work builds on earlier experiments in which the researchers demonstrated that graphene could be produced using materials including pencil lead, tap water, soap, kitchen appliances, and coffee filters.This latest study takes the concept further by asking whether both the equipment and the starting materials could come from inexpensive or discarded sources.  For most experiments, the researchers used commercially available graphite heat-spreading material because a single smartphone contains only a small amount of graphite. However, they also dismantled a discarded phone and recovered enough graphite to demonstrate that real electronic waste could also be processed into much thinner carbon sheets. The researchers are not suggesting that kitchen blenders will replace industrial graphene factories.Instead, the work points toward a potentially more accessible model for early-stage research. Schools, community laboratories, and smaller research groups could potentially perform the initial processing using inexpensive materials, while relying on universities or shared facilities for advanced characterization.It also offers an intriguing example of circular materials research. Yesterday’s newspaper and discarded electronics could help create a material being explored for tomorrow’s technologies. In this case, the most sophisticated part of the experiment was not making the graphene but proving that the blender had actually done it.

title: SpaceX to build world's biggest $100B spaceport with 10 launchpads
content: SpaceX plans to spend at least $100 billion on a massive new spaceport in Louisiana, setting the stage for what could become the world’s biggest launch site.The project, called Starbase Louisiana, will rise near Pecan Island in Vermilion Parish. SpaceX expects construction to begin in 2027 and aims to launch its first Starship from the site in 2029.The project reportedly represents the largest capital investment in the state’s history. SpaceX also plans to create more than 3,000 jobs, with hiring focused heavily on nearby communities.The new complex would give SpaceX a third major operational hub alongside its South Texas Starbase and Florida launch operations.Spaceport built for scaleStarbase Louisiana will cover roughly 125,000 to 130,000 acres of coastal land. SpaceX plans to build five launch complexes with two pads each, giving the site 10 launchpads.That scale reflects the company’s ambitions for Starship. SpaceX says the facility could eventually support thousands of flights every year.The site will also need far more than launch towers. Plans include vehicle processing facilities, on-site propellant production and dedicated power generation.Deep-water shipping infrastructure will move large hardware through the facility. SpaceX also plans to build an airport and residential areas for employees and their families.Elon Musk has suggested the site could eventually grow beyond its initial footprint. He said Starbase Louisiana could ultimately host more than a dozen launch towers and support over 30 Starship flights each day. “SpaceX makes sci-fi real,” Musk wrote on X.Starbase Louisiana will ultimately have over a dozen launch towers, enabling more than 30 Starship flights per day and making it the biggest launch site on Earth! SpaceX makes sci-fi real. https://t.co/C7Ht0U12ba— Elon Musk (@elonmusk) August 25, 2026If those targets materialize, Louisiana would host a launch operation unlike anything currently operating in the United States.Third Starship hubLocation plays a major role in SpaceX’s plans. Launches from Pecan Island could head south over the Gulf of Mexico and support missions into polar or near-polar orbits.Those trajectories could become increasingly important as SpaceX expands Starlink and pursues plans for orbital data centers. The company also expects Starship to play a central role in NASA’s future lunar missions.Starbase Louisiana could help distribute Starship operations across multiple sites as launch demand grows. Texas has served as the vehicle’s main development and test center, while Florida provides another path for future missions.The Louisiana site would add a purpose-built facility designed around high-frequency operations from the start.Coastal challenges remainSpaceX will build the spaceport in a region facing severe coastal erosion. Vermilion Parish loses shoreline at rates ranging from roughly 3.3 to 23 feet annually.The company says it will work with state and federal agencies on coastal protection projects. Proposed efforts include Gulf shoreline breakwaters that could reduce wave energy and slow land loss.Construction remains years away, but the project’s schedule already points toward an aggressive expansion of Starship operations.Initial site operations could begin in 2030. If SpaceX delivers on its proposed launch cadence, a quiet stretch of Louisiana’s Gulf Coast could become home to the busiest spaceport on Earth.

title: Tiny infrared sensors cut bulk while sharpening drone vision at night
content: Teledyne FLIR OEM will help the U.S. Army develop smaller, cheaper, and more capable thermal imaging technology under a new modernization initiative.The company has joined the Army’s Delivering Unmatched Thermal Capability Hastened, or DUTCH, initiative. The program aims to improve uncooled infrared sensors for future military systems.Teledyne FLIR OEM will contribute its thermal imaging technology and system integration experience. Army researchers want to improve sensor performance without increasing the size or power demands of military equipment.The effort also targets lower production costs and larger manufacturing volumes. Those goals could prove important as the Pentagon expands its use of drones and other autonomous systems.Shrinking the thermal sensorUncooled infrared sensors allow military systems to detect heat without requiring cryogenic cooling equipment. That makes them useful for smaller and more portable platforms.The technology already supports drones, thermal binoculars, weapon sights, and loitering munitions. The Army now wants better performance from sensors that occupy less space.DUTCH will focus heavily on SWaP-C, an industry term covering size, weight, power, and cost. Engineers often face difficult tradeoffs between those requirements.A more compact sensor can reduce the payload burden on an uncrewed aircraft. Lower power consumption can also extend operating time.Teledyne FLIR OEM plans to advance its uncooled thermal imaging technology under the initiative. Its work will also support demonstrations tied to Army modernization programs.The company has invested in small-pixel thermal sensor designs. Smaller pixels can help manufacturers create compact imaging systems without sacrificing critical thermal detail.Paul Clayton, president of Teledyne FLIR OEM, said the effort supports Washington’s push for stronger domestic production. “Our ability to deliver NDAA-compliant thermal imaging solutions on time and at scale helps reduce program risk,” Clayton said.Preparing for drone dominanceThermal imaging has become increasingly important for unmanned military systems. Drones can use infrared cameras to identify targets when visible-light cameras struggle.That capability matters during darkness, smoke, and other low-visibility conditions. Future systems will also need sensors that manufacturers can produce in large numbers.The DUTCH initiative therefore extends beyond laboratory performance. Army planners want technologies that can move into high-volume production for future programs.Teledyne FLIR OEM says its manufacturing experience could help meet that requirement. The company operates as a U.S.-based supplier of uncooled thermal imaging systems.Its role could also support the Army’s broader Drone Dominance effort. That program seeks to accelerate the development and fielding of uncrewed capabilities.Securing domestic productionThe initiative also reflects wider concerns about America’s supply of critical defense electronics. Defense officials have increasingly emphasized secure domestic supply chains for microelectronics and other military technologies. Thermal imaging components form an important part of that industrial ecosystem.George Bobb, president and CEO of Teledyne Technologies, said reliable access to advanced camera modules remains important for national security. “A trusted, scalable, and resilient domestic supply of high-performance thermal imaging camera modules is vital,” Bobb said.For the Army, the DUTCH program could help turn advanced thermal sensing into a technology that reaches more systems. Success will depend on improving performance and scaling production.That combination may become increasingly important as drones take on a larger role across future U.S. military operations.

title: US Navy wants anti-submarine torpedo that glides to destroy targets
content: The United States Navy is the most powerful in the world, and it keeps on upgrading itself to ensure naval dominance. In one such move, it is now looking to add a new anti-submarine torpedo, which will be a glide weapon, to its arsenal.The US Navy is currently looking at two options for its Silent Anvil air-launched torpedo, and both of them are for a glide weapon.The Naval Air Systems Command (NAVAIR), operating under the Department of the Navy, has issued a Request for Information (RFI) for the Silent Anvil air-launched torpedo (SAA-LT) standoff delivery solutions.The SAA-LT is being considered a next-generation anti-submarine warfare system that will be used to counter evolving undersea threats. It is being considered that the weapon should be able to launch from both manned and unmanned aircraft platforms operated by the US Navy.Acquisition plans by the US Navy for the glide weaponThe US Navy is looking at two design options for the standoff air-launched torpedo. The first is a fully integrated weapon, which can cover the entire process from aircraft separation to underwater target engagement.The second is a wing kit design, an unpropelled glide wing kit, which is designed to carry a government-issued torpedo to the target.The RFI issued mentions that the glide weapon will be captive-carried and released “from both internal and external aircraft weapons stations utilizing standard Department of War (DOW) carriage systems.”The glide wing kit will consist of a wing, a radio and guidance system, while the torpedo would consist of an acoustic sensor, a warhead, and a command center alongside propulsion.Although information is being sought from contractors at this stage, the RFI states that the torpedo must maintain a compact, lightweight form factor similar to the GBU-39 Small Diameter Bomb (SDB). It states that the complete weapon system should weigh not more than 268 pounds. The maximum length should not exceed 70 inches (5 feet 10 inches), with a diameter of 7.5 inches.More requirements for the glide torpedoThe launch speed for the glide weapon is considered to be from Mach 0.25 to Mach 0.85 and from an altitude of up to 60,000 feet.It should also be able to mount on a BRU-61/A bomb rack and be compatible with current Navy aircraft mission planning applications. Moreover, it shall maximize aerial flight endurance while minimizing aquatic immersion time, restricting water residence strictly to the minimum duration required for successful mission execution.It intends to find out the maximum range possible for such a weapon from the contractors.The service is looking for an end-to-end prototype capability of the SAA-LT system within eighteen (18) months of agreement award. Further, it wants 180 prototype all-up-rounds (AURs) within the three years of the demonstration.The RFI mentions that vendor responses can be sent by September 29 to NAVAIR. The responses should provide a realistic target date and high-level schedule to perform an end-to-end demonstration of the system. It should also come with the pertinent Technology Readiness Level (TRL) for the overall system and critical subsystems.

title: US firm offers incentive to link solar, EVs, and home power system
content: Eligible California homeowners can access up to $18,300 in combined incentives to install a home energy system that integrates solar power, battery storage, and bidirectional electric vehicle charging.San Francisco-based dcbel announced the offer on August 25 after its Ara Home Energy Station was added to Pacific Gas and Electric Company’s Vehicle-to-Everything program. Fewer than 50 places remain under the available rebate programs, according to the company.The incentives combine up to $13,800 from the California Connected Home Rebate, supported by the California Energy Commission, with as much as $4,500 from PG&E.Incentives reward early adoptersEligible PG&E customers can receive an upfront incentive of $2,500 through the utility’s V2X program. The amount increases to $3,000 for customers living in designated Disadvantaged Communities.The first 250 participants can also receive an additional $1,500 Early Adopter Incentive, bringing the maximum available PG&E support to $4,500.Rebates are being distributed on a first-come, first-served basis. California homeowners can begin by reserving a system through dcbel, after which an energy specialist will confirm their eligibility, help them apply for incentives, and connect them with an approved installer.The company said customers will have a single point of contact throughout the process, from their initial inquiry to installation and subsequent support.EV battery can provide 10 days of powerAra combines the equipment needed to manage solar panels, stationary battery storage, and bidirectional EV charging in one Home Energy Station. This eliminates the need for separate power-conversion and management systems for each energy source.At the heart of the station is dcbel’s energy-management technology, which the company said makes more than 100 decisions every second. It automatically directs electricity between the home, solar panels, storage equipment, an electric vehicle, and the grid.During an outage, Ara can draw electricity from the large battery inside a compatible bidirectional EV.According to dcbel, the arrangement could keep a home powered for up to 10 days, although the actual duration would depend on the vehicle’s battery capacity and household energy consumption.The company also claims that charging an EV with home-generated solar electricity could provide up to 20,000 miles of driving range annually.System could reduce annual energy costs“Every Californian deserves clean, reliable energy, and real control over their power and their costs,” said Marc-André Forget, founder and CEO of dcbel. “dcbel gives homeowners that control, working hand in hand with their utility and the grid to make the whole system more resilient for everyone. With these rebates, California is helping families take a meaningful step toward energy independence,” he added. When paired with solar panels, the system can generate and manage electricity with up to 30 percent greater efficiency than separate power-conversion and energy-management solutions, according to the company.Ara can use electricity stored inside an EV to power a house during expensive peak-pricing periods. dcbel estimates this could help a household save up to $1,300 annually while reducing its exposure to changing utility rates.

title: Westinghouse reactor passes criticality test, targets 8-year run
content: Westinghouse has completed zero-power criticality testing of its eVinci microreactor, validating its core design models.The test was conducted on August 24 at the National Criticality Experiments Research Center (NCERC), a National Nuclear Security Administration facility at the Nevada National Security Site in Nevada. Los Alamos National Laboratory and Idaho National Laboratory worked with Westinghouse on the testing.The test did not generate electricity. Instead, zero-power criticality testing allows engineers to examine the nuclear behavior of a reactor core without operating it at full power. The results are being used to validate the models and assumptions behind the eVinci design.Westinghouse said the milestone is part of an iterative development process that combines physical testing, computer modeling, simulation and design changes. The approach is intended to identify technical issues earlier while the company continues developing and demonstrating the reactor.Core design faces reality“This zero-power criticality milestone reflects Westinghouse’s heritage of innovation and pushing to the next frontier of nuclear,” said Dr. Lou Martinez Sancho, Westinghouse Chief Technology Officer. “We appreciate the support and collaboration of our partners at the U.S. Department of Energy, NNSA, Los Alamos National Laboratory, Idaho National Laboratory and NNSS in achieving this important milestone.”The eVinci is designed around a compact reactor architecture that uses heat pipes to move heat from the reactor core. Its design also combines TRISO fuel, graphite core materials and control drums.Rather than relying on a conventional large reactor configuration, the microreactor is intended to provide a compact source of electricity for locations where building traditional power infrastructure can be difficult or impractical.Westinghouse says the system could provide electricity continuously for up to eight years without refueling. The company is targeting applications in remote locations as well as defense and space missions, where reliable power can be difficult to provide.Built for remote missionsThe zero-power test is one part of a broader development program. Westinghouse plans to use information from prototype testing and demonstrations to refine the reactor’s design and assess its performance, operation and manufacturability.That testing approach could be particularly important for a microreactor, where reducing the size of the system does not eliminate the need to demonstrate how its nuclear components behave together.The eVinci’s heat-pipe system is central to the design. Heat pipes can transfer energy from the reactor core without the large pumping systems used in some conventional reactor designs, potentially helping simplify the overall architecture.Westinghouse is also developing the reactor for uses beyond conventional electricity generation. Its compact format could make it suitable for isolated communities, industrial sites and other locations where transporting fuel or building grid connections can be challenging.The company has not announced a commercial operating date for the eVinci microreactor. The latest criticality test instead marks a technical validation step as Westinghouse moves toward additional testing, prototypes and demonstrations.For now, the result gives engineers experimental data to compare with their models before the reactor progresses to later stages of development.

title: World-first test sends information through light beams without loss
content: A laser beam shot across a university campus may have just solved one of telecommunication’s oldest problems. Researchers at Wits University (South Africa) and the University of Bordeaux (France) have demonstrated a method to transmit optical data through open air without needing complex systems to correct for atmospheric distortion.Sending data through open air has always been a messy thing. Earth’s atmosphere is chaotic. Swirling pockets of warm and cold air twist, scatter, and scramble light signals, often turning to heavy computing power and expensive adaptive optics just to piece the broken data back together.Now, a world-first experiment laser shows we can simply ignore the distortion altogether.The team successfully transmitted data through turbulent open air with its integrity entirely untouched. And it all came down to topology.“We create and transmit these particle-like topologies of light through a 270-meter free-space optical link, revealing their robustness across a wide variety of conditions and turbulence strengths,” the study noted.The coffee mug trickTopology is a branch of mathematics concerned with properties that stay constant even when an object is stretched, twisted, or squished.“To explain its benefits, we can liken it to how a coffee mug can be reshaped into the form of a doughnut,” said Prof Andrew Forbes, Head of the Structured Light Lab in the Wits School of Physics.“Despite their very different shapes, both have a single hole. You can stretch or distort them without changing that fundamental property. In the same way, the light beam can become badly distorted while its topological information remains unchanged,” Forbes added. The team applied this concept to light, encoding information into exotic, particle-like magnetic structures called skyrmions. Encoding information into the light’s topological profile gives the data an invisible layer of armor, rather than relying on its raw brightness or color. To put the theory to the test, skyrmion-encoded laser beams were fired across hundreds of meters between two buildings on the Wits West Campus in Johannesburg. The light hit real-world heat, wind, and atmospheric noise.When the light reached the receiver, the shape of the beam was utterly mangled. But surprisingly, the underlying topological data remained completely intact.As a result, data was transmitted through the open air with over 98 percent fidelity in most conditions, dropping to only 86 percent under extreme turbulence.Laser’s best possible use in space missionsFiber-optic cables protect light signals by shielding color, intensity, and polarization from external disturbances. In contrast, sending unguided light through open air leaves these signals far more vulnerable to environmental disruptions like atmospheric turbulence.Until now, free-space optical (FSO) communication systems required constant, real-time recalculations to undo the damage caused by the atmosphere. Receivers had to measure the distortion and fire off dynamic hardware corrections just to read a clean signal. But now, with this new approach, the topology survives the chaos. Therefore, the receiver can read the encoded payload directly without needing to clean up the beam first. And of course, the usage will be huge if scaled. Removing the need for heavy corrective hardware could lower the energy and computing demands for long-distance optical networks.Particularly, the development could be beneficial in deep-space missions, high-speed satellite downlinks, and quantum cryptography. Closer to home, it might bridge the digital divide without laying miles of costly fiber-optic cable. The tech could soon give rural and isolated communities affordable, high-speed internet beamed straight through the sky.The findings were published in the journal Science Advances.

title: Chromium interlayer and FTO front contact let cheap electrodes match gold's stability in perovskite solar cells
content:
Chromium interlayer and FTO front contact let cheap electrodes match gold's stability in perovskite solar cells
Researchers at the University of Oxford, Philipps-University Marburg, Swansea University, the Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems ISE, the University of Surrey and the Chinese University of Hong Kong have tackled a fundamental barrier to commercializing perovskite photovoltaics: how to make highly efficient devices durable without relying on expensive or scarce electrode materials.
The team shows that a 5-nanometer chromium interlayer beneath a cheap aluminum electrode can match, and in some cases beat, the stability of a gold electrode, while cutting the electrode's raw material cost by more than 100,000 times. In a related finding from the same study, the team also identifies indium migrating out of the standard transparent front electrode and into the perovskite as a degradation pathway that is already active during device processing, and shows that a simple substitution fixes it.
Gold rear electrodes are the reliable choice for stable perovskite solar cells, since more reactive metals like silver, aluminum and copper react with halides escaping the perovskite layer and accelerate its breakdown. But gold is far too expensive for terawatt-scale manufacturing, and the alternative - carbon electrodes - is difficult to integrate into the higher-efficiency p-i-n device architecture. Front transparent electrodes carry their own overlooked risk: indium tin oxide (ITO), the industry-standard transparent conductor, has known chemical and thermal stability limits, but how that translates into device-level degradation had not been thoroughly studied.
The researchers fabricated otherwise-identical devices with silver, aluminum, copper and gold rear electrodes, with and without the chromium underlayer, then aged them under heat and simulated sunlight for over 1,000 hours. Unprotected copper and aluminum degraded even faster than silver, but adding the chromium nanolayer roughly doubled the time each metal's champion device took to lose half its efficiency, with chromium/aluminum ultimately matching or exceeding gold's stability - a reversal, since aluminum alone was the fastest-degrading electrode of all four metals tested. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy on aged devices showed the chromium layer forms a mixed metallic/oxidized, likely carbide-containing barrier that suppresses halide transport to the aluminum beneath, blocking the aluminum-bromide formation seen in unprotected electrodes.
On the front-contact side, depth-resolved mass spectrometry revealed indium ions distributed throughout the perovskite layer in both fresh and aged ITO-based devices, with evidence that leaching begins during fabrication itself, not just under later heat or light stress. Photoluminescence measurements confirmed the damage: perovskite films on ITO collapsed from over 1% to below 0.01% quantum yield during aging, while identical films on fluorine-doped tin oxide (FTO) held between 1% and 5% throughout. Deliberately doping perovskite with indium iodide reproduced the same accelerated degradation, confirming indium itself, not just the ITO interface, as the culprit.
Combining both fixes (FTO in place of ITO, plus the chromium/aluminum rear electrode) and reproducing the result in a second laboratory in Oxford, the team's best device retained 66% of its initial efficiency after more than 1,000 hours of aging at 75°C under simulated sunlight, and reached 24.7% power conversion efficiency in a narrower-bandgap composition. The chromium/aluminum electrode also proved more resistant to reverse-bias breakdown than gold and recovered performance more readily afterward. The authors frame the combined result as a practical, terawatt-compatible route to durable perovskite photovoltaics that avoids both gold and scarce indium.

title: Tandem PV secures $7.7 million US DOE ARPA-E SCALEUP Ready award
content:
Tandem PV secures $7.7 million US DOE ARPA-E SCALEUP Ready award
Tandem PV
has been selected for the US Department of Energy's ARPA-E SCALEUP Ready program, winning approximately $7.7 million to support the commercial scale-up and US manufacturing of its tandem technology. SCALEUP Ready is ARPA-E's "disruption wing," aimed at helping promising advanced energy technologies move from development toward market adoption and commercial deployment.
The award will support Tandem PV's Tandems for American National Dominance in Energy Manufacturing (TANDEM) project, which the company says will help move its high-efficiency tandem panels toward large-scale commercial production and support US solar PV manufacturing. Tandem PV's technology combines an ultra-thin perovskite layer with conventional silicon, a design the company says packs more power into the same panel footprint and helps lower costs; it claims up to 29.7% efficiency for its tandem modules under internal testing.
The award follows a string of recent moves toward higher-volume manufacturing. Tandem PV
opened a 40 MW demonstration factory in Fremont, California in April 2026
to validate large-format production, and more recently
acquired Oregon-based thin-film metal oxide coating company nexTC Corporation
, bringing that manufacturing process in-house. The company has previously received a $4.7 million DOE SETO award as part of the TEAMUP tandem-perovskite consortium and a $4 million California Energy Commission grant.
"Being selected by ARPA-E for SCALEUP Ready is a strong validation of our technology, our team and our path to scale," said Tandem PV CEO Scott Wharton, adding that the project would help the company move faster toward high-volume US manufacturing. To date, the company says it has raised $100 million in venture capital, debt and government funding from investors including Eclipse, Constellation Energy, 8090 Industries, Trellis Climate, the US Department of Energy and the California Energy Commission. Former US Energy Secretary and Michigan Governor Jennifer Granholm joined Tandem PV's board of directors earlier this year.

title: AI optimizer to trade Baltic hybrid solar-storage assets - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
Finnish battery optimizer Capalo AI has partnered with Danish developer European Energy to provide trading and market-access services for two hybrid solar-plus-storage projects in Lithuania and Latvia.
Brian Publicover
26 Aug 2026
Applications & Installations
Batteries
Energy Storage
Highlights
Utility-scale
Capalo AI, a Finnish company that optimizes battery energy storage systems across European electricity markets, has agreed to provide route-to-market and trading services for two hybrid solar-plus-storage projects owned by Danish developer European Energy in the Baltic region.
The first asset is the Anykščiai hybrid project in Lithuania, comprising a 78.5 MW solar park co-located with a battery connected in June 2026 at 25 MW/65 MWh. European Energy had
previously announced financing for a 50 MW battery
at the same site, but it is unclear from public disclosures whether the 25 MW/65 MWh system represents the final project configuration, a phased deployment, or a change from earlier financing plans. Capalo AI’s release describes commissioning and market prequalification for the asset as finalized in August 2026.
The second asset is the Saldus Hybrid Park in Latvia, where Capalo AI and European Energy describe the battery component as 46 MW/105 MWh. The project remains under construction.
European Energy’s own prior announcements have described the battery differently: an October 2025 announcement of European Energy’s sale of a 50% stake in the project to Danish pension fund Sampension cited a 46 MW rating, while a November 2025 financing announcement cited 92 MWh. It is not clear from public disclosures whether these figures describe the same final configuration as the newly announced 105 MWh.
Capalo AI said it will provide day-ahead, intraday and balancing-market trading, along with coordinated dispatch of the solar and battery components as a single flexible unit. The company also said it will provide balance responsible party (BRP) services for the Baltic assets. In Poland, by contrast, Capalo AI holds its own
electricity-trading license
but a third party, AARX Energy, serves as BRP, indicating the role can vary by market.
Capalo AI manages 1.6 GW of batteries and 460 MWp of solar under its
Zeus VPP platform
, with 600 MW and 300 MWp of that already live under trading and optimization. The company, founded in 2022, now operates in six European markets and plans to expand into five more this year. It also raised €11 million ($12.8 million) in a Series A round led by Heartcore Capital earlier this year.
Henri Taskinen, Capalo AI’s CEO, noted that European Energy has a large renewable-energy development portfolio. He said that Capalo AI expects the Anykščiai and Saldus assets to participate in Baltic balancing and wholesale power markets through its optimization platform.
European Energy Deputy CEO Jens-Peter Zink said battery storage and the hybridization of energy parks is becoming an increasingly important part of the company’s portfolio, and added that the Baltic countries are a particularly interesting market.
European Energy, headquartered in Copenhagen, reported €766 million in revenue and €170 million in EBITDA for 2025, with 662 MW of renewable capacity grid-connected during the year and a battery-storage development pipeline that grew from 2.4 GW to 7.4 GW over the same period.
The Baltic states have moved toward common regional balancing arrangements since synchronizing with Continental Europe, with Lithuania becoming one of the region’s most active battery storage markets. The country’s government has approved support for up to approximately
1.7 GW/4 GWh of new storage capacity

title: Ecoprogetti upgrades PV module line in South Africa - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
The solar equipment manufacturer completed a project rescue on a PV module line in South Africa that previously faced integration challenges. The newly-operational 200 MW line produces modules primarily for the local market.
Patrick Jowett
26 Aug 2026
Applications & Installations
Highlights
Manufacturing
South Africa
Italian PV equipment manufacturer Ecoprogetti has upgraded an existing PV module manufacturing line in South Africa.
The company explained its upgrade follows an initial installation carried out by a different supplier which had left the production line with integration challenges and unable to reach expected output levels.
A spokesperson for Ecoprogetti told
pv magazine
the upgraded manufacturing facility has an increased nominal annual production capacity reaching approximately 200 MW.
“The line is designed to manufacture different module formats depending on the intended application,” the spokesperson said. “This includes high-power PV modules of up to 650 W, mainly for larger-scale installations and solar parks, as well as modules of around 500 W for off-grid and stand-alone applications.”
Ecoprogetti says it delivered the upgrade through key phases including a detailed technical assessment and identification of critical issues.
It supplied advanced testing equipment, including the latest-generation Ecosun Nova solar simulator and Ecolab EL electroluminescence testers for in-line module testing and quality control, as well as an automatic interconnection machine, Ecobussing, for automatic cell interconnection soldering. The company then offered IEC certification support and on-site services during installation and restart phases.
The production line is now fully installed and operational. Ecoprogetti’s spokesperson also told
pv magazine
production is primarily intended for the South African local market, with target applications including solar parks, agriculture, rural electrification and off-grid installations.
“In particular, the smaller modules are suitable for stand-alone systems serving local homes and agricultural applications, including solar-powered water pumping,” the spokesperson added. “The facility is therefore positioned to support both larger solar projects and decentralized energy solutions for local communities and the agricultural sector.”
Ecoprogetti CEO Laura Sartore commented that a project rescue is not simply about fixing a problem but stepping into a critical situation, restoring control and performance, and delivering tangible value back to the client and investors.
“What truly matters is ensuring continuous output of high-quality PV modules, and this is what we consistently guarantee as a turnkey line provider and PV process expert,” Sartore said.
Ecoprogetti added that Africa represents a key strategic market. The company has also been expanding in the Middle East, most recently with
Iraq’s first solar module production line
and previously with
production lines in Oman

title: Endesa tests voltage control system to integrate more low-voltage self-consumption - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
Endesa’s distribution unit, e-distribución, is testing a voltage control system on low-voltage grids in Aragon and the Balearic Islands. The technology is designed to manage voltage fluctuations and increase grid capacity for self-consumption, renewables and EV charging.
Pilar Sánchez Molina
26 Aug 2026
Applications & Installations
Commercial & industrial
Residential
Endesa is testing a new solution to improve low-voltage grid stability as self-consumption deployment increases in Spain.
The growing adoption of self-consumption and distributed generation is changing power flows in low-voltage grids in Spain, increasing the need to monitor and manage electrical parameters in real time. E-distribución, the distribution arm of Spanish utility
, is testing the LV Line Manager, a system designed to control voltage levels and facilitate the connection of new energy resources while maintaining supply quality.
The device provides real-time monitoring and management of voltage on low-voltage networks. Its deployment comes as electricity generation increasingly shifts from centralized power plants toward distributed generation closer to points of consumption.
E-distribución’s network currently serves more than 438,500 connected self-consumption installations, including around 45,000 collective systems. The resulting bidirectional electricity flows pose new technical challenges for distribution networks.
The pilot will be deployed on networks in Aragon and the Balearic Islands to assess the LV Line Manager’s performance under conditions associated with distributed generation and fluctuating demand.
One challenge is overvoltage during periods of high photovoltaic generation, particularly around midday. Demand peaks, meanwhile, can cause voltage drops. Networks can also experience voltage imbalances due to the uneven distribution of users and differences in their consumption and generation profiles.
The system continuously monitors electrical parameters, including voltage and current, and can automatically intervene to correct imbalances and maintain grid conditions within operating limits.
It is also designed to facilitate the connection of additional low-voltage resources, including renewable energy systems and electric vehicle charging infrastructure.
E-distribución said the technology could increase the capacity of existing networks to accommodate additional distributed energy resources while reducing voltage quality issues.
Real-time voltage management could allow distribution operators to make greater use of existing infrastructure and increase grid flexibility in response to fluctuations in generation and demand.
The LV Line Manager was developed as part of an
Enel Group
innovation project involving different grid environments in Italy and Spain. Enel selected the technology through its Open Innovability platform after evaluating market-ready solutions for testing under real-world grid conditions.

Southampton FC fans can access discounted rooftop solar panels through leasing company Utilita Home, with potential annual energy savings and a chance to win match tickets and a signed shirt.

26 Aug 2026

Commercial & industrial
Southampton FC has teamed up with Utilita to offer fans a buy one, get one free solar promotion.
Southampton FC fans who spy an opportunity to improve their household energy efficiency are being offered a buy one, get one free discount on solar panels via UK solar leasing company Utilita Home.
New customers looking to score discounted rooftop solar panels are invited to apply for a free online quote from Utilita Home using promotional offer code. Those that do so before Aug. 31 will be entered into a prize draw, with the chance to score hospitality tickets for Southampton v Bolton, plus a signed shirt.
Installing rooftop solar panels can save Southampton fans up to GBP 1,275 ($1,737) per year according to Utilita, netting them bill savings and cutting their carbon footprint.
The savings estimate is based on a large electricity usage home in the United Kingdom, using roughly 5,700 kWh per year, with Utilita claims could save GBP 916 on a 16-panel system with 5.32 kWh of battery storage, plus a further GBP 359 in savings in exports to the grid.
To qualify for the promotion, entrants must be new domestic solar customers aged 18, and must complete and submit a desktop survey. Eligibility for promotion is subject to terms and conditions.
Southampton FC is not the only English club with ties to the solar industry. Premier League runners-up Manchester City signed a multi-year global partnership with JinkSolar in June 2024.

title: Hinen launches 13.68 kWh residential energy storage system - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
Hinen’s A15 residential energy storage system combines 3.6 kW to 15 kW hybrid inverters with 14.4 kWh LFP battery modules, each offering 13.68 kWh of usable capacity. Up to six batteries can be connected in parallel for 86.4 kWh nominal and 82.08 kWh usable capacity, with more than 8,000 cycles, IP65 protection and a 12-year warranty.
Tristan Rayner
26 Aug 2026
Technology & Products
Batteries
Energy Storage
Residential
A Hinen A15 installation shown on YouTube
China-based inverter and energy storage system provider
has launched its A15 residential energy storage system in the United Kingdom. The system combines hybrid inverters with modular, high-voltage lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries.
The A15 pairs Hinen’s A-series hybrid inverters with its B15 high-voltage battery module. Each B15 module has a nominal capacity of 14.4 kWh and an initial usable capacity of 13.68 kWh. Up to six battery modules can be connected in parallel, providing up to 86.4 kWh of nominal capacity and 82.08 kWh of usable capacity.
Each B15 battery weighs 117 kg and is equipped with handles. The system is compatible with Hinen’s single-phase and three-phase A-series hybrid inverters. Single-phase models are available with power ratings ranging from 3.6 kW to 15 kW.
The 3.6 kW inverter option falls within the scope of the United Kingdom’s G98 connection process, under which qualifying systems can generally be installed before the distribution network operator (DNO) is notified. Higher-power systems may require a different grid-connection process, depending on the installation and DNO requirements.
The A15 has a depth of 180 mm and can be installed in garages, utility rooms and other areas where space is limited. It supports wall- and floor-mounted installation, with adjustable feet available for floor mounting.
Hinen said the battery is rated for more than 8,000 cycles and comes with a 12-year warranty. The company said the system does not require an external battery management system (BMS), reducing the amount of wiring required during installation.
The battery incorporates a heating system designed to enable operation at temperatures as low as -20 C. The system has an IP65 enclosure and what Hinen describes as a five-layer protection system.
According to Hinen, the A15 also includes a built-in circuit breaker, automatic fault isolation designed to allow continued operation if an individual battery module fails, and an internal aerosol fire-suppression system.
Users can monitor real-time energy consumption through the Hinen app, which also supports over-the-air (OTA) firmware updates. The system can be used for applications including solar self-consumption and supplying loads such as electric vehicle chargers and heat pumps.
“The UK is an important market for Hinen. The A15 launch marks more than a new product – it strengthens our commitment to local partnerships and the support network needed to help installers and homeowners adopt energy storage with confidence,” said Dustin Wang, country general manager at Hinen UK.
Hinen unveiled the A15 during an online event aimed at installers. Participants included the company’s technical team, UK distributors and installers, industry representatives and homeowners. The event featured installation and commissioning demonstrations, information on Hinen’s experience in the Australian market, and introductory pricing for installers.
