title: PJM’s Power Shortfall Puts Data Center Growth in Focus
content:
PJM’s latest capacity auction left the RTO 6.8 GW below its Reliability Requirement for the 2028/29 delivery year, increasing pressure on the grid operator as it develops rules for rapidly growing large-load demand, including data centers, and seeks additional power supply.
PJM has responded with a proposed
Reliability Backstop Procurement
, an accelerated process intended to secure additional generation and address the shortfall. PJM filed the proposal with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission July 31 after its board advanced the plan.
For data center operators,
PJM’s large-load decisions
increasingly determine whether proposed projects can secure the power they need to move forward, how much generation they may need to bring or contract for, and how much certainty they can have around long-term electricity costs.
The approach is also testing a lesson from PJM’s first major attempt to address large load growth through its stakeholder process.
Related:
DOE Keeps Eddystone Power Plant Online Amid Data Center Demand Surge
That process, launched in 2025, produced 12 proposals but no consensus. With none receiving the required stakeholder support, PJM’s board used the record to set its own policy direction and direct further work.
The question now is whether PJM can move faster while keeping policy direction, stakeholder implementation and the evidence supporting major planning assumptions clearly separated.
Twelve Proposals, No Decision
A recently released transcript of a July 23 FERC
technical conference
on PJM governance shows how sharply participants disagreed over the stakeholder process.
PJM’s first Critical Issue Fast Path process for large loads produced 12 proposals, but all 12 were voted down by stakeholders and none advanced as a recommendation to the PJM Board of Managers.
Pennsylvania Deputy Secretary of Policy Jacob Finkel, speaking at the conference, recalled the reaction when he returned to PJM’s Valley Forge headquarters for a postmortem.
“The members went around patting themselves on the back for what a thoughtful, deliberative, creative process they had just gone through,” Finkel said.
He saw it differently.
“This is a failure,” Finkel said. “You have not advanced the ball.”
The problem was not a lack of ideas, said Neil Osnato, founder of Persistence Analytics Group.
The stakeholder process was being asked to resolve a policy question involving participants with materially different economic interests, downside exposures and views of who should pay, Osnato said.
“At some point, more alternatives do not create consensus,” Osnato said. “They create more ways to avoid making the underlying decision.”
Related:
PJM Strategy Targets Data Center Growth, but Policy Gaps Remain
Joseph Bowring, president of Monitoring Analytics and PJM’s independent market monitor, said the stakeholder process itself remains useful, although it could be made more efficient.
“Stakeholders were generally pursuing their narrow self interest and ignoring the broader public interest in efficient, competitive markets that assign costs and risks to those that cause them, in this case the data center load,” Bowring told
Data Center Knowledge
The proposals addressed different pieces of the large load problem, including load forecasting, new generation, interconnection, reliability and the treatment of customers that could not be served under PJM’s traditional resource adequacy framework.
PJM’s board ultimately used the
CIFP record
to develop its large-load framework, incorporating ideas from multiple stakeholder proposals. The January decision addressed load forecasting, bring your own new generation arrangements, expedited generation interconnection and a reliability backstop.
The Board Sets Direction
Osnato said the outcome does not mean the stakeholder process had no value.
It generated information, exposed competing positions and gave the board a menu of possible approaches, he said.
Related:
Can Large-Load Flexibility Ease Data Center Energy Concerns?
But the process did not make the final policy decision.
“The stakeholder process functioned as an input mechanism, but failed as the final decision mechanism on this particular issue,” Osnato said.
Abe Silverman, assistant research scholar at Johns Hopkins University’s Ralph O’Connor Sustainable Energy Institute, made a similar distinction at the FERC conference.
The problem was not necessarily the number of committees in PJM’s stakeholder process, Silverman said.
“It’s when we ask committees to decide policy,” he said.
Large load integration should start with PJM, its board and the states establishing the policy direction, Silverman said. Stakeholders could then work through the technical and implementation questions.
“We would have saved so many hours of meetings,” he said.
Pamela Quinlan, executive director of the New Jersey Energy Resilience Bank, made a similar point while cautioning against abandoning PJM’s technical stakeholder process.
Direction and leadership should come from PJM leadership and the board, Quinlan said, while stakeholders provide the technical expertise needed to work through implementation.
July Base Residual Auction
procured 138,318 MW through the Reliability Pricing Model. Including fixed-resource-requirement capacity, PJM reported total RTO procured capacity of 149,181.6 MW UCAP, which was 6,831.3 MW UCAP below its Reliability Requirement for the 2028/29 delivery year.
RBP proposal
is designed to address that shortfall. The procurement is targeted to begin Sept. 30, subject to FERC approval.
The RBP would secure resources for terms of up to 15 years, with a maximum weighted-average willingness to pay of $555 per MW-day. Qualifying new resources covered by bilateral agreements or otherwise brought to the system would reduce the amount PJM procures through the backstop.
Customers Need Power Path
The reliability gap has direct consequences for the companies driving much of PJM’s new demand.
Google’s Brian George, senior lead for U.S. energy markets, told FERC that his company has billions of dollars invested in PJM and operates data centers throughout the region.
Google has participated in the large load process despite not being a PJM member, working with members and other nonmembers on proposals intended to address the resource adequacy problem.
But George said the company needs greater certainty before committing capital to additional power resources.
The company is expected to make investments in new generation as part of the federal ratepayer protection effort.
“We can’t do that without the certainty that the market rules are going to exist in such a way that we know that investment is going to be worthwhile,” George said.
The RBP is intended to create a mechanism for bringing additional generation into the system while PJM works through its broader large-load framework.
PJM proposed a central procurement to address the 6.8 GW capacity shortfall from the 2028/29 Base Residual Auction. The procurement would run in September and October, with results expected in December, and would give new generation resources a fixed price for 15 years. PJM also proposed reducing the procurement target for large loads already matched with bilateral supply, approved integrated resource plan supply or demand-side participation.
Bowring said the RBP would shift the cost of serving data center load to other customers.
“The RBP process would require other customers to pay for data center load, despite PJM’s assertions to the contrary,” Bowring said. “The RBP approach is going in the wrong direction.”
Faster Decisions, Stronger Evidence
The 6,831 MW auction shortfall is now the basis for a procurement that could involve substantial new generation investment and long-lived infrastructure commitments.
Osnato said that makes the evidentiary question even more important.
Before the shortfall figure drives procurement, cost allocation or infrastructure decisions, PJM should be able to identify the assumptions behind the number, the evidence supporting those assumptions and which large-load additions are executable and durable, Osnato said.
PJM should also establish which dependencies must remain true and what changes would require the calculation to be revisited, he said.
The goal should not be to slow PJM down.
“Speed matters,” Osnato said. “But speed and verification should not be treated as opposites.”
The same principle applies to PJM’s broader large-load planning.
“Before a large load representation becomes an infrastructure planning assumption,” Osnato said, “someone should be able to answer: Who proved it?”
The question is increasingly consequential as PJM tries to accommodate a wave of new data center demand while addressing the capacity shortfall.
PJM expects roughly 70 GW of new large load could come to the system by 2038.
At the same time, PJM is turning to an accelerated procurement process to address the immediate reliability shortfall.
Authority Or Execution?
The disagreement over how to fix PJM’s process extends to whether the grid operator needs more authority.
Mason Emnett, senior vice president for public policy at Constellation, said the problems drawing the most attention, including resource adequacy and infrastructure, are already areas where PJM has Section 205 filing authority.
Changing that authority would not necessarily address the problem.
“PJM is the chef,” Emnett said. “It has different tools in its toolbox. And we don’t believe that those tools need to be changed; we believe they should be used.”
Emnett said PJM had already spent substantial time working through large load solutions and should not simply begin another lengthy process.
“That is about leadership and execution of responsibilities,” he said.
Osnato said the RBP does not fundamentally change his view of the first CIFP.
If anything, he said, the new procurement sharpens the lesson.
The RBP addresses a more immediate problem, with PJM facing a stated capacity shortfall and an accelerated process intended to produce a backstop solution. But the governance risk remains if stakeholders are again being asked to determine core policy choices rather than implement a direction established by PJM and its board.
“The lesson from the first CIFP is not that PJM needs fewer ideas. It is that policy direction has to come before stakeholder implementation, and faster decisions need stronger evidence, not weaker evidence,” Osnato said.
The first large-load CIFP showed that a stakeholder process could generate a dozen serious proposals without producing a decision.
The test for PJM now is whether it can move faster without lowering the evidentiary standard for the assumptions behind those decisions.

title: Australia completes first solar-BESS hybrid dispatched as a single generator - Energy Storage
content: Australia’s first approved single hybrid generator performance standard (GPS) project has now been built and connected. A project joint venture (JV)-owned by Italian utilities major Enel Group and Japanese oil and gas giant Inpex, Potentia Energy with its construction partners have completed the $190 million (USD 136.4 million) Quorn Park solar hybrid in New South Wales (NSW). Located inland from Sydney, the hybrid 98 MW solar and 20 MW / 40 MWh battery energy storage system (BESS) Quorn Park hybrid, was the first hybrid project in the National Electricity Market (NEM) to receive approval for a single hybrid generator performance standard (GPS). Historically, the NEM in Australia required co-located solar and storage assets to register as two separate entities with independent connection agreements. Under the new single hybrid standard, Quorn Park and its 160,000-panels and 16-unit BYD BESS system are licensed and dispatched as one integrated generator under the GPS. It therefore uses a single power plant controller with AC-coupling to govern dynamic interactions between the solar and battery inverters behind one point of connection. The outcome means that the AC-coupled plant can freely store its own solar output, or import from the grid. The energy can then be time-shifted or arbitraged for higher prices as it operated in three distinct modes – solar only, battery only, and solar battery hybrid. Potentia Energy has previously noted it had engaged Beon Energy Solutions to deliver the BESS, and had made use of BYD Cube Pro utility-scale battery units. SMA supplied inverters for the solar park and battery system. Potentia Energy Chief Executive Officer Werther Esposito said Quorn Park is an example of where the energy system is heading . “As more renewables enter the grid, the challenge isn’t simply how much clean energy we can generate but how flexibly we can use it,” Esposito said. Esposito added that combining solar generation and battery storage as a genuinely integrated facility, Quorn Park creates greater flexibility to generate, store and dispatch renewable energy according to the needs of the grid. Potentia Energy Chief Operations Officer Gabriele Mallarini said delivering an integrated hybrid facility required close coordination across every aspect of design, construction, commissioning and grid connection. “Bringing solar and battery storage together as one plant adds a level of technical and operational complexity that goes well beyond simply building the two assets next to each other,” Mallarini said. “What matters now is how these technologies perform together in the real world. Quorn Park gives us an opportunity to demonstrate the value that truly integrated renewable generation and storage can provide to the electricity system.” Quorn Park was delivered with Beon Energy Solutions, SMA Australia, LONGi, BYD, Nextracker and Proa Energy Intelligence. The project is also supported by a 10-year power purchase agreement with South Australia-headquartered renewable energy gen-tailer Zen Energy. title: Battery boom brings round-the-clock solar closer, Ember says - Energy Storage
content: A study by British energy think tank Ember suggests that the prospect of round-the-clock solar photovoltaic (PV) availability is drawing closer. Solar PV generated just over 10% of global electricity in the first half of 2026, up from 8.9% in the same period of 2025. Its share has nearly doubled from the 5.6% recorded in the first half of 2023. Over the past three years, solar PV generation has grown seven times faster than total electricity generation. While global electricity generation rose by 12% between the first half of 2023 and the first half of 2026, solar generation more than doubled, from 769 TWh to 1,564 TWh. However, this growth remains heavily concentrated around midday. On an average day in the first half of 2026, solar met more than 25% of global electricity demand between 11:00 and 14:00, before falling to near-zero levels between 20:00 and 05:00. In markets with higher levels of solar PV penetration, this concentration is even more pronounced. In Chile, where solar met 26% of electricity demand in the first half of 2026, its contribution reached 71% at midday but had virtually disappeared by 21:00. In the Netherlands, solar met 58% of demand at 13:00, while in Germany it covered 55% at midday. In both markets, however, solar’s contribution fell to zero a few hours later. Fossil-fuel generation maintains its position after sunset The expansion of solar PV is displacing fossil-fuel generation during the day, but hours without sunlight remain a key domain for conventional generation. Between the first half of 2023 and the first half of 2026, average fossil-fuel generation between 11:00 and 14:00 fell from 86 GW to 69 GW. During the evening peak, between 19:00 and 21:00, however, the decline was much smaller, from 106 GW to 101 GW. New battery storage installations in 2026 are projected to reach 459 GWh, up 50% from the 307 GWh added in 2025. According to Ember data, this capacity could theoretically shift 34% of new daily solar generation to non-solar hours. This proportion is nearly double the 18% estimated for batteries installed in 2025 and compares with just 4% five years earlier, in 2021. Falling battery installation costs have been a key driver of this progress. Average global costs fell by 95% between 2010 and 2025, from $2,634/kWh to $140/kWh. Bulgaria and Chile lead the rollout While batteries installed globally in 2025 could shift the equivalent of 18% of new daily solar generation, some countries achieved significantly higher shares. Bulgaria installed enough storage to shift 77% of its new daily solar generation, followed by Chile at 76% and Australia at 60%. Bulgaria’s growth has been particularly rapid. The country went from virtually no battery storage capacity in 2023 to adding around 3 GWh in 2025. By May 2026, installed capacity had surpassed 8.6 GWh. Chile followed a similar trajectory, adding 4 GWh of battery storage in 2025 and bringing its installed capacity to 7.6 GWh. Most of the new storage was installed alongside solar plants, helping to reduce curtailment and shift solar generation into the evening hours. The United States added 58 GWh of storage in 2025, enough to shift approximately one-quarter of its new daily solar generation. The European Union, meanwhile, added 27 GWh of battery storage in 2025, equivalent to shifting 16% of new daily solar generation and below the global average. Solar power begins to extend into the evening In California, the combination of solar and battery storage met more than a quarter of electricity demand during the evening peak, between 19:00 and 21:00, on an average day in the first half of 2026. In the first half of 2023, the figure stood at 6.8%. In the first half of 2026, batteries enabled solar energy to meet more than 10% of evening electricity demand in Chile. In Bulgaria, solar and storage together covered nearly a quarter (24%) of electricity demand between 19:00 and 21:00 and supplied an average of 10% of demand between 19:00 and 07:00. However, developing solar generation capable of supplying electricity beyond daylight hours will require more than additional battery capacity. Electricity markets must also enable batteries to participate effectively and operate where they provide the greatest value to the power system. Ember concludes that batteries do not eliminate the need for a diversified electricity mix. Wind, hydropower, nuclear power, and long-duration energy storage will continue to play significant roles, particularly during extended periods of low solar or wind generation. title: BMW's new iX3 EV is racking up orders, even in China, despite selling only an image
content:
Peter Johnson
| Aug 27 2026 - 8:35 am PT
With global orders for the
near 100,000, BMW dealers in China are reportedly overwhelmed by demand, with tens of thousands of pre-orders coming in in less than a week after it went on sale.
The new BMW iX3 is off to a strong start, even in China
After launching the new iX3, the first from its Neue Klasse (“New Class”) lineup last September, BMW’s former CEO Oliver Zipse revealed the electric SUV
secured 50,000 orders
in its first six months on the market.
BMW said on Thursday that orders were now nearing 100,000. To meet the stronger-than-expected demand, the company added a second shift at its plant in Debrecen, Hungary, earlier this year.
While the promising start has caught even BMW off guard, the new iX3 is reportedly now drawing big interest in China, where the luxury automaker, like most foreign OEMs, is quickly losing market share to domestic EV makers like BYD and Xiaomi.
BMW launched the new iX3 in China at the Chengdu Auto Show on August 21 in three variations, with prices ranging from 269,900 yuan to 339,900 yuan ($40,200 to $50,500).
Several BMW dealers told
that “Once the pre-sale price was announced, the sales team has barely stopped working, working until 10 pm every day,” adding that “there are just too many interested users.”
Shao Bin, Senior Vice President of Marketing at BMW Brilliance Automotive Ltd at the 2026 Chengdu Auto Show (Source: BMW)
In just under a week, each BMW store in the core area has received nearly 80 “small orders,” the dealers claimed. Since it went on sale, the new BMW iX3 has reportedly secured “tens of thousands” of small blind pre-orders.
The “overwhelming demand” comes despite having essentially zero actual vehicles to show. “We’re not selling cars, we’re just selling pictures, Xiao Zhou, a BMW salesperson, told
In the 10 years that Zhou has worked for BMW, this is the first time that he has had no models to display after opening pre-sales.
BMW expects show cars will begin arriving at dealerships at the end of October, followed by the first customer deliveries in November.
BMW iX3 50L (Source: BMW)
Full-scale deliveries are not expected to begin until 2027. According to BMW’s app, those who place an order can have it confirmed by January 31, 2027.
To keep potential buyers interested, BMW introduced a new “waiting points” system, which many local EV manufacturers use. From the day they place an order, iX3 buyers will receive 100 BMW membership points a day until the vehicle is delivered.
With a total of about 16,000 points possible from now until January 2027, the value is worth around 4,000 yuan,
said, or roughly $600.
The BMW i3 Long Wheelbase (left) and iX3 Long Wheelbase (right) Source: BMW
A source close to BMW’s R&D team told
that some of the new technology included in the iX3 is still in the final stages of testing. BMW “would rather delay delivery than hand over a half-finished product to users,” the source said.
Like in Europe and other overseas markets, BMW’s new iX3 is off to a promising start in China as well.
As the first EV based on BMW’s Neue Klasse platform with its sixth-generation eDrive (Gen6) architecture, the new iX3 is a step change from its first-generation electric vehicles.
BMW iX3 50L prototype drives 500 miles in real-world driving conditions (Source: BMW)
The new BMW iX3 has an official CLTC range of up to 919 km (517 mi). In June, BMW tested an iX3 50L xDrive Long Wheelbase (LWB) prototype, which
covered over 800 km
(500 miles) around the Qinghai Lake grand loop.
BMW put it through the paces, repeatedly climbing hills with an elevation gain of over 6,500 feet (nearly 2,000 meters) and driving through “heavy snowfall, intense rain, and strong high-altitude sunshine.”
The prototype achieved an energy consumption of 20.3 kWh/100 miles (12.6 kWh/100 km), or 4.9 miles per kWh, and still had 2% battery capacity at the end of the journey.
BMW iX3 interior (China-spec) Source: BMW
BMW said that under the same real-world driving conditions, the iX3 LWB could achieve a driving range of about 835-840 km (518-522 miles).
The China-specific iX3 also features nearly 40 “high-value features” as standard on all trims, including BMW’s Panoramic iDrive, a new end-to-end autonomous driving system developed with Momenta, and a new AI-powered Intelligent Assistant with Alibaba Large Language Models (LLMs).
Electrek’s Take
Although the orders in China are blind pre-orders and likely a bit inflated, the new iX3 is still doing one thing — getting buyers interested in the brand again.
BMW still has a long way to go to revamp the brand in China, the world’s largest EV market. In the first half of 2026, BMW Group’s sales in China plummeted by 20% compared to the same period last year.
Its attention to detail has helped BMW get to where it is today, but to keep up with Chinese brands like BYD and Xiaomi, it will need to shorten its development cycle drastically. Generating hype is one thing, but converting it into actual sales is another.
In the US, the 2027 BMW iX3 50 xDrive is
available to order
, starting at $61,500. It has an EPA-estimated driving range of up to 434 miles.
The BMW iX3 40 is on sale in Germany, starting at €63,400 ($73,000), with a WLTP driving range of 628 km (390 miles), while the iX3 50 xDrive is priced from €73,925 ($85,200), with a driving range of up to 805 km (500 miles).
The LWB version’s wheelbase is 108 mm longer than that of the standard iX3, but it’s specifically designed for China.

title: London police are now using the same illegal e-bikes as the criminals they chase
content:
Electric Motorcycles
Micah Toll
| Aug 27 2026 - 2:55 am PT
London police have apparently decided that if you can’t beat them, join them – or at least get yourself the same electric bike.
The Metropolitan Police has expanded its fleet of high-powered electric two-wheelers used to chase suspects across London, adding 20 new electric motorbikes and bringing the fleet to 25. The machines can reach speeds of around 50 mph (80 km/h), hop curbs, tackle stairs, and follow suspects into places where a traditional police motorcycle, electric bicycle, or squad car simply can’t go.
And judging by the photos released by Scotland Yard, those bikes are Sur-Rons – the very same type of lightweight electric dirt bikes that have become infamous for their use by criminals and illegal street riders in London.
The irony is pretty thick. Even an official Sur-Ron social media page
posted a quip
about it.
Sur-Ron-style electric motorcycles have more frequently been referred to by a new colloquialism of “e-motos,” separating it from the more longstanding colloquialism of “e-bikes” that has long encompassed a wide range of two-wheeled EVs from lightweight electric bicycles to higher powered rides. But legally speaking, these Sur-Rons are mostly just electric dirt bikes, far from anything considered road legal in the UK.
Local electrically assisted pedal cycles are limited to 250W of continuous motor power and assistance up to 15.5 mph (25 km/h). Anything exceeding those limits is generally treated as a motor vehicle and must meet the corresponding registration, insurance, licensing, and approval requirements to be legally operated on public roads.
Of course, the police bikes are presumably (or hopefully) being operated under some appropriate legal framework. The point is that unregistered Sur-Rons ridden on public streets – the same machines police routinely seize from illegal riders – are very much illegal.
In fact,
the Met itself lists
illegal e-bike use as a policing priority in parts of London, including enforcement and seizure of illegally ridden machines.
But there’s a good reason police want them.
Phone snatching has become a major problem in London, often involving thieves using fast electric bikes to approach victims and then escape through traffic, alleys, parks, and pedestrian areas. According to Reuters, reported mobile phone thefts fell from roughly 68,000 to 54,000 in the 12 months through May, though fewer than 1% of offenses currently result in what the Met calls a “positive outcome,” such as a charge or caution, according to
Police say combining the fast electric motorbikes with drones has helped officers close the mobility gap. The Met described its expanded e-bike fleet as part of its effort to target gangs using e-bikes and mopeds for crime.
, Mayor of London, said:
“The Met’s new fleet of Sur-Ron e-bikes sends a clear message that London will not tolerate criminal behaviour,” explained London Mayor Sadiq Khan in a statement. “These bikes have been successfully helping the Met to go after offenders who are increasingly using high-powered, illegally modified e-bikes to commit crimes and it’s great to be able to expand the fleet. With record funding from City Hall, the Met are using the latest innovation and technology, alongside neighbourhood policing, to stay one step ahead of criminals.”
And frankly, it makes sense. Sur-Rons became popular with criminals for many of the same reasons enthusiasts love them: they’re quick, quiet, narrow, lightweight, and ridiculously capable off-road.
Now the police chasing them finally have the same advantages.
Sometimes the best tool for catching an illegal bike is, apparently, another one.

title: Storm Sondors is back, teasing mysterious new electric bike [Photo]
content:
Micah Toll
| Aug 27 2026 - 5:24 am PT
Just when you thought the SONDORS story was over, Storm Sondors appears to be mounting another comeback.
The entrepreneur behind one of the most influential – and eventually most controversial – electric bike companies in the US has resurfaced with a mysterious new two-wheeler being teased on the SONDORS website.
For now, details are exceedingly thin. The ⁠SONDORS
has been stripped down to little more than a dark teaser image showing what appears to be a new moped-style electric bicycle, along with “001” and a September 3 date.
Admittedly, it doesn’t show much. But after I cranked up the exposure on that teaser image and tweaked the lighting a bit more, it’s easy to see that there are several clues hiding in the shadows.
The bike appears to feature a long bench-style saddle, relatively small and wide tires, an upright riser handlebar, and what looks like a large triangular central frame section covered by a distinctive slotted panel. There appears to be a bicycle crank and chain, suggesting at least an attempt at a landing in the three-class electric bicycle system in the US.
A substantial-looking dual crown front suspension fork is visible as well, and the overall silhouette falls squarely in the increasingly popular moped-style e-bike category. Basically, it’s pretty obvious that this will be the type of bike we have often referred to as a SUPER73 competitor, though at this point SUPER73 is likely more of a fellow member of that group of e-bikes than the leader it once was.
There simply isn’t enough visible yet to make any useful guesses about the motor, battery, performance, or even exactly how SONDORS intends to classify the vehicle. But if September 3 is indeed the reveal date, we shouldn’t have to wait long.
And perhaps the bigger story isn’t even the bike. It’s the name behind it.
The complicated history of SONDORS
Storm Sondors burst onto the electric bicycle scene
way back in 2015
with a proposition that seemed almost too good to be true: a $500 fat-tire electric bicycle.
At a time when most decent e-bikes in the US still cost several thousand dollars, the original SONDORS bike was disruptive in the truest sense of the word. The crowdfunding campaign raised millions of dollars and quickly turned SONDORS into one of the most recognizable names in the nascent US e-bike industry.
And despite plenty of early skepticism and the many detractors calling it a scam, the comapny delivered. Sure, the bikes came in late, cost a bit more than they should have, and didn’t always live up to the full specs originally promised. But they arrived. And over the following years, Sondors did something important that shouldn’t be erased by what happened later: he actually put a lot of people on electric bikes.
It’s unclear exactly how many bikes were sold under the SONDORS name over the years, but company statements and
SEC filings
put the number in at least the high five figures, if not the low six figures. Whatever number you choose SONDORS made various larger marketing claims over the years – we’re talking about tens of thousands of real electric bicycles that reached real riders.
SONDORS also helped demonstrate just how effective the direct-to-consumer model could be for inexpensive e-bikes. The company developed everything from fat-tire bikes and folders to more sophisticated models, often offering eye-catching designs at prices well below the established competition.
The original SONDORS e-bike that took the industry by “storm” in 2015
But there was another side to the SONDORS playbook.
Delays became something of a recurring theme. Products often arrived later than originally promised, and sometimes with specifications or designs that had changed along the way. For years, though, SONDORS generally managed to pull it off. As I wrote
back in 2023
, the pattern was often something along the lines of “delivered late and under-specced but always getting there. Mostly.”
SONDORS expanded into folding bikes, full-suspension bikes, scrambler-style bikes, and even crazier projects like an
ill-fated three-wheeled electric car.
Then came the Metacycle.
The Metacycle changed everything
When SONDORS
unveiled the Metacycle electric motorcycle in 2021
, it looked like another potential industry disruptor. The $5,000 motorcycle was originally pitched with an 80 mph (130 km/h) top speed and 80 miles (130 km) of range.
The motorcycle was late – very late – and the production version changed considerably from the original concept. But eventually Metacycles really did start reaching customers in 2022. By early 2023, Storm Sondors told
Electrek
that nearly 2,000 had been shipped.
I rode one myself
, and despite the missed specs and changed design, it was actually a fun little electric motorcycle.
Unfortunately, that wasn’t the end of the story.
Deliveries eventually slowed to a trickle while customers continued waiting for motorcycles and, in some cases, refunds. I later learned from SONDORS’ Chinese manufacturer, and revealed in
a detailed exposé
, that hundreds of completed Metacycles and large quantities of components were sitting in China amid a financial and contractual dispute between the factory and SONDORS. The factory accused SONDORS of failing to make required payments on bikes already shipped to him and others still in production; Storm later disputed the characterization of the situation and showed
Electrek
records of millions of dollars in payments, arguing that funds he had already paid on future orders should have been applied differently to settle current debts.
At least hundreds of paying Metacycle customers, but potentially more, were ultimately left without motorcycles, while an unknown number of SONDORS e-bike customers were also caught up in the collapse.
So… is everyone ready for SONDORS 2.0?
That’s what makes this new teaser so interesting.
Storm Sondors has always had an impressive ability to identify the kind of electric two-wheelers people want and package them in designs that generate attention. The original $500 fat-tire bike was the right product at the right moment. Even the Metacycle, for all of the disaster surrounding its rollout, was an incredibly compelling concept. It was the motorcycle that the US needed, at the moment it needed it, and at the right price. A stylish, lightweight, highway-capable electric motorcycle for around $5,000 was exactly the sort of product so many riders wanted.
The question has rarely been whether Storm can make people
the product. He’s repeatedly proved that he can.
The question this time is whether he can convince them to pay for it.
And the market he’s apparently returning to is considerably different from the one SONDORS helped create a decade ago.
Moped-style electric bikes were once a much smaller category dominated by a handful of recognizable brands, particularly SUPER73. Today, that market is packed with competitors ranging from tiny direct-to-consumer startups to established e-bike companies. Even the
reborn Juiced Bikes has returned
under new ownership with its new Scrambler lineup, offering exactly the sort of motorcycle-inspired electric bicycles that this mysterious SONDORS machine appears positioned against.
In other words, Storm isn’t coming back to an empty field.
He may still have one advantage, though: the guy knows how to get attention. I’m writing an article about a mostly black photograph of a bicycle, after all, and all because his legacy is pages longer than almost anyone else in the industry at this point.
But attention and trust aren’t the same thing.
If this new SONDORS project is going to succeed, the most convincing launch strategy should probably have less to do with outrageous specifications or an irresistible introductory price and more to do with demonstrating that finished bikes actually exist, production is funded, and customers won’t be asked to bankroll another ambitious production run with an open-ended preorder like the last few rounds of this game.
Remember, there are still tens of thousands of riders out there who had perfectly good experiences with SONDORS bikes. But on the flip side, there are also many former customers for whom the SONDORS name represents money paid for a product that never arrived.
That’s a cargo e-bike’s worth of baggage landing squarely on the rackless frame of yet another moped-style e-bike.
For now, all we’ve got is a silhouette, the number “001,” and September 3.
Whatever Storm Sondors is planning for his next act, we’ll apparently find out next week.

title: Waymo takes a shot at Tesla's self-driving: it's a 'false summit'
content:
Waymo published a list of “10 AI lessons” from driving more than 200 million fully autonomous miles, and several of them read as a direct rebuke of Tesla’s self-driving strategy — without ever naming Tesla.
The sharpest: trying to turn a driver-assist system into full autonomy is a “false summit,” according to Waymo. That’s exactly what Tesla is attempting with Full Self-Driving.
What Waymo actually said
The post, published Tuesday by Waymo’s head of AI foundations, Srikanth Thirumalai, frames all 10 lessons around safety and the company’s 200-million-mile record in fully driverless operation.
Lesson 10 is the one aimed squarely at the L2-to-L4 playbook:
Simply improving a driver-assist system (L2) for full autonomy is a false summit. True L4 maturity can only be safely achieved by a purpose-built system, validated on closed courses and hardened by the uncompromising experience of driving without a human in the car.
Waymo’s argument is that neither billions of simulated miles nor millions of “supervised” human-present miles can replicate what a system learns once it operates with no human backup. That’s a pointed contrast with Tesla, which trains FSD on data from a fleet of customer cars whose drivers remain legally responsible for the vehicle.
Cameras alone and the ‘black box’
Two other lessons land in Tesla’s lap.
Lesson 1 states plainly that cameras alone can’t deliver safe, full-scale autonomy, and that Waymo combines cameras, lidar, and radar for redundancy. Tesla runs a camera-only “Tesla Vision” stack — a bet Waymo’s co-CEO already picked apart earlier this month when he explained why camera-only self-driving falls short.
Lesson 4 warns against pure end-to-end neural networks that convert raw camera input directly into steering commands: “You can’t build trust with a black box.” Tesla has spent the last two years selling exactly that end-to-end approach as the core of FSD v14 and v15.
However, the approach often results in a two-step-forward, one-step-back situation with every new update.
The widening gap behind the jab
The confidence has numbers behind it. Waymo is now serving more than 500,000 paid, fully driverless rides every week across its US markets, and it has set a target of one million by the end of the year.
Tesla, by comparison, still runs a small “Robotaxi” service that launched in Austin with human safety monitors in the car, and by some counts its fleet has shrunk rather than grown. CEO Elon Musk has promised “unsupervised” FSD would be widespread by year-end — a target he has moved repeatedly.
A year into the program, Tesla confirmed last month that it has driven only 380,000 unsupervised miles – something Waymo does in a day.
Electrek’s Take
Waymo didn’t name Tesla, but it didn’t have to. Every one of these “lessons” maps onto a specific Tesla decision: camera-only sensing, an end-to-end black box, and, most pointedly, the belief that you can incrementally upgrade a consumer driver-assist product into a robotaxi.
The “false summit” line is the interesting one and should ring true to anyone following Tesla’s effort closely. CEO Elon Musk has declared victory so many times when it comes to solving autonomy and each time, it was indeed a false summit.
Top comment by JoeUser
As I’ve posted before, I live in the middle of the robotaxi service area in Austin. I see far fewer Robotaxis now than I did 6 months ago. On the plus side, they are always ‘unsupervised’, but it’s really like one a month, if that. Waymos I see a few dozen every day. If Tesla was even close to solving autonomy the fleet would be exploding. Tesla is undoubtedly winning in the ADAS arena, but they are not even close on autonomy.
Waymo is arguing that the hardest part of autonomy, the long tail of weird, dangerous edge cases, only reveals itself when there’s no human to catch the mistakes. Tesla’s approach assumes it can climb to that summit gradually, learning from millions of Teslas whose drivers are still doing the catching. Waymo is telling the market that path doesn’t reach the real peak; it just gets you to a ledge that looks like one.
Is Waymo right? I don’t know. But it is certainly ahead of Tesla and scaling much faster. Its sensor fusion approach appears much more robust than Tesla’s vision-only.
Now, Tesla fans would argue that none of that matters because Tesla is on the verge of achieving generalization and would quickly overtake Waymo, if that’s the case. But there’s no clear evidence that’s happening.

title: 欣旺达：2026H1储能系统出货14.7GWh，同增64.98%
content:
集邦光储观察获悉，8月26日晚，欣旺达披露2026年半年度报告，并发布投资者关系活动记录。
报告期内，公司实现营业收入381.79亿元，同比增长41.48%；归母净利润6.03亿元，同比下降29.59%；扣非净利润9726万元，同比下降83.32%。
其中，储能系统业务保持较快增长。2026年上半年，公司储能系统实现营业收入17.70亿元，同比增长76.21%；储能系统出货量达14.7GWh，同比增长64.98%。
海外市场成为储能业务增长的重要驱动力。公司表示，储能系统收入主要来自海外市场，海外客户占比超过70%，核心海外客户项目批量交付带动业务持续增长。同时，公司全球化项目交付及本地化服务能力进一步提升。
欣旺达持续推进全球化产能布局，目前已在印度、越南、泰国、摩洛哥、匈牙利等地布局生产基地。其中，泰国电池生产基地一期已于报告期内正式投产，二期同步启动；越南消费类电芯生产基地预计于2026年底投产，匈牙利动力电池生产基地也在逐步建设。
产品与研发方面，公司围绕314Ah、280Ah、588Ah、684Ah等储能电芯及3.125MWh、6.25MWh集装箱、电池包等系统产品持续迭代，完成5MWh液冷储能集装箱大规模火烧测试，推进器件寿命评估、火灾仿真模型、大储实证测试平台、电力电子仿真平台及PCS升压一体机自集成等能力建设，产品安全性、可靠性和系统级解决方案能力持续增强。
截至6月底，公司存货为163.28亿元，较2025年末增长51.77%。公司在投资者交流中表示，存货增长主要源于战略性备货。由于原材料价格持续上涨，同时为匹配2026年第三、四季度业务增长，公司自年初开始积极备货。
除传统储能业务外，AIDC备电也成为公司重点布局方向。欣旺达在投资者交流中表示，AIDC备电市场需求自2025年年底开始快速增长，公司早在2015年前后便已进行相关布局，目前已与国内主流云服务商、互联网企业及数据中心托管商建立合作关系。

title: 通威、晶科、中环发布半年报业绩，出货量刷新高
content:
集邦光储观察获悉，8月26日，通威股份、晶科能源、TCL中环3家光伏企业相继披露半年报。除公布上半年业绩情况外，各家龙头在电池组件出货量、光伏技术迭代、海外布局上均有关键进展。
图：2026年上半年光伏企业业绩（亿元，%）
通威股份光伏电池累计出货超400GW
8月26日，通威股份发布公告，2026年上半年营业收入343.57亿元，同比下降15.19%；归母净利润亏损51.19亿元，同比下降3.31%；扣非净利润亏损52.83亿元，同比下降5.05%。
报告期内，光伏业务方面，通威适时调整经营策略，高纯晶硅业务加强主要战略客户合作，市占率稳居行业第一，并持续加大溢价产品市场拓展力度。其中：
合计实现高纯晶硅出货15.53万吨；太阳能电池实现销量34.78GW，成为全球电池行业首家累计出货突破400GW的企业；组件业务，海内外并举，提升高价值订单占比，上半年国内集中式业务顺利中标华电、华能、中石油等重点央企年度组件集采，分布式业务出货稳步增长，海外市场落地罗马尼亚、波兰等多个大型标杆项目，实现组件销量同比增长，占比提升至近40%。
上半年，通威继续坚持TOPCon、HJT、xBC、钙钛矿叠层等多技术路线并行研发，多项核心技术实现突破性进展。
在TOPCon技术方面，报告期公司率先完成新一代旗舰技术TNC3.0量产落地。量产端组件功率最高达670W，双面率可达85%~90%，全面达到行业一级能效标准。HJT方面，聚焦100%无银铜电镀、低铟TCO、低成本背抛、0BB/SMBB组件等重点技术开发，加速推动具有差异化优势的HJT铜互连产品量产落地，报告期实现THC-G12异质结铜互连组件输出功率突破802.43W，全面积转换效率高达25.83%，第十二次刷新行业功率纪录。在TBC技术路线完成0BB叠栅、铜电镀无银化、全面屏封装三大核心工艺突破，210R组件功率突破660W，HTBC成功研发行业首款三分片双面全面屏组件，峰值功率681W，转换效率25.2%。
与此同时，通威高度关注航天等新兴光伏应用领域，报告期内与商业航天企业协同攻关太空极端环境下的P型HJT和高效叠层电池及组件技术，推进柔性太阳翼等前沿产品开发与航天级验证，持续推动光伏应用场景拓展。
晶科能源上半年光伏组件出货29.64GW
晶科能源披露半年报，2026年上半年实现营收247.27亿元，同比下降22.32%；归母净利润-30.76亿元；扣非净利润-33.61亿元。
上半年，晶科能源光伏组件出货29.64GW，预计2026年三季度组件出货15-17GW。此外，考虑到部分市场需求的变化，晶科能源将更加注重出货规模与盈利、现金流和订单质量之间的平衡，因此将2026年全年组件出货指引调整为60-70GW。
截至2026年上半年，晶科能源组件全球累计出货量突破420GW，Tiger Neo系列高端组件产品已成为公司出货的主力产品。截至报告发布日，公司N型Tiger Neo系列高效组件全球累计出货量已超250GW。
储能方面，晶科能源上半年实现储能系统产品交付3.1GWh，出货量高增。
TCL中环上半年净利同比减亏
8月26日，TCL中环发布2026年半年度业绩报告。2026年上半年，TCL中环实现营收143.15亿元，同比增长6.84%；归母净利润-32.04亿元，同比减亏。
财报显示，面对行业周期压力，TCL中环坚持降本提效、推进组织与流程优化，落地适度一体化、全球化战略，内部各项经营调整逐步反映到财务指标转好，经营修复成效持续显现。
报告期内，TCL中环电池组件业务实现较快发展，出货量逆势增长29%，BC及半片新品等高效产品出货占比超过15%，战略客户集采入围规模居前列，二季度组件销售收入已经超过光伏材料业务。
财报显示，上半年TCL中环国内端完善营销及交付体系，获取多笔战略客户订单。海外市场方面，海外销售收入占总营收比重进一步提升至25%，硅片、组件海外出货均实现增长。TCL中环重点布局欧洲、中东、澳新、东南亚等区域，组件海外销量实现同比增长4倍，产品均价与毛利同步好转。
7月初，TCL中环完成一道新能源控股权交割。7月，TCL中环对电池、组件产能实施BC路线技改，相关产能预计三季度末陆续投产，进一步提升BC高效产品供应能力。

title: 阳光电源、创维等3企储能订单传新动态
content:
集邦光储观察获悉，近日，阳光电源、创维储能、金风科技等3企披露储能业务最新进展，包括大型储能电站并网投运、欧洲储能订单签约等新动态。
阳光电源供货400MWh储能电站
8月25日，阳光电源宣布，近日合肥200MW/400MWh储能电站并网投运。该项目采用阳光电源PowerTitan3.0全维智能方案，搭载600+Ah系列叠片电芯。
据悉，依托自身年产能100GWh的世界级储能智造基地，阳光电源PowerTitan 3.0以高效交付、可靠品质和运维能力，高效交付全球100+国家地区。
当前，阳光电源依托全链路数智交付体系，实现储能系统从订单、智造、物流、调试到智慧运维的数字化、可视化，各节点高效并行。自研灵犀交付平台，可以一键自配置、自检查，叠加储能系统预安装、预调试，将10+天传统人工并网调试缩至1小时，项目17天一次性成功并网。
创维储能签欧洲31MWh储能订单
8月26日，创维储能宣布，在罗马尼亚、塞浦路斯接连拿下储能订单，合计31MWh。
据悉，创维储能户用产品已在欧洲市场积累良好口碑。此次接连签订罗马尼亚、塞浦路斯储能订单，产品覆盖大型园区、工厂、商业综合体等全场景，叠加微电网、光储充一体化等系统解决方案，匹配欧洲客户多元诉求。
在罗马尼亚市场，4套5MWh级大容量集装箱式储能系统已确认采购函，合计20MWh。此外，16台分布式工商业储能设备也同步确认，合计8MWh。
在塞浦路斯储能市场，当地客户采购16台232度电工商业储能柜，合计约3.7MWh，项目进入交付阶段。
金风科技签约罗马尼亚储能项目
8月26日，金风科技宣布，已于近日与Dunarea Power签署合作协议，共同推进罗马尼亚Topalu储能项目建设。
据悉，Topalu项目是罗马尼亚首个风储一体化项目，将采用集中式交流耦合架构进行整体设计，将风力发电与电池储能系统深度融合。项目采用交钥匙建设模式，配置7台金风GWH170-7.2MW风机及10.8MW/23.4MWh金风电池储能系统。
其中，储能系统交付范围涵盖28台储能设备、中压变压器系统及全场能量管理系统（EMS），项目预计于年内并网投运。

Intercontinental Energy (ICE) has scaled back expansion plans for its mammoth Western Australia (WA) green hydrogen and ammonia project, according to reports.
The developer recently requested a termination of its Environmental Impact Assessment on its Australian Renewable Energy Hub (AREH) and will now pursue building up to 15GW of renewables capacity instead of the original 26GW.
H2 View has reached out to ICE for confirmation.
Located in the Pilbara region, ICE had planned to eventually produce 1.6 million tonnes per annum (mtpa) of green hydrogen and 9 mtpa of ammonia.
Plans for the 26GW build-out were backed in February by the Australian Renewable Energy Agency (ARENA), which
granted $21m
(€18m) for its development.
The potential scale-back follows British oil and gas firm
ulling out of the development in July 2025, leaving the WA government scouring for alternative majority
stakeholders in Japan
It comprises a blow for ICE’s ambitions in WA, which also involve the Western Green Energy Hub (WGEH), a 70GW plant in the Goldfields region slated to produce 5 mtpa of green hydrogen.
Asian majors
came on board
with WGEH in February, lining up a final investment decision for 2029.
While near-term outlook for green hydrogen in the region remains cautious as projects face commercial and offtake challenges, it retains long-term potential underpinned by abundant renewable resources, land and export infrastructure.

title: Nobian and Air Products sign RFNBO hydrogen offtake agreement | Hydrogen Tech World.com
content:
The hydrogen is produced at Nobian’s renewables-powered chlor-alkali electrolysis plant in Rotterdam, which in 2025 became the first large-scale European renewable hydrogen producer to receive ISCC EU certification for renewable fuels of non-biological origin (RFNBO). With more than 14,000 tons of annual hydrogen production capacity, equivalent to 1.68 PJ, the facility is described as Europe’s largest RFNBO-certified hydrogen plant.
Under the agreement, Air Products will distribute the certified hydrogen through its existing infrastructure and network, supporting customers seeking to meet RED III compliance obligations. The company said the arrangement reinforces Rotterdam’s role as a hydrogen hub and supports industrial decarbonization strategies.
Markus Mingenbach, Senior Vice President Chlor-Alkali & Chloromethanes of Nobian, said: “This agreement is an important milestone for certified green hydrogen in Europe. Together with Air Products, we continue the build-out of the European hydrogen economy now. This is Grow Greener Together in practice – two leading industrial partners collaborating to advance the European energy transition.”
“By expanding access to RFNBO-certified hydrogen from an established source, we are helping customers navigate RED III compliance while supporting their decarbonization strategies. These certified molecules are available today, and Air Products’ network can bring them to market in a reliable and practical way,” said Caroline Stancell, Vice President, Marketing and Growth, Europe and Africa, Air Products.
RFNBO-certified hydrogen enables fuel suppliers and industrial users, including refineries, to support compliance with the EU’s 2030 decarbonization targets, which require at least 1% of transport fuels and 42% of industrial hydrogen in the EU to originate from RFNBO-certified sources by that date.

title: Here Are Some Of The Biggest Changes On The New Chevy Bolt
content:
Here Are Some Of The Biggest Changes On The New Chevy Bolt
The new Bolt won't be made for long, but it's a big improvement over the old car.
The current Ultium-based Chevy Bolt isn't going to last long, with its planned discontinuation happening in Summer 2027. However, while it's here, it's one of the more intriguing affordable EV options and one that customers should keep their eyes on. There's some understandable confusion surrounding the Bolt, though, and this new video from Ever nicely breaks down some of the biggest and most impactful changes made to this 2027 model for anyone interested in buying one.
Chevy was originally going to discontinue the Bolt after 2023. However, both internal and external pressure led GM to reopen the Bolt's file. Unfortunately, the Bolt that customers knew in 2023 just wasn't gonna cut it among its more modern peers. GM had to refresh it but keep it cheap. So it swapped out its old battery for a new, cheaper battery pack, gave it a new interior with upgraded tech, and freshened up its looks a bit. Despite the penny pinching, the results are actually pretty impressive.
The 2027 Chevy Bolt only comes in EUV crossover shape, which was the more practical, more popular option anyway. It looks mostly the same but it has new split headlights, new taillights, and a lot of black plastic. Where it's visually changed most is inside, where it has a heavily revised cabin with GM's latest tech. While it might feel familiar, the new Bolt's dashboard and tech are entirely new. Its infotainment screen and digital gauge cluster are basically the same as you'll find in every other GM EV, though.
Don't let its looks fool you, though, this new Bolt is entirely different where it matters most: under the skin. The battery is all-new, with lithium-iron-phosphate (LFP) cells instead of nickel-magnanese-cobalt (NMC), and while the 65 kWh capacity is the same, the new model has more range. The new Bolt has 262 miles of range, versus the old EUV's 247 miles. It's still front-wheel drive, with about the same power, now at 210 horsepower instead of 200. However, the new motor loses a ton of torque, dropping from 266 lb-ft to 169 lb-ft. Chevy used some clever final drive trickery to actually improve power delivery. Because of the shorter final drive gear, the new Bolt actually makes more torque to the wheels than the old one.
There are a few other worthwhile changes, so if you're a potential buyer you should check out Ever's video. But the new Bolt, despite being similar looking to the old one, is still worth your consideration even if it won't be on sale in a year's time.

title: How The Volvo EX60 EV Can 'See' Deer Around Corners Through A New Update
content:
How The Volvo EX60 EV Can 'See' Deer Around Corners Through A New Update
It's not just deer, either. The Volvo can even detect people and other hazards before you do.
- Volvo EVs are getting new safety features via a software update.
- The EX60, EX90, and ES90 in the U.S. and Canada will get four new safety alerts based on data collected from other vehicles on the road.
- One could help you avoid hitting a deer or other animal.
The Volvo EX60 can see into the future. Well, sort of. It can see into your future. In 2016, the Swedish automaker launched its connected safety technology, which uses data collected about road hazards from other vehicles to alert you about upcoming dangers. Now, it's expanding on that tech with new features that can let you know about a deer in the road, around a blind corner, before you even get there.
With the latest software update, Volvo EX60, EX90, and ES90 EVs in the U.S. and Canada will gain four new features to help warn drivers of impending danger. Large Animal Alert is pretty self-explanatory, as it warns drivers of big ol' animals in the road, like deer or moose. I imagine the latter is extra helpful in Volvo's home country. There's also Vulnerable Road User Alert, which tells you about humans who might be up ahead, like cyclists or pedestrians, on or near highways. Roadwork Alert and Accident Ahead Alert are again alert you of upcoming road work or accidents.
None of these replace the existing connected safety features, like Slippery Road Alert and Hazard Light Alert. They're all just added to Volvo's safety arsenal.
In Europe, this system works by using data collected from the European Union's "Data for Road Safety" ecosystem. The system is a cooperation between OEMs and the EU, and it pulls safety and road data from all vehicle types, so that all vehicles can share it. And Volvo uses that data to alert its drivers about upcoming dangers, while also sharing its own data with others.
“Every time a Volvo car shares safety intelligence, it helps other drivers prepare earlier to avoid accidents and feel safer," said Head of Volvo Cars Safety Centre Åsa Haglund in a recent press release.
So next time you're driving around in a Volvo, know that even around blind corners, the car is looking out for you. So while it isn't a time traveler, it can know what's coming next even before you do. Volvo says the timing of the features will depend on the car model.

title: Voltpost Is Making A Charger For People Without A Driveway
content:
Voltpost Is Making A Charger For People Without A Driveway
Voltpost's new chargers cut install costs by sticking to ceilings and walls—meaning apartment dwellers could be the real winners.
- Voltpost is releasing two new EV chargers.
- Both products are meant to make retrofitting easy, which means apartment-dwellers may finally have a simple solution for EV charging.
- The company says that its mounting methods cut install costs by as much as 70%.
There's a little assumption that is seemingly baked into EV ownership advice: home charging. Most people assume that anyone buying an EV is just charging in their driveway. After all, most of the convenience and savings in EV ownership comes from home charging.
But relying on public fast charging can often prove to be nearly as expensive as filling up at the pump—plus, you can't just wake up with a fully-juiced battery. That's where a new idea from Voltpost is here to help.
Voltpost is best known for turning lampposts and telephone poles into EV chargers. Now it's tackling the driveway problem by introducing two new Level 2 chargers into its Voltpost Air retrofitting portfolio.
First up is the company's new Air Ceiling Mount that is purpose-built for parking garages. As the name implies, it attaches to the ceiling of a garage with hanging cables to maximize the space available for parking. It also introduced a new Air Surface Mount that attaches directly to walls (and, of course, pedestals). Voltpost says that this is aimed at bringing chargers to parking lots and curbside locations when a pole isn't available—think the side of buildings or a pedestal bolted into pavement.
Both setups use a retractable cable to keep the charging hardware tidy and off the ground. But the real win, according to Voltpost, is how easy the chargers are to retrofit around infrastructure already in place. No ripping up sidewalks or trenching, just mount it on something already there, run some wires, and call it complete in hours rather than days. That approach cuts installation costs by as much as 70%, according to Voltpost.
Voltpost isn't solving apartment or destination charging everywhere overnight. No charging company is. Building and lot owners still need to actually install these chargers (and somebody has to foot the bill). But saving some dough by bolting the chargers onto a building instead of trenching out a lot sure feels like a pretty good place to start.

title: Waymo Just Took A Not-So-Subtle Dig At Tesla’s Self-Driving Strategy
content:
In a blog post, one of Waymo's top engineers wrote that cameras "aren't enough" for autonomous driving.
Photo by:
2:44pm ET
In a new blog post, Waymo laid out 10 takeaways from 200 million miles of autonomous operation.
It took some swipes at Tesla's approach to developing self-driving tech.
Waymo casted doubt on camera-only systems, end-to-end AI, and improving a Level 2 system to full autonomy.
Waymo didn’t name Tesla in its latest blog post. But it didn’t really have to. The two companies have spent years pursuing radically different visions of what self-driving technology should look like. And on Wednesday Waymo made it abundantly clear which it thinks will win.
the post
, the company's vice president of onboard software, Srikanth Thirumalai, laid out 10 learnings from 200 million autonomous miles. Without mentioning any rivals by name, Waymo effectively picked apart the key tenets of Tesla's self-driving philosophy.
For starters, Waymo addresses the elephant in the room: the sensor question. Tesla uses only cameras, and Elon Musk has called lidar a "fools errand." Waymo's latest system in its
Ojai van
, by contrast, relies on 13 cameras, 4 lidar units, and 6 radars, plus microphones. Thirumalai writes that "multimodal sensors are indispensable" and takes direct aim at the vision-only approach.
"Cameras are incredible, but they aren't enough," he says. "By combining inputs from cameras, lidar, and radar, the Waymo Driver creates a rich, redundant world view that no single sensor can replicate."
Tesla Cybercab
Photo by: Tesla
Lidar sensors, he explains, "capture 3D geometry with millimeter precision." Radar tracks velocity and detects objects in conditions that cameras can't, like in heavy fog. Cameras, he says, are good for reading street signs and traffic lights.
Thirumalai also notes the importance of HD maps, which Tesla says it doesn't need. The highly detailed maps, he says, are "incredibly helpful in poor visibility and complex thoroughfares." And he casts doubt on end-to-end AI systems that take in sensor data at one end and spit out driving instructions at the other. This idea is core to Tesla's approach, and it's been adopted by others in the space too.
"Pure end-to-end (E2E) neural architectures, where a model takes in raw pixels and directly outputs steering commands, run the risk of black box failures," he says. "That means, it's hard to understand how decision making happens in full E2E systems."
Stay informed with our newsletter every weekday
Tesla has for years promised that Full Self-Driving (Supervised) would eventually get so good that it could take the human out of the loop. That the vast trove of FSD data collected from Tesla's customer fleet would help it get to true autonomy. But Waymo argues that to really improve an autonomous system, you need to have it operate autonomously.
"Simply improving a driver-assist system (L2) for full autonomy is a false summit," Thirumalai says. "You can run billions of miles in simulation or with human supervision, but an AV system only truly matures when it is solely responsible for the driving task. Full autonomy exposes the system to the true gravity of its decisions and reveals novel situations that humans or simulations might unconsciously smooth over."
It's not surprising that Waymo thinks its philosophy is the right one. Of course it does. But it's making that argument more explicitly than before, right as Tesla finally makes the inroads into autonomy that it's hyped up about for years.
The company appears to have
removed the safety operators from its Robotaxi service
across several markets. It has scheduled a launch event for the purpose-built Cybercab for next week, though it's not clear what exactly that will entail. Tesla maintains that its more streamlined approach is easier to scale. But Waymo has the distinct scale advantage right now, with over 500,000 driverless trips per week. The next few years will show who's really got the edge.

Ferienzeit ist nicht nur Urlaubszeit, sondern auch Übungszeit für den Schulweg. Viele Eltern haben sich in den vergangenen Wochen gefragt, welche Route wohl die beste für ihr Kind ist, damit es auch sicher in der Schule ankommt. Ein Projekt der Bergischen Universität Wuppertal in Zusammenarbeit mit dem Büro für Forschung, Entwicklung und Evaluation (buffee) hat sich zum Ziel gesetzt, diese Entscheidung zukünftig mit einer Web-App zu erleichtern. Bis 2028 wird noch geforscht und entwickelt. Ein Workshop, offen für Vertreter*innen von Schulen und Kommunen, gibt am 23. September aktuelle Einblicke in das Projekt und fragt die Beteiligten nach ihren Bedarfen.
Im Projekt SAFER arbeiten Mathematiker*innen der Bergischen Universität daran, Routen zu berechnen, die einen guten Kompromiss zwischen der kürzesten und der sichersten Strecke liefern. „Aktuell entwickeln und überprüfen wir die Algorithmen, die der Berechnung zugrunde liegen und gehen der Frage nach, welche Wege vorgeschlagen werden sollen“, erklärt Prof. Dr. Michael Stiglmayr aus der Arbeitsgruppe Optimierung.
Denn eine Web-App, die das Ziel des Projekts ist, soll zukünftig nicht alle möglichen Wege präsentieren. Wie bei heutigen Navigationsanwendungen üblich, soll sie eine Auswahl treffen. „Letztlich sollen die Nutzer*innen zwischen einer Handvoll Routen auswählen können, die unterschiedlich genug sind, da auch das Sicherheitsbedürfnis von Mensch zu Mensch verschieden ist. Das Ergebnis soll Kriterien wie Weglänge, Dauer und Sicherheit berücksichtigen und für die Anwendenden sichtbar machen“, so Stiglmayr.
Auch Schulen und Kommunen profitieren
Der Service kommt nicht nur Eltern und Schüler*innen zugute. Für Schulen liefert das Projekt Antworten auf wichtige Fragen wie „Wo verlaufen sichere Wege, damit wir diese bewerben können?“ und „Welche Wege werden wie genutzt?“.
Mithilfe von Einwohnermeldedaten lässt sich prognostizieren, welche Wege besonders frequentiert sind. Informationen, die sich mit den neuen Rechenwegen aus dem Projekt nützlich kombinieren lassen. Indem den verschiedenen Typen von Straßenquerungen – wie Ampel, Zebrastreifen oder Mittelinsel – ein entsprechendes Gefahrenpotenzial zugeordnet wird, können Kommunen unter anderem fundierte Aussagen darüber treffen, wie sich mögliche Veränderungen in der Verkehrsinfrastruktur auf die Schulwegsicherheit auswirken könnten.
Das Projekt SAFER – Sicheres, Algorithmen-basiertes Fußwegerouting – wird im Rahmen des Innovationswettbewerbs NeueWege.IN.NRW durch das Land Nordrhein-Westfalen und den Europäischen Fonds für regionale Entwicklung mit 590.000 Euro gefördert.

Beim Symposium „MORE WITH LESS – Die Leichtigkeit des Bauens“ an der Frankfurt University of Applied Sciences (Frankfurt UAS) am 12. November 2026 informieren und diskutieren renommierte Expert*innen über das Thema Nachhaltiger Leichtbau in Architektur und Bauwesen.
Das Symposium und die Beiträge aus den Bereichen Architektur und Bauingenieurwesen rücken Lösungsansätze zur Reduktion des Ressourcenverbrauchs in den Fokus. Ergänzt wird der Themenbereich im Anschluss an das Symposium durch die Eröffnung einer Ausstellung zu Forschungsarbeiten des Research Lab for Sustainable Lightweight Building Technologies (ReSULT) der Frankfurt UAS.
Vorträge von Prof. Thomas Auer und Anders Lendager
Die Keynote hält Prof. Dipl.-Ing. Thomas Auer, Professor an der TU München und Experte für klimagerechtes Bauen. Der Abschlussvortrag des dänischen Architekten Anders Lendager setzt sich mit dem Thema kreislaufgerechtes Bauen auseinander.
Weitere Fachbeiträge des Symposiums zu den Themen „Mehr Funktion?“ und „Weniger Material!“ stellen u.a. luftreinigende Textilfassaden vor, die durch integrierte Wirkstoffe schädliche Stickstoffe neutralisieren („Anti-Nox-Fassade“). Ein Vortrag widmet sich hydroaktiven Gebäudehüllen („Hydroskin”), die Gebäudekühlung und Verbesserung des Stadtklimas verbinden. Das Institut für Leichtbau Entwerfen und Konstruieren (ILEK) der Universität Stuttgart ist vertreten mit Forschungsprojekten zu wasserlöslichen Zero-Waste-Schalungssystemen zur abfallfreien Herstellung komplexer Betonleichtbauteile.
Ausstellung zum Nachhaltigen Leichtbau
Als Überblick über zehn Jahre Forschungsarbeit präsentiert das ReSULT Forschungsergebnisse in einer Ausstellung, die im Anschluss an das Symposium um 18:00 Uhr eröffnet wird und bis zum 20. November zu sehen ist.
Gezeigt werden laufende Projekte wie textilbasierte Grünfassaden und Solartextilien für Plug & Play Anwendungen (fabricGREEN, 3D-Solartextil). Abgeschlossene Arbeiten umfassen Projekte wie Adaptive Sun Skins und WiFaPu (Wickelverfahren für hochbewehrten Faserbeton am Beispiel eines Pumpensumpfes) ebenso wie 3D-Druck auf 3D-Textilien (6dTEX) und ausgeschäumte Leichtbauteile. Außerdem werden neuartige Projektansätze im Bereich der Materialökologie sowie myzelbasierte Leichtbauweisen gezeigt, die derzeit in der Gruppe entwickelt werden.
„Die Projekte verbindet die integrale Betrachtung von Material, Herstellprozess und Gestaltungsoptionen. Dabei werden klassische Themen des Leichtbaus – minimales Gewicht der Bauteile bei gleichzeitig maximaler Funktionalität – mit Fragen zur Kreislauffähigkeit und zum CO₂-Fußabdruck verbunden“, erläutert Prof. Claudia Lüling, die sich als Professorin für Entwerfen und Gestalten schwerpunktmäßig mit textilem Leichtbau befasst.
Die Teilnahme am Symposium ist kostenfrei, die Anmeldung ist bereits jetzt möglich. Das Programm und der Anmeldelink finden sich auf der Webseite unter: www.frankfurt-university.de/?id=15798

Mit dem Railway and Infrastructure Laboratory erweitert die TU Graz den Bereich der Eisenbahnforschung um ein hochmodernes Prüflabor. Hier lässt sich das gesamte Gleissystem unter realitätsnahen Bedingungen testen.
Wie belastbar ist ein Gleis, wenn Züge jahrzehntelang darüberfahren? Und wie verändert sich sein Verhalten, wenn sich die Bedingungen im Untergrund verändern? Antworten auf solche Fragen lassen sich an der TU Graz künftig unter kontrollierten, realitätsnahen Bedingungen untersuchen. Mit dem neuen Railway and Infrastructure Laboratory (RaIL) am Institut für Eisenbahn-Infrastrukturdesign nimmt eine europaweit einzigartige Laborinfrastruktur für die Eisenbahnforschung ihren Betrieb auf. Im RaIL können vollständige Eisenbahn-Fahrwegsysteme auf ihre Belastbarkeit und Haltbarkeit während des simulierten Realbetriebs geprüft werden – von Schiene und Schwelle über Schotter und Unterbau bis in den Untergrund. Das ermöglicht neue Erkenntnisse über die Wechselwirkungen zwischen Verkehrsbelastungen und den verschiedenen Schichten des Gleisaufbaus.
Realisiert wurde die rund vier Millionen Euro teure Einrichtung aus Mitteln der TU Graz, der Forschungsförderungsgesellschaft FFG und mit finanzieller Unterstützung der voestalpine. Die technischen Prüfmaschinen stammen vom deutschen Unternehmen Form + Test.
Bisher erfolgt die Forschung zu neuen Lösungen für den Eisenbahnfahrweg vor allem im Zusammenspiel von analytischen Berechnungen, numerischen Simulationen und Messungen im realen Betrieb. Das Labor erlaubt es nun, das Gesamtsystem Schiene sowie einzelne Entwicklungen für etwa Weichenkomponenten oder Befestigungssysteme zu testen, bevor eine aufwendige Prüfung im laufenden Bahnbetrieb erfolgt. Das kann Entwicklungszyklen verkürzen und die Grundlage für leistungsfähigere und langlebigere Fahrwegsysteme schaffen. Das RaIL ermöglicht zudem normgerechte Prüfungen des Eisenbahnoberbaus sowie Versuche in der Produktentwicklung und für die Zulassung.
Oberbausimulator, Aufspannfeld und Schotterbox
Das Herzstück des Labors ist ein fünf Meter langer, 3,5 Meter breiter und 1,8 Meter tiefer Oberbausimulator. Mit hydraulisch und elektronisch angesteuerten Prüfzylindern lassen sich dort statische und dynamische Belastungen nachbilden, denen Gleise ausgesetzt sind, wenn ein tonnenschwerer Zug über sie hinwegrollt. Untersuchen kann man damit die dynamische Kraftübertragung im System von Schiene, Befestigung, Schotterbett, Unterbau im Gleisrost und bis zu acht Schwellen. Auch kritische Bereiche wie Isolierstöße, Dehnfugen oder Brückenübergänge sowie die Auswirkungen von Stopfarbeiten im Schotter lassen sich untersuchen.
Für größere Systeme steht ein neun mal fünf Meter großes Aufspannfeld zur Verfügung (erweiterbar auf 14 mal fünf Meter), bei dem ebenfalls die Prüfzylinder zum Einsatz kommen. Dort können beispielsweise Weichenbereiche und Auszugsvorrichtungen, die temperaturbedingte Längenänderungen von Schienen ausgleichen, normgerecht geprüft werden. Eine flexible Schotterbox ermöglicht die Untersuchung einzelner Komponenten, etwa Weichen-, Rahmen- oder Holzersatzschwellen, um das fundamentale Verschleißverhalten des Schotters unter spezifischen Frequenzen und Lasten zu erforschen. Dies hilft dabei, elastische Elemente und Schwellen optimal aufeinander abzustimmen und so den Verschleiß des Oberbaus zu minimieren.
Tests mit durchfeuchtetem Gleisbett
Ein Alleinstellungsmerkmal des RaIL ist die Möglichkeit, die Feuchtigkeitsbedingungen gezielt zu verändern. Dadurch lässt sich experimentell untersuchen, wie unterschiedliche Wassersättigungsgrade die Steifigkeit, Lastverteilung und das Langzeitverhalten des Ober- und Unterbaus beeinflussen. Damit können die Auswirkungen veränderter Umweltbedingungen auf die Dauerhaftigkeit von Eisenbahninfrastruktur erforscht werden.
Forschung an der resilienten Bahn der Zukunft
„Die Eisenbahnforschung ist für die TU Graz ein wichtiger Kernforschungsbereich, mit dem wir europaweit zu den Top-3-Universitäten gehören“, sagt Horst Bischof, Rektor der TU Graz. „Im Research Cluster Railway Systems arbeiten wir eng mit der Industrie zusammen, mit unseren Eisenbahn-Instituten, mehreren Professuren und hochmodernen Prüfständen betreiben wir international anerkannte Forschung auf höchstem Niveau. Das Railway and Infrastructure Laboratory ist die logische Ergänzung dieser Forschungsinfrastruktur, die in ihrer Gesamtheit in Österreich einzigartig ist. Ich bedanke mich bei der FFG und der voestalpine für die Unterstützung bei der Realisierung des neuen Labors.“
„Die Eröffnung des Railway and Infrastructure Laboratory „RaIL“ am Institut für Eisenbahn-Infrastrukturdesign stellt einen wichtigen nächsten Schritt in der Zusammenarbeit zwischen der TU Graz und der österreichischen Bahn- und ihrer Zulieferindustrie im Rahmen des Research Clusters Railway Systems an der TU Graz dar“, sagt Franz Kainersdorfer, Vorstandsmitglied der voestalpine AG und Leiter der Metal Engineering Division. „Der von der TU Graz gemeinsam mit den ÖBB, Siemens, voestalpine, Plasser & Theurer sowie dem Virtual Vehicle gebildete Forschungscluster ist in dieser Form weltweit einzigartig und wird durch das neue Labor wesentlich weiterentwickelt und unterstreicht sowohl die Leistungsfähigkeit der österreichischen universitären Forschung als auch jene der österreichischen Bahn- und ihrer Zulieferindustrie.“
„Mit dem RaIL wollen wir das Eisenbahn-Fahrwegsystem als Ganzes besser verstehen. Gleichzeitig schaffen wir eine Infrastruktur, mit der neue Komponenten unter reproduzierbaren Bedingungen entwickelt und geprüft werden können und Studierende direkt am realen System lernen. Unser Ziel ist es, wissenschaftliche Erkenntnisse schneller in die Praxis zu bringen und damit einen Beitrag zu einer leistungsfähigen und klimaresilienten Bahn zu leisten“, sagt Ferdinand Pospischil, Leiter des Instituts für Eisenbahn-Infrastrukturdesign der TU Graz. Die Laborleitung übernimmt der stellvertretende Institutsleiter Julian Torggler.

title: Is Slate Auto’s new electric truck the EV Americans need?
content:
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
EVs account for under 10% of total new-vehicle sales in the US, and the numbers are declining. From a climate perspective, that’s pretty dismal, especially because the transportation sector is the single biggest source of greenhouse-gas emissions in the country.
One thing that could help turn that around? Slate Auto’s new truck—a vehicle that seems to buck every convention about selling cars in the fully loaded, range-obsessed US market.
The company is going all in on simplicity, to the point of austerity. The Slate is a tiny, two-door pickup that’s shorter than a Honda Civic. Much of the media coverage has obsessed over the fact that the base model’s windows use hand cranks, a feature straight out of the 20th century.
Slate is also breaking away from other EV manufacturers’ efforts to compete with gas-powered vehicles on range. The truck sports a small lithium iron phosphate battery, ringing in at 65 kilowatt-hours, and its quoted top range is just 205 miles. For comparison, the most basic Tesla Model 3 can go over 320 miles on a charge.
It might seem an odd choice to go so small and simple in a market that’s increasingly sizing up—but the status quo hasn’t exactly been working for EV makers. A few years back, the hero for US automotive electrification was supposed to be the Ford F-150 Lightning. Announced in 2021, it was an electric version of the country’s best-selling vehicle.
But Ford discontinued the truck in December 2025, just four years after its introduction. It’s not entirely the Lightning’s fault: The second Trump administration slashed tax credits and other support designed to boost EVs.
The Lightning was also plagued by price increases. The base model cost roughly $40,000 when shipments started in 2022; during its final year, prices topped $54,000. One factor behind the increase was its massive battery; to reach an almost 300-mile range, the truck needed a battery with a capacity roughly twice that of Slate’s truck.
That obsession with range is largely unwarranted. While Americans have historically chased distance, the average driver puts under 35 miles a day on the odometer, and nearly 90% of trips in a personal vehicle are
20 miles or less
Surveys of EV drivers show a similar trend: One recent
found that people tend to use less than 20% of their EV’s range on a typical day.
The notion that drivers need far less range than they think they do might sound a lot more persuasive these days—even for Americans who tend to buy cars for their longest road trip instead of their everyday errands. Roughly half the country is
struggling to pay for basic necessities
such as gas and groceries, and 95% of Americans believe we’re in an affordability crisis, according to a
recent Harris poll
. An inexpensive vehicle that allows you to skip the gas station sounds like an attractive prospect.
Affordable EVs have already found willing buyers in other parts of the world—even with reduced range. China currently has over 40 million EVs and plug-in hybrids on the roads, and roughly half of new vehicles sold are electric. On average, new EVs sold in China in 2025 had a range of just 247 miles. For the US over the same period, the average was 329 miles. (Europe falls between the two, at 281 miles.)
Slate is set to start delivering on preorders in late 2026. Its factory will have a capacity of 100,000 vehicles in the first year and 150,000 soon after. Thousands of customers have already put in preorders, according to the company.
Some people obviously believe in the truck’s prospects: Investors, including Jeff Bezos, have put nearly $1.4 billion into the company over three major funding rounds. Ford is jumping (back) into this space soon too. The automaker is working on its own
small electric truck
, which is expected to debut in 2027 at a retail price of around $30,000.
The key question that will determine Slate’s success or failure is whether drivers can get on board with a small, short-range vehicle for the sake of its price tag. At this moment, I’d bet the answer is yes.
