title: DHL Lands New SAS Ground Handling Deal in Manchester
content:
DHL Lands New SAS Ground Handling Deal in Manchester
Prioritise Us
on Google
The new agreement between DHL and SAS will run for three years (Image source: Getty Images/Kirillm)
David Johnson of DHL Supply Chain explains “huge team effort”, as a new three-year ground handling partnership with SAS at Manchester Airport is launched
DHL Supply Chain has been appointed as SAS Scandinavian Airlines' ground handling partner at Manchester Airport, as part of a new three-year partnership announced on 25 August 2026.
The contract will support up to five SAS flights a day, covering the airline's operations between the UK, Scandinavia and beyond. DHL will provide baggage operations, customer service, aircraft loading, dispatch and pushback.
The speed here is something to note: DHL completed the mobilisation in 30 days, standing up a
live aviation operation
while maintaining service continuity throughout.
A fast-growing corner of DHL's supply chain business
Ground handling sits within DHL Supply Chain's wider aviation and travel portfolio, which the company positions around bringing a logistics mindset to airport operations. It applies the same principles of efficiency, visibility and process discipline it uses across contract logistics more broadly.
The SAS deal is not an isolated case. Earlier this year in April,
DHL Supply Chain was appointed by Air France-KLM
to deliver full ground handling services at London Gatwick, supporting the airline's new route to Paris Charles de Gaulle, and covering a similar scope of baggage, aircraft turnaround and dispatch work, alongside cabin cleaning. Taken together, the two contracts show the way the company is steadily building out its airport footprint across the UK.
At a Glance: DHL Supply Chain and SAS at Manchester Airport:
supports up to five SAS flights a day between the UK, Scandinavia and beyond
covers baggage operations, customer service, aircraft loading, dispatch and pushback
runs for three years under the new agreement
reflects a 30-day mobilisation from signing to live operation
follows DHL's April 2026 ground handling contract with Air France-KLM at London Gatwick.
DHL positions itself within aviation and aerospace logistics more broadly as a Lead Logistics Partner capable of managing supplier relationships and coordinating complex, multi-tier supply chains for airlines, OEMs,
engine manufacturers
and suppliers alike. Its reach extends well beyond ground handling into spare parts logistics and Aircraft on Ground support.
DHL Supply Chain describes itself as the world's largest contract logistics specialist and its aviation and travel division applies that scale to ground operations specifically, combining
technology, data and process
discipline with the aim of improving on-time performance and passenger experience for airline customers. Manchester Airport, which is the UK's third-busiest by passenger volume, adds another significant hub to that growing UK footprint.
Why mobilisation speed matters
David Johnson, Interim MD, Healthcare & Specialist Logistics at DHL Supply Chain UKI, explains how the 30-day mobilisation demonstrates the operational capability behind the contract.
Mobilising a new operation in just 30 days required a huge team effort and demonstrates the agility and expertise of our aviation teams.
David Johnson, Interim MD, Healthcare & Specialist Logistics, DHL Supply Chain UKI
Ground handling has a narrow margin for error. A late bag run, a slow pushback or a delayed loading sequence can cascade into missed slots and knock-on disruption across an airline's wider schedule, which is why airlines increasingly treat their choice of ground handler as a supply chain decision, not just an airport formality.
David Johnson, Interim MD, Healthcare & Specialist Logistics, DHL Supply Chain UKI (Image source: David Johnson via LinkedIn)
The SAS side of the equation
Hans Henrik Spangenberg, MD SAS Ground Handling International, points to Manchester's role as a UK gateway connecting customers to Scandinavia and SAS' wider international network. Crediting DHL's
operational expertise
and speed of mobilisation, he calls the partnership "a smooth transition," adding that SAS looks forward to continuing the collaboration.
SAS has operated as Scandinavia's leading airline since 1946, running hubs at Copenhagen, Oslo and Stockholm. The airline serves more than 25 million passengers and transports 55,000 tonnes of cargo annually across 135 destinations in Europe, the US and Asia, and joined the SkyTeam alliance in September 2024.
This latest deal follows DHL's April 2026 ground handling contract with Air France-KLM at London Gatwick (Credit: Unsplash)
What this signals for supply chain leaders
Airlines outsourcing ground handling are essentially extending their supply chain to a third-party partner at the exact point where service failures become visible to passengers fastest. The choice of provider carries reputational weight well beyond the operational contract itself, particularly on routes like Manchester-Scandinavia, where connecting passengers have little tolerance for missed transfers.
For DHL, the SAS and Air France-KLM contracts reinforce a pattern: aviation ground handling is becoming a repeatable, scalable service line within its broader supply chain business, built on the same mobilisation playbook applied twice in under six months.
For supply chain and procurement leaders evaluating outsourced
logistics partners
more broadly, that repeatability, standing up a compliant, safety-critical operation from a standing start in 30 days, is arguably the more transferable capability than the aviation specifics themselves.
Key partner cited: SAS Scandinavian Airlines
SAS Scandinavian Airlines is Scandinavia's flag carrier, operating hubs at Copenhagen, Oslo and Stockholm airports since 1946. Hans Henrik Spangenberg serves as MD SAS Ground Handling International. The airline carries more than 25 million passengers and 55,000 tonnes of cargo a year to 135 destinations, and is a SkyTeam member.

title: Q&A: Jim Mellon, Agronomics on Food Supply Chain Risk
content:
Q&A: Jim Mellon, Agronomics on Food Supply Chain Risk
Prioritise Us
on Google
Jim Mellon, Co-Founder and Executive Chairman of Agronomics, shares his thoughts on upcoming risks to the food supply chain
As rising temperatures and ongoing climate disruptors create significant risk for the food supply chain, Jim Mellon shares his thoughts on upcoming risks
Around the world, supply chains have been tested by changing weather patterns and increasing demands. Food and agriculture supply chains are particularly vulnerable to the effects of climate change, with ongoing turbulence making harvests unpredictable.
A strong El Niño is impacting climates and supply chains around the world, with an increasing concern that it will grow to become the largest on record.
Though these events are damaging to current operations, the real concern is for the harvests in 2027, as agricultural impacts typically follow a climate event by six to 12 months.
This means we could be facing lower yields and higher prices in 2027, following unpredictable weather, record-hitting temperature heights and fertiliser disruption caused by issues in the Strait of Hormuz.
Agronomics is a company focused on investing in clean and alternative food production, moving towards
building resilience
in a critical – yet vulnerable – supply chain.
Clean food is that which is produced in controlled environments, away from pesticides, microbial contamination and insecticides. Sustainable and resource-efficient production methods are used, such as cell-cultivation and precision fermentation.
The aim is to develop supply chain and food security, alongside reducing the environmental impact of industrial agriculture.
Supply Chain Digital spoke to Jim Mellon, Co-Founder and Executive Chairman of Agronomics, about the current state of the food supply chain and how resilience can be developed.
None of this argues for sidelining traditional farming. The goal has to be to complement it, freeing land and farmers to focus on higher-value, more resilient practices rather than absorbing every shock at the root.
Jim Mellon, Co-Founder and Executive Chairman of Agronomics
What has been a core concern for food supply chains in recent years? Has that changed over recent months?
The conversation around food security has usually centred solely on sustainability; emissions, land use, water consumption. That's still true and vitally important – agriculture generates 17% of global greenhouse gas emissions and consumes 70% of the world's freshwater. But this year, the emphasis has shifted. The core concern has
become resilience
and supply security. The FAO's Food Price Index hit 130.7 points in April 2026, and the UK's Food and Drink Federation has revised its food inflation forecast to at least 9% by year-end. Fertiliser and energy costs have risen sharply, driven by geopolitical instability, pushing prices for UK farmers up by as much as 70%.
What we're seeing is that food price shocks no longer correct themselves, the evidence suggests they drive prices up indefinitely. So the question has moved from "can we produce enough calories globally?" to "can we guarantee reliable, and accessible supply at a national level, even under stress?"
Food supply chain resilience has become a critical concern. Credit: Unsplash
How is a strong El Niño revealing vulnerabilities in agriculture supply chains?
El Niño has returned to the Pacific, and forecasters believe it could rank among the most powerful on record, alongside 1997-98 and 2015-16. Its agricultural impact typically lags the underlying climate signal by six to twelve months, so the real pressure on yields and prices is still growing through the rest of 2026 and into 2027.
It's also landing on a system already buckling under strain from a live fertiliser crunch. Climate risk and geopolitical risk are compounding rather than operating as separate problems, and a food system built almost entirely on open fields, rainfall and stable input markets has very little, if any, protection against that.
Why are perennial crops like cocoa and coffee demonstrating structural deficits, rather than rare reactions to weather issues?
Farmers can’t replant their way out of a bad season. Soil is degrading, herds have been culled and will take years to rebuild, and perennial crops in particular carry damage forward rather than resetting. Cocoa illustrates this clearly: after a
run of deficits
driven by ageing trees, disease and erratic West African rainfall, the market has only recently rebalanced into a fragile surplus, and that recovery depends entirely on the weather holding. The underlying structural problems, low farmer incomes, thin reinvestment in irrigation, remain unresolved.
Coffee shows the same pattern, with Brazil's crop outlook now a central swing factor for the whole market. Beef tells the story from another angle:
years of drought
have pushed the US cattle herd to its smallest size in generations, and ranchers can't rebuild quickly because doing so requires feed and pasture the drought hasn't allowed. These are structural problems and the effects are already being felt.
Cocoa harvests in Africa are vulnerable to weather events. Credit: Getty
What are clean ingredients and why is producing them becoming vital in today’s world?
Clean food covers technologies like precision fermentation – which uses microbes to produce ingredients such as proteins, fats and flavouring compounds – and cell cultivation – which grows real animal and planet cells directly in bioreactors. Both remove production from agricultural land, weather conditions and the volatility of traditional farming. This is incredibly important because it allows food production to be more localised, reducing reliance on global networks and exposure to cross-border disruption.
Instead of a crop absorbing sunlight over a season, microbes and cells are fed a nutrient broth in a controlled tank, multiplying into the target ingredient in days. None of this depends on this season's rainfall, this year's fertiliser price, or the state of a shipping lane thousands of miles away. And the good news is, it's happening already. Take Clean Food Group, a UK company that has a million-litre facility in Liverpool that produces CleanOil, a palm oil alternative that requires no tropical
deforestation
and no transoceanic shipping.
Jim explains
Agriculture is responsible for 17% of global greenhouse gas emissions
70% of the world's freshwater is consumed by the agriculture sector
In April, the FAO's Food Price Index hit 130.7 points
UK farmers are facing price increases of up to 70%
What can organisations do to develop agricultural resilience in today’s modern world?
The response cannot simply be to absorb each shock and wait for it to pass, because the next one is already visible on the horizon. Organisations need to invest now in production that sits outside the climate and geopolitical risk cycle. That means treating clean food technologies as
strategic infrastructure
rather than experimental science and backing companies scaling these processes commercially. We also need companies to work with policymakers on regulatory pathways.
It’s important to caveat that none of this argues for sidelining traditional farming. The goal has to be to complement it, freeing land and farmers to focus on higher-value, more resilient practices rather than absorbing every shock at the root.

title: Shein's Stock Market Debut: Pressure on Supplier Networks
content:
Shein's Stock Market Debut: Pressure on Supplier Networks
Prioritise Us
on Google
Shein is targeting the Hong Kong Stock Exchange with a US$27bn valuation. Credit: Shein
Shein is making its Hong Kong stock market debut, but supply chain concerns and ongoing scrutiny has the company targeting a lower valuation than expected
Global ecommerce platform Shein rose to prominence in the late 2010s and early 2020s, becoming a major player in how consumers buy clothing.
With this, there has been growing demand for the site, alongside rising scrutiny for the way it operates.
Now, Shein is making its debut on the Hong Kong stock exchange, targeting a US$27bn valuation.
The lesson for online retailers is that visibility and contingency plans are crucial for the bottom line, including for situations where a supplier becomes unusable because of new regulatory or ethical concerns coming to light.
Ben Wright, Managing Partner at Argon & Co UK
The rise of Shein
Initially set up in 2008 by Chris Xu (Xu Yangtian), Shein began its worldwide operations in 2012, initially selling wedding dresses. Now, it sells around the world, offering apparel and products at an affordable price. A core aim is to make fashion accessible to all, using a digital-first approach to
meet its customers
head-on.
It uses technology throughout its entire process, relying on social media and trends to stay informed of consumer demand. Its digital supply chain aims to deliver products to customers around the world at a fast-paced manner, ordering in small batches and tracking sales at all times.
The company grew significantly in 2020, driven by closed retailers amid the COVID-19 pandemic and bored consumers looking to rejuvenate their look. It reported US$10bn in revenue in 2020, and was the world's largest online-only fashion firm.
Since then, the company has continued to grow – but so has its
public scrutiny
. In 2024, Shein attempted to become listed on the London Stock Exchange for an initial public offering (IPO), following a failed attempt at the New York Stock Exchange. Public scrutiny and policy queries led to this being a failed attempt, with heavy concerns regarding the standards of care throughout its supply chain.
Now, the organisation will list itself on the Hong Kong stock exchange on 1 September, with a valuation of approximately US$27bn. This low number has proven to be a shock to many analysts, as the company reached a private-market valuation of almost US$100bn in 2022.
"The US$73bn question for Shein is how much
poor supply chain visibility
can ultimately cost a business," explains Ben Wright, Managing Partner at Argon & Co UK.
Ben Wright, Managing Partner at Argon & Co UK
"Its fall from a valuation of almost US$100bn at its 2022 peak to around US$27bn today cannot be attributed to supply chain concerns alone. But the scrutiny surrounding its sourcing and labour practices shows that supply chain transparency is now an investor issue as much as an operational one."
The hidden risks
Though ecommerce has skyrocketed in recent years, there has also become a greater awareness of ethics and sustainability. Consumers want reliable and fast delivery of products, but they are also prioritising organisations with transparent supply chain operations and clear sustainability initiatives.
Much of the scrutiny facing Shein is its lack of visibility and the implications which come with
fast-fashion
– particularly as Shein's prices are as low as they are. While it still has a relatively large market – 273 million active customers in 160 markets throughout 2025 – investors have greater concerns.
For a company with as much scrutiny as Shein has, investing in it is a risk – does it still have a capacity for growth, or have new standards meant that the retailer has reached its peak? If so, investors could see less benefit in taking that chance.
In the first three months of 2026, Shein faced a net loss of US$99m, following its US$395m profit in 2025. Much of this has been a result of lacking clarity across supplier base and ethics of production.
“Shein’s tumble in valuation should be a warning to e-commerce firms that investors are really laser-focused on the story behind the growth story," Ben tells Supply Chain Digital.
“Its valuation decline can’t be attributed to supply chain concerns alone, but for e-commerce businesses built on complex, global supplier networks, it does show that issues around sourcing, governance, and transparency are now investor issues as much as operational ones.
Chris Xu, CEO of SHEIN, founded the company in 2008.
“Before, e-commerce firms like Shein and Boohoo were rewarded for scale, speed and low prices. But now, investors also want evidence that these models are sustainable. Technology and AI are making much greater supply chain visibility possible, which means investors are much less tolerant of companies that can’t answer fundamental questions about where their products come from, whether
child labour
is used, and under what conditions workers are living.
“The lesson for online retailers is that visibility and contingency plans are crucial for the bottom line, including for situations where a supplier becomes unusable because of new regulatory or ethical concerns coming to light.”
Key facts
Shein is targeting a US$27bn valuation on the Hong Kong stock exchange
The company began in 2008
In 2020, Shein reported a US$10bn revenue
Shein has faced a net loss of US$99m in Q1 2026
Meeting modern standards
Though Shein has a
dedicated sustainability strategy
, evoluSHEIN, with a focus on empowering people, driving resilience and reducing waste, it is generally deemed unethical and unsustainable. Its introduction of cheap items, heavy use of synthetic materials, encouragement of hyper-consumption and low durability contribute to high levels of waste.
Ethical consumerism is growing, as more shoppers recognise their impact on the planet. The 2026 E-Commerce Trends Report by DHL found that 35% of shoppers have abandoned an online purchase due to a lack of sustainability credentials.
Though the LSE missed out on the IPO, therefore potentially putting it at a disadvantage in competitiveness with Hong Kong, it is demonstrating its focus on governance, responsible sourcing and scrutiny.

title: Lyten to acquire insolvent battery cell manufacturer Morrow Batteries - electrive.com
content:
US battery developer Lyten is now seeking to acquire the insolvent Norwegian battery cell manufacturer Morrow Batteries, after acquiring Swedish battery maker Northvolt. If the deal goes through, Morrow's battery technology activities could continue to be based at the company's site in Arendal.
Morrow's battery factory in Arendal, Norway.
Image: Morrow Batteries
Lyten has signed a letter of intent to acquire Morrow Batteries, in collaboration with Innovation Norway —Norway’s state-owned economic development and investment bank— and Morrow’s insolvency administrators. The
Norwegian battery specialist
initiated insolvency proceedings
earlier this year
for Morrow Batteries ASA, Morrow Technologies AS, and Morrow Industrialisation Center AS, and declared insolvency in early summer. Morrow opened a smaller industrial plant for
LFP battery cells in 2024
, and stated in June this year that it aimed to salvage at least part of its operations. These prospects now appear promising with the recently signed letter of intent from US battery developer Lyten.
Bidding process with multiple interested parties
According to their statements, the insolvency administrators and Innovation Norway had been negotiating with several bidders and finally selected Lyten as the preferred bidder. The three partners have agreed to keep the details of the letter of intent confidential.
Leon Bakkebø, Executive Vice President at Innovation Norway and responsible for financing and banking, stated: “As a secured creditor, our priority throughout the process has been to maximise value recovery and reduce execution risk.” He said they support the trustee’s decision to proceed with Lyten “because their proposal provides the strongest overall combination of financial recovery, transaction certainty and industrial credibility.” The executive further noted that, if completed, “the transaction could also create a foundation for future battery-related activity in Arendal.”
70 jobs secured in the short term
Lyten is already familiar with the acquisition of insolvent Nordic battery makers from its acquisition of the r
emaining assets of Swedish battery manufacturer Northvolt
. Christian Bohne, the lawyer administering Morrow’s insolvency estate, explained that the goal is to preserve value and seek a solution for the company’s continued existence. He pointed out that employees have been severely affected by the insolvency. “Under demanding circumstances, they have made an important and highly valued contribution to the work to continue battery production in the Arendal region. Their commitment has been instrumental in enabling us to enter into this agreement”
In the short term, Bohne said the process secures around 70 jobs until autumn. In the long term, several hundred jobs at Morrow and orders for local material and service providers could be safeguarded. However, the insolvency administrator also warns that there are circumstances and conditions beyond their control that must be met before the transaction can be completed. Nevertheless, Bohne said, “Although we do not yet know whether those circumstances can be met, I am optimistic about Lyten’s ability to execute”
Lyten aims to establish European production base
Dan Cook, CEO and co-founder of Lyten, sees significant potential in Europe. He pointed out, “Europe has entered a sustained period of infrastructure investment, and batteries are now an important part of this critical infrastructure.” Lyten aims to build a financially robust and scalable production base for batteries and energy storage in Europe, coupling technologies, supply chains, and production sites in the USA and Europe. “The Morrow team has built a business aligned with this strategy, making the assets a strong strategic fit for Lyten in Europe,” said Cook.
According to Lyten, the company is evaluating the expansion of the Morrow site into a potential “Lyten Industrial Hub.” The US company said it should be able to integrate battery production, upstream and downstream activities in the energy storage value chain, and industrial activities to support other critical sectors—including AI data centres, mobility, and defence. Lyten also plans a similar hub in Skellefteå at the former Northvolt site.
Northvolt and Morrow Batteries were long regarded as two of the few companies capable of producing battery cells in Europe but were unable to sustain activities. While Northvolt struggled with production quality during its ramp-up phase, Morrow Batteries fell victim to its small size in a consolidating market. The plant opened in summer 2024 at its headquarters in Arendal for the production of prismatic LFP cells with an annual capacity of just 1 GWh—far too small to supply a major car manufacturer. This capacity is sufficient for only around 25,000 small cars with a 40-kWh battery. For comparison, Volkswagen’s subsidiary PowerCo states that its
new cell factory in Salzgitter
has an annual capacity of 20 GWh, enough for around 250,000 small cars.
Morrow lacked investors for expansion to 43 GWh
Morrow Batteries was also targeting the construction of such a gigafactory. The Norwegian company had planned to expand the Arendal site in four stages to eventually reach 43 GWh. But this never materialised due to a lack of investors. Even the ramp-up of the existing 1-GWh plant proved to be a significant challenge, and the cell factory never achieved series production. As recently as January 2026—nearly a year and a half after the plant’s opening—Morrow Batteries stated that it was now ready for series production but was adopting a “partnership-based approach,” seeking long-term investments and strategic alliances to accelerate technology validation and secure offtake agreements. Morrow Batteries’ management commented on the insolvency in June, stating that the background was complex. “The company has been operating in an early and capital‑intensive industrialisation phase, while at the same time the global battery market has become more competitive with oversupply and resulting price pressure. In addition, increased capital costs, delays in the industrialisation process, and a more restrained investment market have made it significantly more difficult to secure financing.”

title: 40,500-ton USS Boxer warship gets $150M upgrade to stay battle-ready
content: BAE Systems has secured a $149.8 million U.S. Navy contract to repair and modernize the USS Boxer, an amphibious assault ship weighing about 40,500 tons at full load.The firm-fixed-price award could grow to roughly $180 million if the Navy exercises every contract option. Work will take place at Naval Base San Diego.The USS Boxer, designated LHD 4, will undergo a Selected Restricted Availability, or SRA. That maintenance period allows crews and contractors to address repairs and upgrades before returning the ship to operational duties.Navy workhorseCommissioned in 1995, the USS Boxer belongs to the Wasp-class of amphibious assault ships. The 844-foot vessel serves as a seagoing platform for Marines, helicopters, and advanced combat aircraft.Its roughly 40,500-ton full-load displacement places the ship among the Navy’s largest conventional surface combat vessels. The Boxer can support amphibious operations and aviation missions from its expansive flight deck. It can also operate aircraft such as the F-35B Lightning II, giving the vessel a growing role in modern Marine Corps operations.That combination makes maintenance periods especially important. Shipboard systems face constant wear from aviation operations, deployments and extended time at sea.BAE Systems will handle the modernization and repair work through its Maritime Solutions operation in San Diego. Eric Icke, the unit’s vice president and general manager, said the work would support the Navy’s mission. “Critical maintenance of the USS Boxer will support the U.S. Navy’s vital mission to continue defending our nation,” Icke said.Modernization during restricted availabilityA Selected Restricted Availability provides the Navy with a scheduled window for significant maintenance and modernization. The process can involve repairs across propulsion, electrical and combat-related systems. BAE Systems did not disclose the complete list of upgrades planned for the Boxer.However, the scope includes critical maintenance, repair and modernization work. The project will take place in San Diego, where the company operates major ship repair facilities.Keeping a 40,500-ton amphibious assault ship ready for deployment requires extensive industrial support. The Boxer warship carries complex aviation, command and amphibious systems within a hull designed for global operations.Work on vessels of that size also demands specialized waterfront infrastructure. BAE Systems operates three full-service shipyards across California, Florida and Virginia. Those facilities provide drydocks, shiplifts, railways and pier-side support for Navy and government vessels.Keeping Boxer mission readyThe Boxer has spent nearly three decades supporting U.S. naval operations around the world. The upcoming availability aims to extend that service through repairs and selected modernization.The $149.8 million award gives BAE Systems responsibility for a substantial portion of that effort. Additional options could lift the program’s value by more than $30 million.For the Navy, the project represents another investment in sustaining its existing fleet. New ships take years to design and build, making maintenance essential for preserving available combat power. Once completed, the work should help prepare the USS Boxer for future operations from San Diego.

title: 5 MWe microreactor that works in extreme environments to support US Army
content: A San Diego-based company’s tactical energy system (microreactor) is set to support one of the U.S. Army’s key programs. General Atomics’ Tactical Energy System (GA‑TES) has ben selected by the U.S. Army to support the Janus Program, which is accelerating commercially developed nuclear technologies into operational use. The company revealed that GA‑TES is a liquid-metal-cooled microreactor with a baseline net output of approximately 5 megawatts electric (MWe) and an architecture scalable to approximately 20 MWe. Designed for remote, off-grid and extreme environments, the plant has a design life of 40 years. Its modular architecture supports transport and deployment by truck or rail, while natural-circulation primary coolant flow eliminates pumps and associated mechanical complexity.Microreactor technologies provide safe, dependable and independent power“General Atomics draws on more than 70 years of nuclear innovation and reactor expertise to deliver microreactor technologies that provide safe, dependable and independent power for military installations,” said Scott Forney, president of GA-EMS.“Our experience designing and deploying 68 reactors worldwide and supporting reactor technologies throughout their lifecycles positions us to deliver assured energy solutions that enhance operational resilience and strengthen mission readiness.”General Atomics Electromagnetic Systems (GA-EMS) revealed that it will execute its effort through an Other Transaction Authority-based agreement and milestone-based funding tied to specific technical goals.It was also revealed that under the Janus Program, Fort Hood, Texas, will serve as the installation to advance GA-TES through development, testing and site-planning milestones toward potential deployment. This work supports the Army’s broader nuclear objectives.Reliable commercial hardware that secures energy independence“The Janus Program is about transitioning from designs and experiments to reliable commercial hardware which secures our energy independence,” said Jeff Waksman, PhD., principal deputy assistant secretary of the Army for Installations, Energy and Environment. “The Janus Program vendors were selected through a deeply rigorous evaluation on technical, financial and organizational capabilities conducted by an all-star panel of dozens of experts from across the nation. We look forward to working alongside each team as they proceed toward successfully completing the rigorous technical milestones we’ve agreed upon.”General Atomics’ longstanding nuclear heritageGA‑TES builds on General Atomics’ longstanding nuclear heritage, including its pioneering work in uranium-zirconium hydride (UZrH) fuel technology and the proven safety and operating record of TRIGA reactors deployed globally. GA-EMS carries that legacy forward by integrating nuclear technologies and materials with power and energy systems expertise to develop practical solutions for demanding national security missions, according to a press release. GA-TES combines the self-regulating characteristics of UZrH fuel with pump-free natural-circulation cooling to enhance passive safety and simplify operations while providing secure and reliable power for critical defense infrastructure without dependence on large cooling‑water infrastructure, as per the release.

title: All-solid-state battery withstands temperatures up to 302°F
content: Maxell has developed an all-solid-state battery module that fits the same 1/2AA size as batteries commonly used in industrial equipment, smart meters and IoT devices, while adding wireless charging capability.The module measures 14.5 millimeters in diameter and 25.2 mm in height, matching the form factor of a conventional ER battery. It delivers the same 3.6-volt output while combining rechargeable all-solid-state cells with a wireless charging circuit and a boost circuit.The company has developed two versions of the module. One can operate at temperatures up to 257°F, while the other is designed to withstand temperatures as high as 302°F.That combination could make the battery useful in equipment where replacing a battery is difficult or where openings in the enclosure could compromise protection against moisture and other environmental factors.Tiny battery tackles tough environmentsConventional ER batteries are widely used as backup power sources in industrial equipment, smart meters and IoT devices. Because they are non-rechargeable, however, users must periodically replace them, creating maintenance work and a stream of discarded batteries.Maxell’s module is designed to address both problems. Once installed, it can be recharged wirelessly using a dedicated charger, reducing the need to physically access the battery. The wireless connection can also allow equipment manufacturers to avoid adding openings specifically for battery replacement or charging.That could be particularly useful for devices that need a highly sealed enclosure. The company says one potential application is a temperature logger used during the sterilization of retort food, where equipment needs to tolerate high temperatures while limiting moisture ingress.Maxell is conducting a joint feasibility study with House Foods Corporation on a food-process temperature logger using the new module.The battery’s high-temperature capability is another important part of the design. The 257°F and 302°F versions are intended to extend rechargeable solid-state battery technology into environments that can be too demanding for conventional rechargeable cells.Wireless charging without battery accessThe module is not simply a solid-state replacement for an ER battery. Its integrated electronics are designed to let existing equipment gain wireless charging functionality without requiring a complicated circuit redesign.The dedicated charger is tailored to the customer’s equipment, meaning the system is not a universal wireless charging accessory. Maxell also notes that wireless charging may not work with every enclosure material.Still, the small form factor could make the technology attractive for compact industrial sensors and other devices where space is limited. By retaining the familiar 1/2AA dimensions and 3.6V output, the module is designed to fit applications built around the dimensions and voltage of conventional ER batteries.The use of rechargeable all-solid-state cells could also reduce the frequency of battery replacement. For equipment deployed in large numbers or in locations that are difficult to access, fewer maintenance visits could translate into lower operating costs as well as less battery waste.Maxell has not announced commercial availability or a production timeline for the module. The company is currently evaluating potential applications with partners, including the food-processing temperature logger project with House Foods Corporation.

title: Aluminum fuel converts scrap metal into 2 MW of clean firm power
content: Hayward, California-based firm Voya Energy has unveiled an aluminum-based power system that can generate electricity without combustion, while aiming to provide large energy users with power independent of the utility grid.The company combines a proprietary aluminum fuel with a purpose-built electrochemical generator. Instead of burning fuel to produce electricity, the system uses a low-temperature electrochemical process to convert aluminum into power.Voya says its fuel can be made from low-grade scrap aluminum, giving the system a potential route to turn an abundant waste material into a source of firm electricity. The company is targeting data centers, industrial facilities and other large power users facing grid-access, permitting or fuel-logistics constraints.The company also announced a $35 million Series A funding round led by Energy Impact Partners. The financing includes participation from John Doerr, Mantis VC, StepStone, Founders Fund, Overmatch, Seven Stars and other institutional investors.Aluminum turns waste into powerAt industrial scale, Voya’s system is designed to produce up to 2 megawatts from a standard 20-foot container. The company says its technology could eventually deliver about 100 megawatts of generation capacity and 10 gigawatt-hours of stored energy per acre.That footprint could make the technology particularly relevant where space is limited. Voya estimates that its system could be about four times more compact than diesel generator fleets and 100 times more compact than grid-scale battery installations.The company says its approach can provide “clean, firm” electricity without combustion or air emissions at the point of use. That could give operators an alternative to conventional diesel generators for backup and off-grid power, while avoiding direct combustion emissions.“America needs dramatically more electricity to power our industries, strengthen our communities, and support continued economic growth,” said John Doerr, Founder at Doerr Capital and Chair at Kleiner Perkins. “Meeting that demand requires new technologies that can deliver clean, firm power at speed and scale. Voya is taking a bold approach to that challenge, turning abundant aluminum into a practical source of 24/7 power wherever it is needed.”Two megawatts inside one containerThe system’s proposed scale is aimed at a growing problem for electricity-intensive facilities: getting enough power from the grid quickly. Rather than waiting for new grid connections or relying entirely on conventional generators, Voya wants its technology to provide power directly at the site.The company says nearly a dozen companies spanning data centers, industry, transportation, utilities and infrastructure are already working with it on pilot demonstrations.The initial deployments are planned for 2027, giving Voya an opportunity to test the system with commercial users before moving toward larger-scale manufacturing. The company plans to use the new financing for technology development, those early deployments, and manufacturing scale-up targeted for 2028.The aluminum fuel approach also gives the system an energy-storage component. Rather than generating electricity only when fuel is consumed, the material can serve as a stored energy source that is converted to electricity through the electrochemical generator when power is needed.Voya plans to use the new funding for further technology development and initial deployments in 2027, followed by manufacturing scale-up in 2028.

title: Battery energy storage system predicts risks before failures
content: ELECTRA AI and South Korean battery diagnostics company MinTech are working on a system designed to spot problems in battery energy storage systems (BESS) before they turn into failures.The technical collaboration combines MinTech’s battery inspection and diagnostic equipment with ELECTRA’s Battery Fleet Analytics software. The system will process operational data from batteries and use it to identify emerging risks in real time.The goal is to give operators earlier warnings about battery health instead of waiting for faults to appear. For large BESS installations, earlier detection could help reduce downtime, lost revenue, and potential safety problems.MinTech specializes in battery diagnostics and testing, while ELECTRA provides the software layer that analyzes the resulting data. The companies are using MinTech’s equipment data with ELECTRA’s Battery Fleet Analytics solution, which is delivered as software-as-a-service.Battery data becomes early warningsThe system is designed to perform state diagnosis and deeper battery analysis while also identifying potential risks before they develop into failures. This could give operators a more detailed view of battery conditions across an energy storage installation.BESS facilities can contain large numbers of battery cells and modules operating continuously. Detecting a developing problem early can therefore be important for keeping the wider system available and preventing a localized fault from becoming a larger operational issue.MinTech’s diagnostic technology is based on electrochemical impedance spectroscopy, or EIS, along with proprietary diagnostic algorithms. EIS can be used to examine the electrical characteristics of batteries and provide information about their condition.ELECTRA’s software is intended to build on that diagnostic information by analyzing operational data and identifying patterns associated with battery health and potential risks.“MinTech brings deep expertise at the diagnostics layer, and ELECTRA brings the intelligence layer that turns operational data into predictive insight,” said Fabrizio Martini, CEO and Co-Founder of ELECTRA AI.The companies say the collaboration combines MinTech’s diagnostics capabilities with ELECTRA’s analytics and risk-prediction technology. Rather than treating battery monitoring as a system that simply reports a fault, the companies are aiming to make it more predictive.Predicting problems before they escalateThat approach could be particularly relevant as BESS deployments grow to support renewable energy, electricity grids and data centers. Battery storage systems are expected to operate reliably for years, making continuous monitoring important for maintaining performance over their operating life.MinTech’s technology covers multiple stages of the battery lifecycle, including manufacturing, in-use applications, second-life batteries and recycling. Its diagnostic systems include EV battery testing, second-life battery energy storage and EIS applications for battery management systems.For ELECTRA, the collaboration adds another source of battery data to its analytics platform. The company says its software is designed to monitor battery systems and turn operational information into actionable insights.The partnership is currently a technical collaboration rather than a commercial deployment announcement. Both companies said they expect to explore additional cooperation in battery diagnostics, battery analytics and battery risk prediction.ELECTRA has also entered a definitive business combination agreement with Iron Horse Acquisition II Corp., a special purpose acquisition company. The combined company is expected to list on Nasdaq in the second half of 2026 under the ticker AIBR.

title: Blackbeard Mach 5 hypersonic missile wins $90M to scale 50 units
content: Castelion has secured an $89.99 million U.S. Navy order to move its Blackbeard hypersonic strike weapon toward Early Operational Capability. The California defense startup revealed Blackbeard publicly on August 20. Just days later, the Navy awarded funding for 50 Early Operational Capability weapons.The firm-fixed-price award signals a major shift for the program. Blackbeard must now prove it can move beyond flight testing and into repeatable production.Castelion will provide engineering, technical, logistics, and manufacturing support under the order. The work will also support Blackbeard’s transition into a formal Navy Program of Record. Production will take place in Torrance, California. Castelion expects to complete the work by August 2028.Towards operational serviceBlackbeard takes a different approach from many earlier U.S. hypersonic programs. Castelion designed the weapon around manufacturing scale from the beginning. The company aims to produce large numbers of weapons without relying on low-volume production methods.The compact strike weapon uses vertically integrated propulsion and guidance systems. Castelion says Blackbeard can exceed Mach 5 and strike targets up to 500 nautical miles away. That range could give U.S. forces a new standoff option against heavily defended targets.The Navy initially examined the weapon for land-based applications. Its potential role has since expanded toward carrier aviation.Castelion has positioned Blackbeard for integration with the Navy’s F/A-18E/F Super Hornet fleet. That could give carrier air wings a hypersonic weapon designed for rapid launches against distant targets.Modern anti-access and area-denial networks increasingly threaten aircraft operating near contested waters. Longer-range weapons can allow naval aircraft to strike from outside some defensive zones. Blackbeard’s speed could further reduce the time available for an opponent to detect, track, and respond.Different hypersonic modelCost sits at the center of Blackbeard’s design philosophy. Many hypersonic weapons involve highly specialized components and limited production runs. Those systems can cost millions of dollars per weapon.Blackbeard Unveiled🏴‍☠️ pic.twitter.com/MXX1uMO0P8— Castelion (@Castelion) August 20, 2026Castelion instead aims to keep Blackbeard below $500,000 per round. The weapon makes a deliberate tradeoff to pursue that goal. It carries a smaller payload than larger hypersonic systems but targets much greater production volume. That approach could matter on aircraft carriers, where magazine depth remains a major operational concern.A lower-cost weapon could allow the Navy to field more hypersonic rounds across its carrier air wings. Higher inventories could also support repeated conventional strikes during a prolonged conflict.The new order also funds Defense Exportability Features for Blackbeard. Those modifications could help accelerate future sales to U.S. allies and partners. Export versions would require designs that meet American technology protection requirements.Castelion’s new Navy award does not guarantee Blackbeard’s entry into full-rate production. The program still faces engineering, manufacturing, and operational milestones. Still, funding for 50 Early Operational Capability weapons gives the startup a clearer path toward deployment.Blackbeard has already flown. Now Castelion has to build 50 of them. That transition will test whether the startup’s manufacturing-first approach can work outside prototypes and small test batches.

title: Chinese humanoid robot runs 100 meters in 8.4 secs at Beijing event
content: A humanoid robot developed in China completed a 100-meter race in 8.64 seconds at the 2nd World Humanoid Robot Games, setting a new record for the competition.Tiangong Ultra, built by Beijing-based X-Humanoid, clocked the record time while winning the large-group final on the closing day of the five-day event.Its performance was nearly one second inside Usain Bolt’s official human world record of 9.58 seconds, although robot and human results are not directly comparable.Tiangong Ultra breaks its record againThe 8.64-second run improved upon the previous fastest time of the games, which Tiangong Ultra had set during the repechage.The humanoid completed the race in 8.86 seconds before shaving another 0.22 seconds off its time in the final. It had already rewritten the event record twice before reaching the decisive race.Tiangong Ultra’s final performance also marked a significant improvement over the inaugural World Humanoid Robot Games, where the fastest 100-meter time was more than 12 seconds.The difference highlights the rapid progress made in humanoid locomotion over the past year. Sprinting at high speed requires a robot to coordinate its legs, maintain balance, respond to changes in momentum, and recover from instability without falling.Tiangong Ultra emerged as the most prolific record-setter at this year’s games. Its closest rival in the final was Lightning, a humanoid robot developed by Chinese smartphone maker Honor.Robots challenge human performance marksLightning entered the final with its own record-breaking achievements. In April, the humanoid reportedly completed a half-marathon with a net time of 50 minutes and 26 seconds, beating the official human half-marathon world record.The five-day competition also saw robots produce performances that surpassed human records in events including sprinting and the high jump.Such comparisons, however, come with important differences. Humanoid robots do not compete under the same physiological, technical, or regulatory conditions as human athletes, meaning their results cannot replace officially recognized human records.The games instead allow developers to test how their machines perform under pressure. Athletic events expose weaknesses in balance, joint control, power management, perception, and the software coordinating a robot’s movements.Analysts said the competition serves as a broad benchmark for evaluating overall robot performance while providing a proving ground for future real-world applications.The 100-meter large-group final was the last event on the schedule and brought the second edition of the games to a close.Lightning’s 9.32-second sprintBefore the competition, Lightning had reportedly completed a separate 100-meter test in 9.32 seconds in Beijing.The humanoid reached a peak speed of 14.5 meters per second during the run, placing its reported time 0.26 seconds inside Bolt’s 9.58-second record. Lightning was developed by Honor as part of the company’s work on humanoid robotics.Tiangong Ultra’s 8.64-second performance at the games was 0.68 seconds faster than Lightning’s reported test result. Together, the runs show how quickly Chinese developers are increasing the speed of humanoid robots while maintaining the balance required to complete a full sprint.

title: Cyborg cockroaches can help survivors in disaster zones before rescue
content: Researchers have developed cyborg cockroaches that could help deliver emergency medical care to people trapped in collapsed buildings, caves, and other dangerous locations. Called Paraborgs, the insects are fitted with miniature electronics that allow researchers to remotely monitor their movements and interact with people who may be beyond rescuers’ reach. The system combines cameras or remotely activated injection devices, turning the insects from simple search tools into potential rescue platforms. Developed by researchers at the University of Queensland and the University of New South Wales (UNSW), the technology keeps critical medical decisions under human control while the cockroaches navigate difficult environments.Robots deliver careParaborgs combines the insects’ natural ability to navigate cluttered environments with lightweight electronics and remotely controlled hardware. The system is designed to extend cyborg insects’ capabilities beyond simply locating survivors.The researchers used North Queensland giant burrowing cockroaches (Macropanesthia rhinoceros), whose relatively large bodies provide enough capacity to carry specialized equipment. Each insect can be fitted with a lightweight electronic harness supporting either a camera for visual feedback or a custom-built auto-injection mechanism, according to a statement by the team.The Giant Burrowing Cockroach provides greater capacity to carry specialised rescue and medical equipment.The camera-equipped insects could provide rescuers with a live view of difficult-to-access environments, while the injector-equipped versions are designed to deliver emergency medication under remote human supervision. This approach means the insect handles the physical navigation and positioning, while people control critical medical decisions.According to researchers, one of the biggest engineering challenges was getting the cockroaches into the correct position for an injection. The insect must navigate toward a target, approach it closely, remain stable, and activate the injector accurately. In proof-of-concept experiments, the Paraborgs achieved a 95 percent success rate when performing close-range injections from within 15 centimeters of the target.When navigation and injection were combined into a single task, the system completed 72 percent of the trials. The results demonstrate the potential of using biological locomotion as part of a robotic medical-delivery system, although substantial development and field testing would be required before such technology could be used in real emergencies.Insect rescue swarmsThe concept takes advantage of capabilities that conventional miniature robots can struggle to reproduce. Cockroaches can naturally move through uneven, confined, and debris-filled environments, potentially allowing them to access gaps and spaces where wheeled or larger robotic systems may become trapped.The researchers envision eventually deploying swarms of specialized cyborg insects rather than relying on a single multifunctional machine. Some insects could carry cameras and environmental sensors to locate survivors and assess their surroundings, while others could transport medical or emergency equipment.The technology also builds on earlier work by the University of Queensland team involving cyborg insects. Researchers previously demonstrated controlled climbing using cyborg beetles, while the larger giant burrowing cockroach offers greater carrying capacity for rescue applications.The insects are anesthetized while electrodes, microchips and harnesses are fitted. According to the researchers, they can live for as long as other cockroaches once the harnesses are removed.The long-term goal is not to replace human first responders but to give them another remotely controlled tool for situations in which direct access is impossible. Researchers say specialized cyborg insect teams could potentially be deployed for urban search and rescue, cave emergencies, and disaster response within the next five to 10 years, provided further research and field testing can accelerate development.

title: Enhanced geothermal system aims to unlock power from hot rock
content: Sage Geosystems, a US developer of enhanced geothermal systems, and Japan’s Chiyoda Corporation, an engineering company specializing in large industrial facilities, are studying a new way to turn heat and pressure deep underground into steady electricity.The companies have signed a memorandum of understanding to assess the surface equipment needed for a commercial-scale enhanced geothermal system (EGS). The study will focus on facilities that can handle high-pressure, high-temperature fluid brought up from engineered underground reservoirs.Sage’s EGS approach starts by drilling into hot rock and creating an engineered reservoir. Water is injected underground, where it absorbs heat and builds pressure before flowing back toward the surface. The system is designed to retain more of that pressure and water, which could improve the efficiency and economics of geothermal generation.Unlike conventional geothermal plants, which depend on naturally occurring underground resources, EGS uses drilling and reservoir-management techniques developed in the oil and gas industry. That could allow geothermal projects to operate in locations that have traditionally been considered unsuitable for geothermal development.Hot rock stores heat pressureThe joint study will examine how the underground resource can be connected to a surface power system. Chiyoda will use information from Sage on wellhead pressure, temperature, fluid properties and operating conditions to assess major equipment configurations, energy balances and expected costs.The companies will also estimate capital and operating expenses and the cost of generating electricity. Those calculations are important because the technical ability to extract heat from hot rock does not automatically translate into an economically viable power plant.Sage’s system is also being developed for energy storage. Instead of using the underground reservoir only to generate electricity, surplus electricity could be used to store pressure energy underground. That stored energy could then be recovered when electricity demand rises.“Chiyoda’s expertise in engineering complex, high-pressure industrial facilities makes it an ideal partner as we move Sage’s proprietary EGS approach toward commercial scale. This collaboration is a significant step in proving out the surface infrastructure needed to convert our subsurface innovation into gigawatt-scale power generation and long-duration energy storage,” said Shayne Dustin, SVP Engineering & Development at Sage.Geothermal moves beyond natural limitsThe ability to generate electricity continuously is one of geothermal power’s main advantages over weather-dependent renewable sources. EGS could potentially make that advantage available across a much wider geographic area.The companies see potential applications in data centers, industrial facilities, community microgrids and critical infrastructure, where reliable electricity is increasingly important.“Geothermal energy has significant untapped potential, and next-generation technologies like Sage’s are key to unlocking it. This collaboration brings together Chiyoda’s engineering strength in high-pressure facility design with Sage’s subsurface methodologies. Together, we aim to accelerate the path to commercial-scale deployment and deliver a dependable, low-carbon power source,” said Ken Kimeta, Head of Business Co-Creation, Assistant Division Director of Business Development & Growth Transformation Division at Chiyoda.The study has been selected for support under the Tokyo Metropolitan Government’s TIB CATAPULT program and aligns with Tokyo’s Zero Emission Tokyo Strategy.

title: Four-hour test recreates 15,000 years of gas trapping in moon dirt
content: It takes roughly 15,000 years of harsh, unshielded exposure to the sun for raw lunar soil to trap enough volatile gases to make off-world mining worthwhile. Interlune just cloned that entire millennia-long process before lunch.In a milestone announcement, the Seattle-based space resources startup revealed it has synthesized gas-bearing lunar dirt on Earth. Years of intense solar radiation damage were recreated in just four hours by bombarding targeted mineral grains with accelerated helium plasma inside a high-temperature vacuum chamber.“This demonstration is a force multiplier not only for Interlune’s broader technology development, but for others building hardware for the moon,” said Rob Meyerson, Interlune co-founder and CEO. “It gives the industry a practical way to validate core processing technology on Earth, learn faster and accelerate progress toward Moon readiness.”Space tech shortcutThe 1970s research of Apollo samples identified ilmenite as the main helium-retaining mineral in lunar regolith. In natural mineral grains, atoms form an ordered crystal lattice structure, but eons of solar wind bombardment disrupt the outer edges of lunar ilmenite. It leads to microscopic defects where volatile gases, like helium, become trapped. In the replication of this phenomenon on Earth, the team energized helium gas into plasma in a vacuum chamber using electron emissions from a heated filament. Next, the process accelerated these helium ions directly into simulated ilmenite at solar-wind energy levels. Overall, the technique disrupted the mineral’s crystal lattice rim and trapped the helium inside artificial micro-defects.Further, the ilmenite was gradually heated in a vacuum chamber to verify the implantation. A mass spectrometer measured the escaping gas, revealing that helium was released between 300°C and 800°C (572°F and 1,472°F) — a profile that directly matches Apollo sample data. The final step involves blending this gas-infused ilmenite with other terrestrial minerals to mimic specific lunar locations, enabling engineers to refine and test resource extraction systems on Earth without depleting rare moon rocks or waiting for future lunar missions.This development provides Interlune and the broader space resources industry with a practical, highly accurate test material to validate extraction hardware on Earth before deploying it to the moon.Standard lunar regolith simulants match the particle sizes and mineral composition of moon dirt. But lack the solar-wind volatiles, like helium and hydrogen, trapped in authentic lunar samples. Interlune’s new demonstration fills this gap by producing a gas-bearing material. Further, Interlune is planning to offer both the material and specialized testing services to space companies, research institutions, and government agencies.Prepares harvesters for the moonInterlune plans to use its new helium-bearing simulant to test the extraction hardware for its Harvesting System, which uses mechanical methods rather than high heat to release volatile gases from lunar regolith at an industrial scale. Compared to other extraction concepts that heat regolith to nearly 1,000°C (1,832°F), this mechanical approach is designed to cut power consumption by up to ten times. It will be a critical efficiency gain on the moon, where both mass and power are severely constrained.Interlune is consolidating its R&D at the Houston-based Interlune Research Lab (IRL), backed by up to $4.84 million from the Texas Space Commission and staffed by experts across geochemistry, plasma engineering, and industrial design. Furthermore, the goal is to tailor the simulant’s mineral composition and gas concentration to mirror specific landing sites across the moon. This new approach could also provide a deeper atomic-level understanding of how eons of solar wind exposure alter lunar materials.

title: New F-16 warfare system hits 500 flight hours after 300 test sorties
content: Northrop Grumman’s Integrated Viper Electronic Warfare Suite (IVEWS) has surpassed 500 flight hours and 300 sorties during testing, demonstrating its ability to protect F-16 pilots from multiple simultaneous radio-frequency threats.Tested at a US government range, the system is designed to detect, identify, geolocate, and counter advanced land, surface, and airborne threats. The upgrade is intended to improve pilot survivability and preserve the F-16’s ability to operate in contested airspace.Electronic protection for the F-16Fifth- and sixth-generation fighters increasingly depend on stealth and advanced connectivity to survive in hostile environments. Older platforms such as the F-16, however, rely heavily on electronic warfare systems to detect and respond to threats.IVEWS provides the F-16 with ultra-wideband protection across a broad portion of the electromagnetic spectrum. According to Northrop Grumman, it can counter multiple threats simultaneously while helping pilots maintain freedom of movement during missions.The system can also geolocate radio-frequency threats using a single aircraft. This allows pilots to determine where a potential threat is located and react before it can place the aircraft at greater risk.“You cannot defeat what you cannot see,” said Shalini Gupta, vice president of electronic warfare and targeting at Northrop Grumman. “A modern EW suite is essential for operations in contested airspace. We are producing fully functional, flight-proven systems now. From day one, our customers gain the ability to geolocate threats with a single aircraft, and the confidence that comes with having a U.S. program of record system on board,” she added. Works alongside the F-16’s radarIVEWS is the only F-16 electronic warfare suite offering pulse-to-pulse interoperability with the aircraft’s AN/APG-83 Scalable Agile Beam Radar, or SABR, according to Northrop Grumman.Electronic warfare equipment and radar can interfere with one another because both operate across the radio-frequency spectrum. IVEWS and SABR are designed to work together without requiring filtering or interrupting either system.Northrop Grumman said this integration avoids blackouts and prevents any reduction in electronic protection or targeting performance. Pilots can therefore continue using the radar while IVEWS searches for and responds to surrounding threats.The US Air Force has selected IVEWS as its F-16 electronic warfare program of record, recognizing the system as a planned protection capability for the Viper.Open architecture supports future upgradesThe threats facing military aircraft are becoming increasingly mobile and difficult to predict. New systems can operate across a wide electromagnetic spectrum and rapidly switch on or off, giving electronic warfare equipment little time to detect and counter them.IVEWS uses an open architecture intended to help the system evolve as those threats change. It also complies with the US Air Force’s Big Iron initiative, an open software standard for electronic warfare systems.The standard is designed to speed up the integration of new capabilities while reducing the time aircraft spend out of service for upgrades.

title: New robot system lets humanoids learn cartwheels, kicks and more
content: Researchers have developed a new framework that enables humanoid robots to perform agile, humanlike movements and transition smoothly between different skills.The system allows robots to execute complex maneuvers, including cartwheels, spin kicks, sports movements, and acrobatics, without requiring separate training for each task. Called BeyondMimic, the framework learns from human motion data and can adapt its movements to new tasks and environments. The researchers say the approach could help overcome limitations of existing humanoid control systems, which often require extensive fine-tuning or produce rigid, unnatural movements. Robots learn human agilityThe BeyondMimic model enables humanoid robots to learn agile, humanlike movements from human demonstrations and then combine those skills to perform tasks they were never explicitly trained for.The system addresses a major challenge in humanoid robotics: robots can be taught individual movements such as walking, jumping, or kicking, but making them perform naturally while switching between different skills remains difficult. Existing approaches often require motion-specific reward functions, extensive tuning, or separate training for each task.BeyondMimic uses a two-stage learning framework to overcome these limitations. In the first stage, reinforcement learning (RL) is used to teach the robot to track a wide range of human motions. Crucially, the researchers use a single motion-tracking formulation, shared reward structure, and common hyperparameters rather than tuning the system separately for every movement.The researchers trained the system using about 2.5 hours of diverse human motion data. It learned hundreds of skills, ranging from ordinary walking and running to single-leg balancing, jumps, dance movements, martial-arts-inspired actions, spin kicks, and cartwheels. Twenty-one representative motion clips were subsequently deployed on a physical humanoid robot, demonstrating reliable transfer from simulation to hardware.Making robots skillfulThe second stage introduces a latent diffusion model, which gives BeyondMimic its ability to generate and combine movements. Instead of simply replaying learned motion sequences, the model learns the underlying distribution of coordinated state-action trajectories. A variational autoencoder first compresses these movements into a smoother latent representation, after which a diffusion model learns how those representations evolve, according to the team. The researchers then use classifier guidance at inference time to steer the diffusion model toward objectives that were not included during training. This allows the robot to adapt its existing skills without retraining or fine-tuning the underlying policy. For example, the system can receive a joystick command and generate appropriate walking or running behavior. It can also navigate toward waypoints, avoid obstacles, or use sparse future keyframes to generate a complete movement between them. In one demonstration, the robot smoothly transitioned from walking into a cartwheel and then returned to walking. It also performed sequences combining four cartwheels with walking and running.The approach can additionally combine multiple objectives. By integrating waypoint tracking with an obstacle-avoidance cost, the robot could detour around an obstacle while continuing toward its destination. The same framework could combine joystick control with collision avoidance.The physical robot demonstrated highly dynamic movements, including aerial cartwheels, spin kicks, and flip kicks. During an aerial cartwheel, it reached a peak acceleration of 31 m/s² and pelvic angular velocities of up to 15.7 rad/s, comparable to reported values for skilled human aerial movements. Beyond agility, the researchers found that the generated walking and running motions appeared more natural to human observers. In a study involving 77 participants, BeyondMimic’s motions were preferred over the robot’s native controller as more humanlike and natural in 70.8 percent of choices, compared with 29.2 percent.The researchers say the key advance is not a single new component but the integration of scalable motion tracking with latent diffusion and inference-time guidance. By separating skill acquisition from task specification, BeyondMimic provides a route toward humanoid robots that can learn large repertoires of human movement and recombine those skills to handle new situations without task-specific retraining.

title: New smart system could help defend Guam from missile attacks
content: Lockheed Martin has demonstrated an artificial intelligence-driven battle management prototype designed to help coordinate the complex mix of air and missile defense systems planned for Guam.The company tested its Guam Defense System (GDS) Battle Manager Suite prototype in a simulated operational environment at the Army Tactical Systems Integration Lab at Fort Bliss, Texas. The system is designed to combine information from multiple Integrated Air and Missile Defense (IAMD) networks, build a single tactical picture, analyze incoming threats using AI, and recommend how commanders should respond.The demonstration comes as the U.S. military works toward building a layered air and missile defense architecture for Guam, a strategically important American territory in the Western Pacific that could play a crucial role in any future Indo-Pacific conflict.AI helps sort hundreds of potential threatsAccording to Lockheed Martin, the prototype continuously examined hundreds of tracks and used AI-driven analytics to prioritize threats and recommend potential responses. Rather than requiring operators to piece together information from multiple systems manually, the software combines sensor, weapon, and engagement data into a common tactical picture.The prototype integrated information from systems including Aegis Guam and the Integrated Battle Command System (IBCS). Commanders could also view information such as weapon inventories and available engagement opportunities across the broader operational area.The idea is to reduce the time between detecting a threat and deciding which interceptor or weapon system should respond. “In missile defense, seconds can determine whether an operator protects a populated island or exhausts precious interceptors,” said Tiffany Marr, director of CommandIQ, Golden Dome for America C2 and Advanced Concepts at Lockheed Martin.The company says the system can recommend the optimal weapon for an incoming threat, potentially helping commanders preserve expensive interceptors while maximizing the number of threats that can be engaged.Moving from manual coordination to algorithmic shot selectionTraditional integrated air and missile defense operations can require operators to coordinate through documents, voice communications, text messages and manual calculations. Lockheed Martin’s prototype attempts to automate much of that process through its CommandIQ software platform.The system uses AI-driven, algorithmic shot selection informed by thousands of simulations, according to the company. Rather than replacing human decision-makers, the technology is intended to provide recommendations that allow operators to process more information and make decisions faster.The open-architecture approach also allows the system to integrate new software and data sources rapidly. During the demonstration, the suite incorporated pre-planned warfighter responses, Air Task Orders, Airspace Control Orders and IAMD defense planning information, as well as capabilities supplied by defense technology partners. That flexibility could become increasingly important as missile defense networks incorporate new sensors, interceptors and autonomous systems.Built and integrated in less than two monthsLockheed Martin said the prototype was developed after the U.S. Army called for a Guam Defense System Battle Manager Suite solution in June 2026. The company was invited to a second-phase evaluation at Fort Bliss and demonstrated the system less than two months later.According to Lockheed Martin, the prototype was integrated into the Tactical Systems Integration Lab environment within 24 hours of arrival and met all demonstration criteria within a week. The company had previously demonstrated rapid software-driven command-and-control integration during Valiant Shield 2026, and says the Guam prototype builds on that work.In a place like Guam, where an attack could involve multiple types of missiles and aerial threats arriving within a limited timeframe, the ability to turn a vast amount of battlefield data into rapid engagement recommendations could become just as important as the interceptors themselves.

title: New stereo vision algorithm gives humanoid robots depth perception
content: Researchers have developed a new vision algorithm that lets humanoid robots perceive depth more like humans, using two forward-facing eyes.Instead of relying on conventional stereo cameras, the system processes visual differences between the left and right images to build a more accurate 3D understanding of a scene. The approach, developed by a team led by researchers from York University in Toronto, could improve how humanoid robots judge distances, recognize object orientation, and navigate complex environments.Researchers say the advance brings robotic vision closer to biologically inspired human depth perception and lays the groundwork for more capable humanoid visual systems.Robot depth visionThe new stereo vision algorithm allows humanoid robots to calculate depth using a camera arrangement that more closely mimics human vision. Called convergent binocular stereo (CBS), it is designed for robotic heads whose two cameras can point toward the same location instead of remaining parallel.Unlike conventional stereo systems, which mainly calculate horizontal differences between images from parallel cameras, CBS accounts for both horizontal and vertical disparities created when cameras converge on a target. This allows the system to use camera movement as part of the depth-perception process.Areas with different horizontal disparities are marked, with solid lines showing camera views and dotted lines showing axes.The algorithm first fixes both cameras on a 3D point and determines the geometric relationship between the resulting images. It then creates a five-level Gaussian pyramid to analyze the images at multiple resolutions. At coarser levels, CBS detects and matches SIFT features while using epipolar constraints to estimate horizontal and vertical disparities. Gabor filters are then used to analyze texture and edge information at different orientations and scales, helping identify corresponding pixels between the two images.The system progressively refines these disparity estimates from lower-resolution images to the original resolution, narrowing the search area at each stage. The resulting horizontal and vertical disparity maps can then be converted into 3D information and depth estimates. The researchers say CBS can also capture information about surface slant, object pose, and the perceived scaling of depth and size, providing a more humanlike approach to robotic visual processing.CBS boosts accuracyTo test the algorithm, the researchers created the Convergent Binocular Stereo–BenchMark dataset, or CBS-BM. It contains 49 scenes, including ordinary tabletop environments as well as repeated patterns, featureless surfaces and highly self-occluded objects. Each scene includes parallel images, along with between five and 12 convergent fixation image pairs.CBS was broadly competitive with established stereo methods and several deep-learning systems. Across the full dataset, it achieved lower mean horizontal disparity and depth errors than the parallel methods tested. Its strongest advantage appeared in scenes containing repeated patterns, where conventional systems can struggle to determine which visually similar features correspond to each other. In that subset, CBS produced a mean depth error about 0.8 metres lower than the next-best method and a horizontal disparity error about 100 pixels lower.According to a statement by the team, the approach does have limitations. Its accuracy decreases for targets at greater distances, and it depends on precise camera calibration and motor positioning. The current implementation also takes about 69 seconds to run on an AMD Ryzen 7 7700X processor, leaving substantial scope for optimization.The researchers say CBS is not intended to replace parallel stereo in applications where humanlike vision is unnecessary. Instead, it provides a foundation for humanoid robots that need their physical eye movements and visual processing to work together, bringing robotic depth perception closer to the active, convergent vision humans use.
