title: 2026年上半年数字产业收入超20万亿元
content:
日前，工业和信息化部发布2026年上半年我国数字产业运行情况。数据显示，上半年，我国数字产业加快发展，总体呈现向优向好发展态势，业务收入保持较快增长，盈利水平大幅改善，出口需求保持旺盛，核心技术加快创新突破，新领域新赛道发展动能增强，为稳定经济增长、培育发展新质生产力、赋能千行百业数智转型提供了有力支撑。
发展质效稳步提升。上半年，数字产业收入稳中有进，实现收入20.71万亿元，同比增长13.6％，增速同比加快4.1个百分点，环比一季度加快0.7个百分点。受国内人工智能需求增长和出口增势强劲双重拉动，数字产业盈利水平持续改善，实现利润总额1.79万亿元，同比增长19.3％，增速较上年同期加快10.3个百分点。收入利润率达8.6％，较上年同期提升0.7个百分点。
重点区域、重点集群带动有力。东部大省（市）产业集聚态势显著，广东、江苏、北京、上海、浙江等数字产业收入前10大省（市）合计完成业务收入17.21万亿元，同比增长13.2％，占全国总量的83.1％，占比较上年同期提升0.3个百分点，对全国数字产业收入增长贡献率达87％。中部地区增速加快，实现数字产业收入2.86万亿元，同比增长28.3％，较上年同期加快18.7个百分点，高于全国14.7个百分点，其中安徽、湖北增速领先。产业集群蓬勃发展，截至目前，围绕集成电路、人工智能等数字产业领域，各地累计培育建设16个国家级先进制造业集群，依托集群培育一批骨干数字企业，这些企业成为推进技术创新、促进产业高端升级、塑造集群竞争优势的关键支撑。
数字基础设施持续优化升级。“双千兆”网络建设提质升级，截至6月底，5G基站达到510.2万个，具备千兆网络服务能力的10G PON端口达3286万个，5G-A商用网络加快建设应用，5G RedCap基站数达224.7万个，万兆光网在小区、工厂、园区等场景试点部署。算力基础设施体系加速完善，我国智能算力规模达2185 EFLOPS（FP16），同比增长177％，全国算力设施整体上架率达71.4％，建成万卡以上智算设施52个。融合应用效能持续释放，建成5G行业虚拟专网超8万个，5G、千兆光网应用已融入94个国民经济大类。全国“5G+工业互联网”在建项目超2.6万个，建成1260家分类分级、特色鲜明的5G工厂。
数字制造业继续保持“量效”齐升。上半年，生产保持较快增长，电子行业增加值同比增长14.8％，增速较一季度加快1.2个百分点，高于整体工业9.4个百分点。其中，电子器件、电子元件及专用材料、智能消费设备行业增速较快。效益显著提升，规模以上电子信息制造业实现营业收入12.15万亿元，同比增长17.8％；实现利润总额7036亿元，同比增长66％。其中，集成电路、计算机整机制造、电子专用材料行业的利润拉动作用最大。
数字服务业保持稳步增长。信息通信业总体运行平稳，按上年不变单价计算的电信业务总量同比增长8.3％，增速较上年同期提高0.6个百分点。软件和信息技术服务业业务收入同比增长9.5％，其中，软件产品收入同比增长6.9％，信息技术服务收入同比增长10.4％。规模以上互联网企业业务收入同比增长10.1％，增速较上年同期加快7个百分点，利润总额同比增长16.6％。　（布轩）

title: 今年服贸会着力打造“服务贸易发展系列论坛”品牌
content:
26日，2026年服务贸易发展系列论坛主题论坛媒体通气会在京举办。记者从会上获悉，2026年服贸会论坛会议将着力打造“服务贸易发展系列论坛”品牌，相关单位将举办190余场论坛会议和洽谈推介活动。其中，主题论坛共计15场，覆盖文旅、医疗、建筑、数字贸易、绿色发展等重点领域。
服贸会组委会相关负责人介绍，2026年服贸会论坛会议下设开放融合、合作共赢、数智创新、绿色发展四大核心板块。每个板块的论坛会议按照权威性和专业性，可归类为主题论坛或专题论坛。
主题论坛是服贸会立足国际性、综合型定位打造的核心专业交流活动，15场主题论坛通过设置高端对话、标准发布、成果首发、项目签约、商贸对接等环节，将发挥趋势引领、规则输出、资源聚合的优势作用。
其中，开放融合板块包括服务贸易发展论坛、数字贸易发展趋势和前沿论坛、人力资源服务业开放协作与融合发展大会3场论坛，旨在聚焦区域协同、规则议定、跨境合作、走出去等领域的对话与协作，促进高水平对外开放，构建互利共赢新格局。
合作共赢板块包括2026首都国际医学大会、2026国际消费趋势大会暨服务消费高质量发展论坛、2026前沿科技大会3场论坛，将推动产业链上下游协同与跨行业资源整合，突出金融、科技、医疗、服务消费等领域跨界合作，构建“政产学研用”协同生态，打通从技术研发到产业应用的全链条。
数智创新板块包括2026电子商务大会、2026世界旅游合作与发展大会、2026全球服务贸易企业家大会、建筑业全产业链数智创新论坛、2026雄安数字贸易创新发展大会5场论坛，关注数字经济、人工智能、大数据、新一代信息技术等前沿技术对产业升级、社会治理、贸易形态的驱动作用，旨在推动数字技术与实体经济深度融合。
绿色发展板块包括第五届气象经济论坛、第三届绿色经济发展论坛、2026总部经济大会暨（第六届）楼宇经济论坛、2026丝路金桥国际合作大会——数字城市发展与智慧绿洲建设论坛4场论坛。该板块旨在围绕“双碳”目标，聚焦产业绿色低碳转型路径、零碳实践与可持续解决方案，助力实现经济社会与生态环境协调发展。（记者 孙明源）

title: 我国首次实现地月双向高速激光通信
content:
地月“信息高速路”通了！记者26日从中国科学院空间应用工程与技术中心获悉，我国地月激光通信试验任务取得重要突破，成功在超过40万公里的地月距离上建立起双向激光链路，首次实现地月双向高速激光通信。这标志着我国空间激光通信正式从近地轨道迈入地月空间。
空间激光通信是一种利用激光传输信息的通信方式，具有带宽大、速度快、方向准、保密性好等优势。但距离越远，技术挑战越大。中国科学院空间应用工程与技术中心研究员杨雷说：“深空激光通信一直扛着三座大山：距离动辄几十万公里，光束极难精准对准；信号传到地面时已经弱得几乎收不到；传输速度也一直提不上去。”
首先难在“瞄准”。地月间通信好比在40万公里外，将一束极细的光线精准穿过一个高速运动的“针孔”。发射端哪怕出现极其微小的角度偏差，抵达目标附近时也会产生数公里的位置误差。为此，科研团队想出了一套新办法：综合考虑卫星轨道、望远镜安装误差、大气折射、激光飞行时间等各种因素，让天上的卫星和地面的望远镜在运动中始终对准，确保激光能精准照到预定位置。
解决了“瞄准难”，新的问题又来了：激光跑完40万公里到达地面时，已经微弱到只剩几个光子。地面望远镜能收到的信号少得可怜，而月光、星光、城市灯光还会混进来捣乱。为此，团队用上了能探测单个光子的“超灵敏探测器”，并开发了一套复杂的信号识别算法，硬是从海量噪声中把有效信号“捞”了出来。这就好像在千里之外喧嚣嘈杂的闹市中，准确听清一根针落地的声音。
信号能收到了，传输速度也得跟上。团队通过技术攻关，大幅提升了数据处理效率。此次试验初步实现上行1.25Mbps（兆比特每秒）、下行100Mbps的通信速率。杨雷举例说：“以一幅8K月面高清图像为例，用传统5Mbps微波链路下传约需4到5分钟；换成百Mbps激光通信后，只要约12秒。”
“目前地月之间的‘信息高速路’已经打通，未来我们将会获取到更多、更有原创价值的科学数据。”杨雷表示，相关技术还将为我国载人登月、月球科研站建设和深空探测提供高速信息传输的新手段。（记者 陆成宽）

title: 湖北一智能网联和电动汽车产业园开工建设
content:
园区位于湖北省汉川市马口镇，距离武汉经开区核心产业板块约30分钟车程，规划面积1.84平方公里，按照首开区365亩、中期2753亩、远期10000亩的三级梯次开发建设。
图片来源：武汉经开区
8月25日，湖北武汉经开区智能网联和电动汽车产业园（西区）揭牌并开工建设，武汉经开-汉川共建区、湖北车谷金马投资有限公司同步揭牌。
智汽园（西区）由武汉经开区与汉川市合作共建，是武汉都市圈发展重点合作园区，与武汉经开区智汽园同园同链。园区位于汉川市马口镇，距离武汉经开区核心产业板块约30分钟车程，规划面积1.84平方公里，按照首开区365亩、中期2753亩、远期10000亩的三级梯次开发建设。其中，首开区总投资约15亿元，分两期建设，一期规划建设生产厂房、研发办公大楼、生活服务等配套设施，打造综合配套完整的产业园区。
在产业规划上，智汽园（西区）将聚焦新能源与智能网联汽车零部件产业，重点发展智能座舱功能材料、汽车内外饰、电气系统零部件、车身轻量化材料、底盘系统结构件五大核心领域；同步布局先进材料、汽车半导体、工业机器人零部件、新型储能设备、数智家居五大同源新兴产业，全力构建整车与零部件协同、制造与研发联动、产业与创新融合共进的“汽车+”产业新生态。

title: 2026年1—7月全国电力市场交易电量同比增长23.4%-索比光伏网
content:
2026年7月，全国各电力交易机构完成交易电量7404亿千瓦时，同比增长18.5%。从交易范围看，省内交易电量5491亿千瓦时，同比增长19.0%；跨省跨区交易电量1913亿千瓦时，同比增长17.2%。从交易品种看，中长期交易电量6786亿千瓦时；现货交易电量618亿千瓦时。绿电交易电量277亿千瓦时，同比增长2.7%。电网企业市场化代理购电电量872亿千瓦时。
2026年1—7月，全国各电力交易机构累计完成交易电量44252亿千瓦时，同比增长23.4%。从交易范围看，省内交易电量34626亿千瓦时，同比增长26.8%；跨省跨区交易电量9626亿千瓦时，同比增长12.5%。从交易品种看，中长期交易电量39354亿千瓦时；现货交易电量4898亿千瓦时。绿电交易电量1918亿千瓦时，同比增长5.6%。电网企业市场化代理购电电量4857亿千瓦时。

title: 福建漳州梳理滞后项目清单，推进集中式光伏电站项目建设-索比光伏网
content:
为加快推进全市集中式光伏电站开发建设，破解滞后项目建设难题，漳州市发改委于近日赴漳浦、云霄、东山等县区开展实地督导调研。督导组现场排查项目建设堵点，组织属地发改部门、项目业主、相关乡镇召开攻坚座谈会，深入分析项目工期滞后原因，分类制定差异化处置方案和攻坚举措，明确下一阶段重点工作任务。
一是精准梳理台账，分类攻坚推进。各县区发改部门要全面梳理滞后项目清单，聚焦用地报批、土地流转、送出工程等关键环节，区分客观要素制约、外部协调难题、企业主观推进不力等各类问题。对具备施工条件的项目，针对性制定专项推进方案，逐项疏通建设堵点、破除落地障碍;对无法实施或无法按期推进的项目，按规定及时分类处置。各项目业主单位要切实履行建设主体责任，配齐工作力量、强化内部统筹，全力提速项目建设，力争早日竣工投用、发挥效能。
二是优化服务保障，健全推进机制。要发挥发改部门牵头统筹作用，联动属地乡镇及自然资源、林业、水利等职能部门，主动靠前服务，搭建政企常态化沟通渠道，打破部门协作壁垒，畅通项目审批、要素保障、并网投产等关键流程。实行全过程跟踪督办、闭环管理，倒逼滞后项目加快建设，抢抓施工窗口期，全力追赶既定建设进度。
三是严守安全底线，筑牢建设根基。坚持“人民至上、生命至上”理念，压紧压实光伏项目安全生产责任，健全施工现场安全管理制度，将安全管控贯穿土建施工、设备安装、线路架设全流程，常态化开展安全隐患排查整治，守牢新能源领域安全生产底线。
下一步，漳州市发改委将依托项目管理“44336工作机制”，持续强化统筹协调，深化部门协同联动，压实企业主体责任、属地管理责任和行业监管责任，推动全市集中式光伏电站项目落地投产、并网发电，为加快建设现代化滨海城市提供坚实能源保障。

title: 粤发改能源〔2026〕267号解读｜广东绿电直连新规 源荷比例考核与交易规则全解析-索比光伏网
content:
2026年8月14日，广东省发展改革委、省能源局正式对外发布《关于有序推动我省绿电直连发展有关事项的通知》(粤发改能源〔2026〕267号)，自发布之日起施行。作为全国外贸规模与用电负荷双第一省份的省级落地细则，本次政策核心是将国家层面倡导的绿电直连模式，转化为带量化考核、带惩罚机制、带退出通道的闭环管理体系，通过三条刚性数字杠锁定“以荷定源、自用为主” 的核心定位，彻底结束了绿电直连“概念大于实操”的阶段。
本次新规构建了全流程约束体系：核心设置三道比例门槛，新能源年自发自用电量占总可用发电量比例不低于60%，占总用电量比例不低于30%(2030年前提至35%)，上网电量占总可用发电量比例原则上不超过20%;明确总可用发电量按“装机容量 × 年发电利用小时数标杆”计算，而非实际发电量，直接堵住“限发凑比例”的操作空间。惩罚机制同步落地：上网电量超20% 上限且因项目自身原因确需上送的，按现货市场出清价格下限(-0.05元/千瓦时)结算，超发面临倒付电费的刚性约束。
收益与定位同步重构：参与绿电直连的项目视为自愿退出机制电价，存量项目0.453元/千瓦时、增量分布式项目0.36元/千瓦时的保底收益需主动放弃;配建新型储能不得作为独立主体参与电力市场交易，价值定位从峰谷价差套利转向保障自用率达标、平滑上网波动的合规工具;明确电网企业不得参与投资运营，电源与负荷非同一主体的，申报前必须签订多年期购电协议，“先锁定负荷再启动项目”成为硬性准入门槛。同时设置动态退出机制，5年内累计3年运行指标不达标须主动申请退出，纳入清单后1年未开工直接调出项目清单。
政策精准锚定四类核心场景：重点支持出口外向型企业、国家和省零碳园区改革试点、算力设施、绿色氢氨醇新兴产业，与广东应对欧盟碳边境调节机制、推进零碳园区建设、布局未来产业的现实需求高度契合。整体来看，广东绿电直连已从政策概念进入可落地、可考核的实操阶段，行业竞争逻辑正式从“资源优先”转向“负荷优先、运营优先”。
为帮助出口制造企业、园区运营方、新能源投资商、售电服务商全面吃透新规规则、测算成本收益、评估项目适配性、抢抓10月申报窗口，索比光伏网结合政策原文与广东电力市场运行数据，推出深度解读报告，覆盖规则逐条拆解、源荷比例测算工具、成本收益模型、申报流程指引、分场景落地方案、风险避坑指南等全维度内容。
以下为报告节选内容，完整成本收益测算模板、申报材料清单、四类场景落地方案、源荷匹配测算工具、退出机制应对指南，可扫码跳转小程序查看全文完整版报告。

title: 100GW光伏计划发布！他们将不再需要进口石油-索比光伏网
content:
印度尼西亚总统普拉博沃宣布启动建设100吉瓦太阳能发电能力的计划，目标在三年内完成。该计划于巴厘岛正式启动，总统强调“这不是开玩笑”，并将之作为国家能源转型核心举措。
截至今年4月，印尼总装机容量约108吉瓦，其中太阳能仅占1.5吉瓦，煤炭仍是主力电源;可再生能源(含水电、地热)整体占比为17.9%。若100吉瓦光伏全部建成，太阳能将成为该国电力供应主体。
印尼能源与矿产资源部长巴赫利尔·拉哈达利亚指出，项目全面建成后，每年可节省能源补贴支出739000亿印尼盾(约合人民币280亿元)。印尼目前为石油净进口国，国内燃料消费依赖大规模补贴。
普拉博沃表示，配合现有地热资源、新发现天然气田及提高石油开采量，100吉瓦太阳能装机将使印尼不再需要进口任何石油。其8月中旬国情咨文提出，仅2026年就计划新增30吉瓦光伏装机，包括在每个村庄建设一座1兆瓦电站，并借此提前关停13吉瓦柴油发电厂。
启动仪式涵盖14个光伏项目：2个已运营、6个在建、6个待投资。官方披露这14个项目总投资额为135万亿印尼盾(约合76.2亿美元)。巴赫利尔透露，实现100吉瓦总目标预计需730亿美元投资，并同步在全国部署电池储能系统以应对夜间供电缺口。
印尼国家电力公司承诺以每千瓦时5至6美分价格收购光伏电力，高于火电采购价(3至4美分)。

title: 吉林油田45万千瓦风光发电项目即将全面投产-索比光伏网
content:
近日，吉林油田35万千瓦风电项目通过国家电网吉林省电力有限公司专家组并网验收，45万千瓦风光发电项目即将全面投产，吉林油田持续转型升级再添力量。
吉林油田45万千瓦风光发电项目是新能源重点建设工程。整个项目规划总容量45万千瓦。其中，10万千瓦光伏发电项目已于今年2月份投运;35万千瓦风电项目新建220千伏升压站1座，安装单机容量
6.25兆瓦风力发电机组56台，于5月份吊装完成。目前，各设备并网前调试工作已全部完成，相关生产准备就绪，已具备并网发电条件。
吉林油田依托吉林西部得天独厚的风能、太阳能资源禀赋，统筹土地资源、电网消纳条件，继15万千瓦自消纳风光发电项目、昂格55万千瓦风电项目建成投运后，进一步在乾安地区统筹推进新能源重点建设项目，即45万千瓦风光发电项目。该项目充分盘活了油田闲置土地、低效井场、排涝区、废弃场站等空间，采用“光伏+风电”复合布局，所发绿电规模外输，通过国网统一调度实现跨区域互济，从而为千家万户安全可靠用电提供坚实保障。
2025年7月9日，该项目正式启动开工建设。吉林油田新能源生产一线广大干部员工克服任务繁重、气候多变、协调困难等多重挑战，上下一心，协同攻坚，全力以赴保安全保进度保工期。
“进入5月以来，伴随着整体吊装作业的完成，我们就开始备战验收工作了”，吉林油田新能源公司副经理刘晓光介绍说，为保障验收工作效率，吉林油田新能源事业部、新能源公司派驻专人与国网省公司相关部门协调，高效完成了并网试运行申请等各项工作，做好了并网验收准备。
据了解，该项目投产后，将形成大规模稳定绿色电力供给，持续扩大油田自产绿电规模，进一步降低外购网电比例，不断压降生产环节碳排放，实现老油田经济效益和环保效益的“双赢”。

辽源市人民政府关于支持辽源高新区建设国家级零碳园区的实施意见
辽府发〔2026〕6号
各县、区人民政府，辽源高新区管委会，市政府各委、办、局，各直属机构，驻市各中省直单位：
为深入贯彻落实国家、省关于碳达峰碳中和重大战略决策和国家级零碳园区建设部署要求，积极稳妥推进辽源高新区国家级零碳园区建设，探索资源枯竭型城市绿色转型新路径，根据《国家发展改革委 工业和信息化部 国家能源局关于开展零碳园区建设的通知》(发改环资〔2025〕910号)精神，结合我市实际，制定本实施意见。
紧密围绕国家级零碳园区建设标准与重点任务，立足辽源高新区纺织袜业、高精铝加工、医药化工、新能源汽车配套、现代服务业“4+1”产业格局，以能源结构清洁化、产业发展低碳化、资源利用节约化、基础设施绿色化、运行管理智慧化为核心，系统构建绿色能源供给、产业低碳转型、资源循环利用、智慧能碳管控体系。力争到2028年底，园区绿色能源结构全面建成，绿色低碳产业体系初步形成，“以绿制绿”发展模式有效运行，单位能耗碳排放、清洁能源消费占比等指标全面达到国家标准，成功通过国家级零碳园区验收。将辽源高新区打造成为符合国家标准、具有示范引领意义的零碳发展高地和产业低碳转型标杆，为资源枯竭型城市能源转型、产业升级提供可复制、可推广的“辽源方案”。
(一)加快能源结构清洁化转型。
以保障能源安全稳定供应为前提，全力推进天楹风光储氢氨醇一体化、辽矿增量配电网风电、园区分布式光伏等重点项目建设，规模化开发厂房屋顶光伏。加快构建以新能源为主体的园区供电形态，做强增量配电网，积极探索推广“绿电直供”模式，为园区内出口型、外向型企业提供具有竞争力的绿色电力，打造服务长春现代化都市圈企业的低碳要素保障基地。构建“电、热、冷、气、氢”多能互补系统，合理布局电化学、重力、氢能等多类型储能设施，提升系统调节能力与绿电消纳水平。积极推进工业余热、生物质、地热能等清洁能源在供热领域的多元化应用。到2028年，园区清洁能源消费占比达到90%以上，绿电供给能力明显提升，成为“长春研发、都市圈制造”产业协同格局中重要的绿色能源支撑点。(市发展改革委、市工业和信息化局、市能源局、国网辽源供电公司、辽源矿业集团、辽源高新区管委会按职责分工负责。以下各项任务均需辽源高新区管委会落实，不再重复列出。)
(二)推进产业体系低碳化升级。
支持园区依托风光资源与“绿氢+”核心优势，构建“风光发电—绿电制氢—绿色化工”全产业链，打造“以绿制绿”发展模式。围绕现有纺织袜业、高精铝加工、医药化工、新能源汽车配套等主导产业，实施节能降碳改造和能效对标行动，推广先进工艺与高效设备，推动重点行业能效水平整体提升。聚焦主导产业实施精准产业链招商，大力引进上下游配套企业、绿色低碳关联项目，着力补齐产业链短板、延伸价值链链条，集聚上下游企业集群化、低碳化协同发展。重点围绕汽车轻量化材料、新能源电池、新能源汽车关键零部件等领域，深化与汽车及轨道列车龙头企业合作，吸引其绿色供应链企业落户，建设服务一汽、辐射长春现代化都市圈的核心低碳配套基地。积极承接长春现代化都市圈数字经济、低空经济等新质生产力配套环节，加快建设算力中心，推动“绿电”与“算力”结合，发展绿色数字产业及配套服务业。支持企业争创智能工厂、未来工厂、绿色工厂、零碳工厂，三年内力争新增智能工厂(数字化车间)2家以上，培育省级以上“专精特新”中小企业3家以上，省级绿色工厂、零碳工厂6家以上。对园区内所有规上企业开展节能监察和节能诊断服务工作。到2028年底，园区企业产出产品单位能耗100%，达到或优于二级能耗限额标准，单位能耗碳排放降至0.29吨二氧化碳/吨标煤。(市发展改革委、市工业和信息化局、市生态环境局、市商务局、市政务服务和数字化局、市能源局按职责分工负责。)
(三)强化资源利用节约化循环。
严格落实国土空间规划，优化土地利用结构，盘活存量工业用地，提升土地集约利用水平。全面推进工业余热、固体废弃物、水资源三大核心资源的节约集约与循环利用。统筹回收工业余热用于生产生活供热，提升余热综合利用效率;加快建设资源循环利用产业园，健全一般工业固体废弃物回收、储运、资源化利用体系，推动废旧纺织、废旧塑料、动力电池、废弃电器电子产品、风光发电淘汰件等循环利用，探索固废跨区域协同处置与资源化利用机制;完善园区水资源循环利用体系。到2028年，园区工业余热、余冷、余压综合利用率达到50%，工业固体废弃物综合利用率达到80%，工业用水重复利用率达到80%，成为长春现代化都市圈重要的资源循环利用节点。(市发展改革委、市工业和信息化局、市自然资源局、市生态环境局、市住房城乡建设局按职责分工负责。)
(四)推动基础设施绿色化改造。
系统推进园区供电、供热、供水、污水处理等基础设施的绿色化、智能化改造与建设，标准与长春现代化都市圈核心城市看齐。对园区既有建筑开展节能改造，新建建筑全面执行绿色建筑标准，加快构建园区绿色交通体系，完善电动汽车充电网络、加氢站等配套设施布局，推广电动、氢能等清洁能源车辆。积极对接长春现代化都市圈交通网络布局，谋划园区与长春、四平等地的绿色货运专线，探索多式联运发展。开展多领域降碳示范，打造零碳建筑、绿色交通等应用场景。(市发展改革委、市住房城乡建设局、市交通运输局、市交发集团按职责分工负责。)
(五)提升运行管理智慧化水平。
支持建设覆盖园区、贯通企业的智慧能碳一体化管理平台，实现能耗与碳排放数据的实时监测、精准核算与智能分析。运用物联网、大数据、人工智能等技术，集成能源调度、碳资产管理、虚拟电厂运营、碳足迹溯源等关键功能。推动平台与省、市碳监测管理平台以及长春现代化都市圈相关智慧系统对接，探索区域碳数据互联互通，提升管理效能与协同能力。鼓励平台运营方开发标准化、模块化服务产品，为园区内外企业提供碳管理服务。到2028年，建成符合国家标准的碳排放核算、监测、核查体系，提供多维度能碳分析报告，提出能耗异常预警、减排潜力评估、碳效优化建议等决策支持，形成园区能源体系智慧管控中枢。(市发展改革委、市工业和信息化局、市生态环境局、市政务服务和数字化局按职责分工负责。)
(六)拓展技术创新协同化应用。
健全“政产学研用”协同创新机制，深化与高校院所开展校地合作，支持园区企业联合共建技术创新中心、中试中心等研发平台。聚焦新能源高效利用、节能降碳、碳捕集利用、氢能储运、固废资源化等关键技术开展联合攻关。加快组建辽源市氢能产业综合研究院，深化与吉林省氢能产业综合研究院合作。加大创新主体培育力度，打造一批低碳零碳负碳技术示范应用场景，加速先进适用技术成果转化落地。(市教育局、市科技局、市工业和信息化局、市生态环境局按职责分工负责。)
(七)深化要素保障市场化配置。
鼓励园区及企业依法依规开展合同能源管理、能源费用托管等市场化节能模式。支持以虚拟电厂等形式整合可调节负荷资源，参与省内及区域电力辅助服务市场与绿电交易。依托吉林省电力现货市场交易平台，指导相关企业开展绿证、绿电交易，满足园区内外企业绿色消费需求。探索碳资产开发与运营管理。鼓励各类市场主体参与零碳园区投资、建设、运营。鼓励企业通过国家工业产融平台填报项目融资需求，结合零碳工厂建设资金使用特点，引导银行机构提供多元化、适配性强的信贷产品，按需保障零碳园区项目融资需求。大力发展绿色金融，有效发挥银行机构绿色金融评估激励作用，鼓励金融机构加大高质量绿色金融服务供给。落实好有利于绿色低碳产业发展的税收政策。(市发展改革委、市财政局、市能源局、市税务局、辽源金融监管分局、中国人民银行辽源市分行按职责分工负责。)
(八)优化零碳管理标准化服务。
将项目碳减排效果作为节能审查的重要考量因素。探索弹性年期出让、先租后让等灵活土地供应方式，保障绿色产业项目用地需求。全面对标长春现代化都市圈一流营商环境，在政务服务“跨市通办”、知识产权保护、市场监管等方面加强协同，提升园区综合服务竞争力。实施积极的人才招引与培养政策，加强与都市圈内人才资源互动，强化柔性引才力度，为零碳园区建设提供智力支撑。(市发展改革委、市教育局、市科技局、市人力资源社会保障局、市自然资源局、市市场监管局、市政务服务和数字化局按职责分工负责。)
成立辽源高新区零碳园区建设工作专班，统筹推进园区建设各项工作，明确各专班成员单位职责分工，凝聚合力推动任务落地;持续强化要素保障、夯实建设根基，积极争取上级各类资金支持，统筹落实市级财政配套资金，优先保障绿色低碳项目用能、用水、环境容量、土地等要素供给，落实人才引育举措，撬动金融与社会资本参与项目建设，实行项目全过程闭环管理，及时疏通建设堵点，全力保障园区按期达标并通过国家创建验收;持续加大宣传推广力度，系统梳理总结能源转型、产业升级等领域典型经验，依托多种渠道宣传建设成效，做好成果向上申报，普及绿色低碳理念，凝聚企业、公众多方力量，营造全社会共建零碳园区的良好氛围。

title: 澳大利亚推进78亿澳元多晶硅项目，计划2030年前投产-索比光伏网
content:
Quinbrook基础设施合伙公司与汤斯维尔市议会签署谅解备忘录，推动位于澳大利亚昆士兰州的 Northern Quartz Campus 多晶硅项目进入下一阶段。该项目预计将在建设和运营阶段创造最多 1,200 个就业岗位，目标于 2030 年实现商业运营。
汤斯维尔市议会与Quinbrook签署谅解备忘录，推动昆士兰州多晶硅制造项目。（配图来源：Juan Alejandro Bernal/Shutterstock.com）
汤斯维尔市议会与 Quinbrook 旗下项目公司 Solquartz 近期签署谅解备忘录，以推动位于昆士兰州 Lansdown 生态工业园区的 Northern Quartz Campus 项目。该项目拟建设成为澳大利亚首个从石英砂到硅材料的一体化制造园区，并将澳大利亚石英砂加工为用于光伏、半导体及其他先进技术领域的高附加值硅材料。
该项目投资额为 78 亿澳元，Quinbrook此前已获得汤斯维尔市议会对项目用地的有条件批准。此次双方签署了谅解备忘录，并计划在 2026 年底前最终签署项目开发与基础设施协议。
项目开发与基础设施协议将明确市议会在基础设施交付方面的责任，以及 Solquartz 对项目第一阶段基础设施成本的出资安排。Northern Quartz Campus 项目预计将在建设和运营阶段创造最多 1,200 个就业岗位，商业运营预计于 2030 年启动。
Quinbrook高级副总裁 Vignesh Bandi 表示，这份谅解备忘录是推动 Lansdown 融合可再生能源、储能与制造业的重要一步。他说：“如此规模的工业项目有赖于配套基础设施、政府支持和私人资本协同发挥作用。”
汤斯维尔市市长 Nick Dametto 表示，这项协议标志着 Lansdown 正在推进最终签署首份项目开发与基础设施协议。他说：“经过多年的规划和前期准备，Lansdown 正从概念阶段走向建设阶段。”
Quinbrook还在推进位于 Lansdown、与 Northern Quartz Campus 同址布局的 Supernode North 电池储能系统项目。该长时储能项目旨在支持高耗能制造业，并帮助释放园区更多电网容量。

Ecomara is ready for commercialisation following inshore trials
Encomara's Squid connection system reached commercialisation on August

title: US declares ‘national emergency’ amid fears of cyber attacks on BESS, power sector – Batteries International
content: The US has declared a cyber security national emergency in a bid to protect battery energy storage systems and the wider power infrastructure from Trojan horse-style attacks. BESS and UPS systems are specifically included in an extensive list of potential cyber warfare targets among bulk-power system electrical equipment (BPSEE) produced abroad — which the US fears are at heightened risk. The energy systems cyber alert was outlined in an executive order signed by US president Donald Trump on August 26. The order — covered by the International Emergency Economic Powers Act and the National Emergencies Act — largely prohibits certain foreign-made equipment from being bought or installed in the US, including critical software and digital capabilities. BPSEE covers a wide range of equipment and installations including power stations, backup power systems and grid-connected inverters. Trump said energy secretary Chris Wright will now work with cabinet colleagues and others to identify BPSEE that may pose risks and draw up a safeguards action list, with a particular focus on equipment linked to US-designated foreign entities of concern (FEOC). ‘Supply disruption’ “Since my first term, the threat to the US regarding foreign supply of bulk-power system electric equipment has become even more acute,” Trump said. “The rapid growth of advanced manufacturing, datacentres, artificial intelligence and defence production has increased the nation’s dependence on abundant, reliable electricity and magnified the consequences of a successful attack or supply disruption on the bulk-power system.” The president’s directive follows a report issued last month by the US Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA), which warned as solar and energy storage continues to expand, cybersecurity protections become increasingly important to support grid reliability and resilience. SEIA cited a 2022 ransomware attack against the IT infrastructure of a wind turbine manufacturer in Germany, followed a year later by an attack that saw a third-party service provider lose remote data monitoring capabilities for around 2,000 turbines. ‘New risks loom’ Separately, in 2025, Poland successfully thwarted what officials described as the largest cyberattack on its energy infrastructure in years, SEIA said. Emerging technologies, including the deployment of advanced artificial intelligence models to optimise energy assets, create new cybersecurity risks and expand the attack surface. The association revealed it now runs a monthly cybersecurity working group dedicated to sharing latest cybersecurity policy, threat information and defence tactics for solar and energy storage systems. In the UK, the government confirmed that a power plant was shut down during a cyber attack in July 2026. Reliable media sources reported that the attack was carried out by hackers affiliated to the Iranian regime. The UK government declined to give details but said the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero and National Cyber Security Centre have since warned power companies to be on their guard. EU cyber concerns A white paper published in December 2025, by global consulting firm the Brattle Group and US-based international operational technology cybersecurity specialists Dragos, said experts agreed that US infrastructure security concerns would likely lead to more stringent security measures towards FEOCs. In terms of the European Union, the white paper said the bloc’s Cyber Resilience Act, which goes into effect in 2027, will certify every product for sale in the EU meets European cybersecurity standards. However, while experts agreed that consistent, EU-wide policy was the correct method to approach grid cybersecurity, the white paper warned that member states without the same agenda or policies would create a lack of harmonisation among operators on the same grid. “Diverging rules between European countries create vulnerability to the highly interconnected European power network, resulting in higher regulatory compliance costs for investors and differing levels of cybersecurity implementation in the European internal energy market.” The white paper said BESS deployment over the next five years is expected to grow at 30% annually in the US, 45% in the EU and 20–25% across Japan, South Korea, Southeast Asia and India. “As BESS deployment accelerates, it is important that the increasing role of batteries in facilitating efficient clean energy and grid reliability is not undermined by cybersecurity vulnerabilities. “Conversely, BESS additions with strong cyber protection will contribute to lower levels of vulnerability for the grid as a whole.” Image credit: Envato The post US declares ‘national emergency’ amid fears of cyber attacks on BESS, power sector appeared first on Batteries International .

title: Cummins Wins Its Largest BESS Contract for US Data Center
content:
Stationary Batteries
Battery Manufacturing
Battery News
The 5MWh lithium iron phosphate system will manage AI-driven load fluctuations and help address community concerns about diesel generator noise and emissions.
August 27, 2026
3 Min Read
Cummins' LFP battery system
At a Glance
Cummins' largest BESS deployment will support AI-driven power fluctuations at a major U.S. data center facility
The 5MWh lithium iron phosphate system offers a quieter, cleaner alternative to diesel backup generators
Battery storage helps data centers overcome community opposition related to noise pollution and carbon emissions.
Cummins Inc. has secured a contract to supply battery energy storage systems (BESS) for a large U.S. data center project, marking the company's largest BESS deployment to date. The project underscores growing demand for energy storage solutions capable of managing AI-driven power fluctuations in hyperscale computing environments.
The BESS installation will support utility-defined requirements for managing load fluctuations associated with artificial intelligence workloads. The system is designed to rapidly charge or discharge to reduce demand spikes, improve power quality, and maintain stable load profiles at utility interconnection points. This capability helps mitigate the oscillating power demands characteristic of AI processing while enhancing ride-through performance during grid disturbances.
BESS as a path around community opposition
Data center projects increasingly face fierce community pushback over environmental concerns. According to a
Gallup survey
, 70% of Americans oppose data center construction in their area, with half of opponents citing excessive resource use and 16% mentioning pollution concerns including noise, air, and water pollution. Communities from
Chandler, Arizona to Greenbrier, Arkansas
have complained about constant humming from cooling systems and diesel generators, with residents reporting headaches, sleep disturbances, and hypertension from 24/7 noise.
Related:
7 Residential Battery Storage Systems Worth Buying in 2026
BESS technology is emerging as a solution that addresses many of these objections. Unlike diesel generators, battery storage systems operate with minimal noise—typically comparable to an HVAC unit—and produce zero on-site emissions during operation, eliminating the need for fuel storage and the associated pollution.
Studies show
that adding BESS can reduce a data center's overall carbon emissions by up to 60% when it displaces diesel usage. Major tech companies including Microsoft, Google, and Meta have initiated programs to replace diesel generators with BESS, with Microsoft committing to eliminate diesel by 2030. The lack of noise and emissions means
batteries can be deployed in urban or sensitive areas with far less community opposition
compared to diesel gensets.
However, BESS deployments face their own challenges.
Community concerns about fire safety and long-term environmental impacts
have emerged as deployment accelerates, making some projects harder to approve. Modern BESS designs address these concerns through advanced thermal management, fire suppression systems, and environmental safeguards built into the system architecture.
Related:
Understanding Base Power’s role in energy storage solutions
Cummins expands its power portfolio
The contract reflects Cummins' broader strategy to support data center infrastructure with diverse power solutions. According to Jenny Bush, president of Cummins' Power Systems business, the company now offers customers a range of options from diesel standby and natural gas prime power to BESS and integrated microgrid solutions.
"As demand for data center capacity continues to grow, Cummins is well positioned to support customers with a broad portfolio of power solutions," Bush said. "This project reinforces our commitment to helping customers build reliable, resilient and increasingly sustainable power infrastructure."
For data center developers facing grid constraints, lengthening interconnection queues, and rising energy costs, BESS is becoming a critical power enabler. The technology can accelerate deployment timelines, enhance resilience, and optimize available power capacity—particularly important as AI workloads drive unprecedented energy demands. Cummins' utility-scale BESS solution can be deployed as a bridge-to-grid solution, integrated with backup power systems, or incorporated into broader microgrid architectures. The flexibility allows customers to maximize available grid capacity, manage peak demand, and meet utility load-management requirements.
Related:
Advanced Testing Methods in Battery Manufacturing BESS Explained
Technical specifications
Cummins' BESS for data center applications features:
5MWh nominal capacity
Lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery chemistry
Liquid cooling thermal management
Flexible DC block architecture compatible with multiple power conversion systems (PCS) and energy management systems (EMS)
Bridge-to-grid ready with integration capability for diesel and natural gas generators
Compliance with UL 9540A, UL 9540, UL 1973, NFPA 855, NFPA 68, IEEE 1547, and UL 1741 SA/SB standards
The system is designed specifically for hyperscale workloads and resilient operation in demanding data center environments. Cummins launched its BESS solutions in May 2025, backed by more than 100 years of power generation expertise.

title: Schneider Electric home EV charger uses smart load management
content:
Charging
Automotive & Mobility
SmartAmp tech dynamically adjusts charging speed based on real-time household energy use to prevent overloads.
August 28, 2026
2 Min Read
Schneider Electric's new Schneider Charge residential EV charger features built-in SmartAmp technology that automatically adjusts charging speed based on real-time household energy use, helping homeowners add Level 2 charging with less complexity.
Schneider Electric
At a Glance
The charger delivers up to 11.5 kW AC power and includes OCPP 1.6 compliance for grid programs.
Installation is simplified with built-in load management, eliminating need for separate monitoring devices.
Schneider Electric Launches Home EV Charger
Electric component supplier Schneider is expanding beyond household plugs and
receptacles
EV chargers
with the announcement of
Schneider Charge
, an SAE Level 2 AC home EV charger.
Schneider Charge Pro
is the company’s existing commercial Level 2 EV charger for multi-unit dwellings, workplaces, fleets, and destination charging.
This new charger’s purpose is to simplify EV ownership for homeowners who aren’t interested in spending a lot of money upgrading their home’s electric service to meet the demands of EV charging. Sometimes electric service or the circuit breaker panel need to be upgraded to support a circuit for an EV charger, which can cost between $2,000 and $6,500.
The Schneider Charge EV charger is designed to work within the home’s existing electric capacity, avoiding the need for upgrades. Its SmartAmp technology is designed to automatically adjust charging speed based on real-time household energy use.
The UL 3141-compliant load management monitors household electrical use and adjusts the charger’s power level downward when appliances need power. It does this without separate monitoring devices or additional components.
When the home’s electrical supply can support it, the Schneider Charge system can deliver 11.5 kilowatts of AC power. It is OCPP 1.6 compliant to support future grid service programs too, but is not currently bi-directional.
"As homeowners buy EVs and add high-power electric technologies, many are realizing their existing electrical systems were not built for that level of demand," said Shawn Bonacorsi, Head of Electrification Solutions, Schneider Electric, North America Operations. "Schneider Charge helps remove that installation hurdle by enabling safe, reliable Level 2 charging within a home's existing electrical capacity, making EV charging simpler and easier at home, where most charging takes place."
There is even support for the installation process through home EV charger installer Omerit.
"For electricians and contractors, Schneider Charge is designed to make installation simpler and more efficient," Bonacorsi said. "By building load management into the charger, we're making home EV charging easier to install with less complexity and disruption for homeowners."
The Schneider Charge app lets homeowners monitor charging in real time, adjust settings, and schedule charging during lower-cost overnight hours.
Schneider Charge is available with either a traditional SAE J1772 plug or a Tesla-style North American Charging Standard (NACS) connector on its 25-foot cable that provides flexibility for reaching the EV’s charge port without hazardous extension cords. It will be available in both a hardwired version and a plug-in version, and hopefully Schneider will also provide EV-certified receptacles for the plug-in chargers, avoiding the
fires that are possible when using a range-grade 240-volt receptacle
for the continuous high load of an EV charger.

title: AI Rack Density’s Real Limits: Power, Cooling, Failure Risk
content:
For decades, each new generation of hardware has packed more compute into less space. AI accelerated that trend to a pace data centers have never seen before, as operators try to squeeze maximum performance from every rack in AI factory deployments.
The change has been dramatic. Racks that seemed extreme two years ago now look ordinary, with the next jump already on the build sheet. The numbers tell the story. One common benchmark is “modal rack density,” the most frequently reported power draw per rack. In 2026, that figure reached 11 kW, up from 9 kW in 2025, according to Uptime Institute’s 16
Annual Global Data Center Survey. The 11 kW profile describes a typical enterprise server room – the kind you’d actually walk past in most data centers today – not an AI training cluster.
AI racks live in a different power class entirely. Nvidia’s GB300 NVL72 – central to AI training clusters through 2025 and early 2026 – requires up to 142 kW per rack, according to Nvidia’s NVL72 AI Factory
reference architecture
. Nvidia’s newest platform, Vera Rubin NVL72,
entered full production
in June 2026 and is slated to ship to cloud providers this fall. While Nvidia hasn’t published an official rack power figure, trade-press supply chain reports place it between
190 kW and 230 kW
. Behind it, Nvidia’s Rubin Ultra NVL576 “Kyber” rack is already specified at
roughly 600 kW
in the second half of 2027.
Related:
AI Infrastructure Pushes Data Center Capex Forecast Above $3 Trillion
So, what really caps density? Three questions define the ceiling: how much heat a rack can remove, how much power the chips draw, and how much power the facility can safely deliver.
The problem isn’t chip count, and it isn’t something bigger fans can fix. “The biggest misconception about what’s limiting density is that it’s capped by the number of GPUs per chassis, or that it’s a cooling issue that you solve with bigger fans,” Joseph Wolff, founder and CTO of eRacks Systems, told
Data Center Knowledge.
Air Cooling Has Reached Its Limit, and Liquid Has Taken Over
More compute means more heat, and for years, heat removal has set the hard limit on density. That limit keeps shifting as cooling technology improves.
Air Cooling Becomes Impractical
Air cooling becomes impractical above roughly 50 kW per rack, according to
Uptime Institute
. Past that point, fans just can’t move enough air to keep up with the thermal load.
Direct-to-Chip Is Now Standard
Liquid delivered through cold plates on the chip now handles 100 to 150 kW per rack and has become the dominant liquid method, holding
55% market share
as of 2026, according to Schneider Electric.
Related:
AI Drives Data Center Uncertainty in Uptime’s 2026 Survey
Two-Phase Immersion Is Recovering, Not Dead
Once touted as the endgame, two-phase immersion was knocked back when PFAS restrictions choked off coolant supply. Adoption hasn’t fully recovered. A replacement fluid was
qualified in early 2026
, though the regulatory outcome won’t be resolved until 2027. “Microfluidics is the one I would still call ‘roadmap talk.’ The science is proven, but mainstream deployment is still a few years off,” said Omkar Nimbalkar, vice president, multi-vendor support services, at IBM, in an interview with
Data Center Knowledge
The Next Step Is Inside the Chip
In September 2025, Microsoft and Swiss startup Corintis
reported lab tests
showing that microchannels etched directly into a chip can remove heat up to three times more effectively than a standard cold plate.
Power Delivery, Not Cooling, Sets the Real Ceiling
Thermal physics isn’t the only constraint. Power delivery is proving just as binding, and it’s not the chip specifications that ultimately decide the limit.
“People benchmark density against chip specs when, in practice, it’s bounded by electrical engineering and failure planning,” Nimbalkar said.
Legacy 54 VDC Hits the Copper Wall
Legacy 54 VDC power distribution runs into a hard limit above
roughly 200 kW per rack
, when the copper required to carry that current becomes too thick, heavy, and unwieldy to build.
Related:
Stargate Update: AI’s Biggest Data Center Buildout Meets Reality
Redundancy Imposes a Capacity Tax
A typical power distribution unit (PDU) handles about 20 kW, with a double-redundant configuration, while servers draw up to 6 kW each, Nimbalkar noted. “The design question is never how many GPUs you can buy, but how many you can safely run if a power supply fails,” he said.
The Power Feed, Not the Chip, Ultimately Sets the Limit
Chip vendors already design around these constraints, offering the same GPU at different power levels to fit within practical envelopes. “The real limit is the power and thermal budget per box, and it’s set by the GPUs themselves,” Wolff said. “Nvidia sells the same 96GB RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell as a 600 W part and as a 300 W Max-Q part – that second SKU exists because eight 600 W cards in one 4U is a 5 kW-class thermal problem most air-cooled rooms can’t feed or exhaust.”
Fixes Are Already Moving from Pilot to Standard
Several efforts are underway to narrow the gap between what a rack demands and what a facility can deliver.
Higher-Voltage DC Distribution Is Moving Beyond Pilots
Vera Rubin NVL72 already
ships with 800 VDC
. The transition has moved beyond pilots: Vertiv, Schneider Electric, Eaton, and Delta all have
commercial 800 VDC offerings slated
for the second half of 2026, and
Foxconn’s 40 MW Kaohsiung-1 facility
in Taiwan is being built for it. But hardware availability isn’t the same as widespread adoption. “Ultimately, we’re asking organizations to digest a generation’s worth of change in 18-24 months,” Chris Butler, president of embedded and critical power at Flex, told
Data Center Knowledge
Power Delivery Is Being Disaggregated from Compute Racks
The Open Compute Project’s Mount Diablo project reached a
finalized 0.7.0 specification
in March 2026; Microsoft and Meta demonstrated
working hardware built on it
in July 2026. By separating power delivery from compute, facilities can scale power independently of the racks it feeds.
On-Site and Behind-the-Meter Generation Are Gaining Traction
More operators are building their own power capacity rather than waiting on utility timelines. Campus-level power “on paper” doesn’t guarantee you can deliver it reliably to a single rack.
“Once you start operating at those densities, power distribution and cooling really have to move together, so the number I pay more attention to isn’t necessarily how many megawatts a campus has on paper,” said Christopher Miglino, CEO of Axe Compute, in an interview with
Data Center Knowledge
. “It’s how much of that power you can actually deliver, cool, and operate reliably.”
Where the Ceiling Will Likely Sit Three to Five Years Out
Heat removal, power delivery, failure risk, and cost each carry an open question over the next three to five years. Where those four land together will shape what “typical” looks like.
The Grid, Not the Rack, Will Be Decisive
Power availability will be decisive. As of the end of 2025, more than 2,060 GW of generation and storage were waiting in US interconnection queues, according to Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory’s
Queued Up report
“On-site generation is a little more dependent on the project, but it’s becoming a much more serious part of the conversation for mega-scale AI campuses because, in many markets, the constraint isn’t demand or access to GPUs – it’s how quickly you can actually get enough power from the grid,” Miglino said.
As Racks Become Denser, Failures Become Costlier
As density climbs, a
single failure
knocks out more compute than it used to. That raises the bar for detection and graceful degradation.
“The smarter approach is building in firmware-level failure detection that can throttle a rack down in seconds, which allows you to run denser than a conservative static number would normally allow,” Nimbalkar said.
The most likely default is 100 kW or more per rack. “A typical high-density AI rack in 2028 is probably a 100 kW-plus deployment with direct liquid cooling standard, 400 V power delivery, and failure-handling logic built into the firmware rather than added as an afterthought,” Nimbalkar said.
Miglino expects the same threshold, with the leading edge well beyond it.
Wolff, however, expects a bifurcation: most enterprises will stay air-cooled, while a smaller set of headline racks will charge far past 100 kW. “The typical high-density AI rack – what most enterprises will actually deploy – is air-cooled 4U nodes with eight GPUs each at 300 W-class power, about 4 kW per box, three or four boxes per rack on ordinary 208 V feeds,” Wolff said.

title: DOE Retreat on Transmission Corridors Tests Grid Planning
content:
Data center developers can seek gigawatts of power years before a transmission line can be permitted and built. That mismatch is putting new pressure on grid planners just as the US Department of Energy (DOE)
has decided
not to designate three proposed National Interest Electric Transmission Corridors (NIETCs) that had advanced to Phase 3 of federal review.
DOE’s decision came after its draft
2026 National Transmission Needs Study
identified accelerating electricity demand from data centers, domestic manufacturing, large industrial loads, and electrification as major drivers of future transmission needs. The draft finds a pressing need for additional transmission capacity to accommodate that growth.
That leaves utilities and regulators with a familiar problem: build transmission early enough to support new demand, or risk making the grid the bottleneck after projects are committed. Building too far ahead, however, may leave utilities and customers paying for infrastructure that serves a load that never materializes.
Related:
Trump Targets Foreign Grid Equipment as Data Centers Expand
Texas offers an example of proactive planning that delivered results at scale. The state’s Competitive Renewable Energy Zones (CREZ) program was designed to move electricity from resource-rich West Texas to major load centers, with transmission planned ahead of the full generation buildout. Nearly two decades later, data center developers are gravitating toward parts of the same grid because of the transmission and power infrastructure that CREZ helped create.
DOE’s NIETC Decisions: What It Means
Former DOE Secretary Jennifer Granholm questioned the NIETC decision. In a
LinkedIn post
, Granholm pointed to the timing of the decisions, noting that DOE’s own transmission study identified a “pressing need” for new transmission to accommodate load growth and maintain reliability.
“You can’t declare an energy emergency, demand that America pump out more electricity, and then purposefully make it harder to deliver that power where it’s needed,” Granholm wrote.
The decision not to designate the three corridors does not necessarily conflict with the broader finding that the country needs more transmission, said Neil Osnato, founder of Persistence Analytics Group. “The Needs Study identifies a national transmission problem,” Osnato said. “The NIETC process asks a different question: whether specific geographic corridors satisfy the statutory and evidentiary basis for federal designation.”
DOE concluded there was not a sufficient basis to designate any of the three potential NIETCs that advanced to Phase 3 – the Tribal Energy Access Corridor, Southwestern Grid Connector Corridor, and Lake Erie-Canada Corridor – citing the 2023 National Transmission Needs Study, public and governmental input, and other information gathered during the designation process.
Related:
PJM’s Power Shortfall Puts Data Center Growth in Focus
A NIETC is a geographic designation, not approval for a specific transmission project. Designation can unlock certain federal transmission tools and, in limited circumstances, trigger
Federal Energy Regulatory Commission
(FERC) authority to issue permits for eligible transmission facilities within the corridor.
Osnato said the episode highlights a broader problem: the US has tools to identify transmission needs, but fewer to turn those needs into timely, coordinated interstate projects. Compounding that, transmission planning and large-load development operate on very different timelines.
Lessons from Texas CREZ Planning
Data Center Knowledge
previously reported
, Texas built CREZ to connect expected wind development in West Texas to population centers, planning the transmission ahead of the generation buildout. Nearly two decades later, major data center projects are locating in areas where CREZ-enabled infrastructure provides access to substantial power.
Galaxy Digital’s Helios campus
in Dickens County, for example, is being developed as a multi-gigawatt data center platform in an area with significant transmission capacity not built specifically for data centers.
Related:
DOE Keeps Eddystone Power Plant Online Amid Data Center Demand Surge
July 2026 report
Illinois Renewable Energy Access Plan
Osnato noted that while the CREZ approach can inform data center planning, the evidence supporting the two types of development differs. “CREZ showed the value of identifying development zones, planning transmission at scale, and avoiding a sequence of one-off upgrades that become slower and more expensive over time,” Osnato said. “That logic absolutely applies to clustered data center growth.”
But whereas CREZ was built around geographically concentrated generation development, data center planning often relies on future load that remains conditional on customer contracts, power delivery, financing, permitting, site readiness, and technology decisions. “I would borrow the CREZ concept of proactive zones and scale planning,” he said, “but pair it with a much stronger requirement to prove which loads have actually earned the right to drive that investment.”
Build Ahead, Not Ahead of Evidence
Transmission planning, permitting, and construction can take five to 10 years or longer, while large-load projects can seek interconnection within months or a few years, according to the ESIG report. Waiting until every customer is fully energized risks making transmission the bottleneck, but building billions of dollars in infrastructure around every announced gigawatt creates stranded capital and cost allocation risks.
“In some places, yes,” Osnato said when asked whether today’s data center pace justifies building transmission ahead of firm commitments. “But ‘ahead of firm commitments’ should not mean ‘ahead of evidence.’”
Osnato favors a staged approach: develop broad scenarios; preserve transmission corridors and development options early; then release increasingly irreversible capital as the underlying load passes defined evidence gates. For example, a utility might secure rights-of-way or design a scalable transmission solution before every megawatt is contracted, while deferring full capital investment until the evidence of durable load is stronger.
He suggested separating the process into three questions: What is represented? What is independently supported today? What change would invalidate that conclusion?
ERCOT’s Queue Tests the Model
The ESIG report underscores how today’s large loads differ from historical demand growth: individual facilities can reach gigawatt scale; projects can cluster geographically; and development can move faster than major transmission projects. That creates a persistent mismatch between the time required to build transmission and the speed at which large loads can seek interconnection.
ERCOT’s large-load pipeline shows the scale of the problem. As of June 2026, ERCOT
was tracking
about 474.7 GW of large-load interconnection requests, including roughly 420.8 GW – about 90.2% – associated with data centers. These requests are not equivalent to committed demand and span a range of development stages.
The size of the queue has prompted Texas officials to scrutinize which projects are real enough to shape grid planning. On June 10,
Gov. Greg Abbott directed
the Public Utility Commission of Texas (PUCT) and ERCOT to review data center projects and address development risks and costs that could otherwise fall on Texas customers. In August, Abbott
ordered a comprehensive audit
of data centers advancing through ERCOT’s interconnection process.
For transmission planners, the central question is how much of that pipeline should influence today’s investment decisions. The ESIG report recommends moving beyond isolated, project-by-project upgrades toward proactive, scenario-based, and multi-value planning that can scale as evidence of durable load accrues.
Plan Early, Commit Capital in Stages
Utilities may need to start planning years before a data center signs a final power contract. That raises the stakes for the evidence behind load forecasts and for how much capital is committed at each stage. Development zones, scenario-based planning, and expandable transmission designs can give planners more options as demand takes shape.
Texas shows how early transmission can enable future development in ways planners might not fully anticipate. For Osnato, the lesson is not to wait for every megawatt to be certain before planning – it’s to distinguish between early planning decisions that preserve options and later irreversible capital commitments that require stronger evidence.
“The real discipline is not choosing between ‘build early’ and ‘wait,’” Osnato said. “It is deciding which decisions are reversible, which are irreversible, and how much evidence should be required before crossing each one.”

title: Data Center Backlash Reaches the Ballot Box
content:
At least 18 incumbent officeholders lost elections between August 2025 and August 2026 after taking documented action on a data center project or becoming associated with a political fight over its development, according to a
Data Center Knowledge
review of election results, government records, campaign materials, and local reporting.
The cases are not equally conclusive. In some, defeated officials directly attributed their losses to data center votes. In others, challengers made data centers a prominent campaign issue alongside electricity costs, taxes, land use or local control.
Data Center Knowledge
counted an incumbent officeholder only when the official lost a completed election after a documented vote, approval, incentive, zoning action or public advocacy connected to a data center project or policy controversy. The review does not treat timing alone as proof that the issue determined the result.
Related:
Land Banking Explained: A Novel Strategy for Data Center Expansion
The count includes one officeholder, Bridget McCandless in Missouri, who sought the mayor’s office while serving as an incumbent council member. It is a count of documented losses, not a measurement of how often data center involvement causes an incumbent to lose.
The officials themselves have generally been reluctant to publicly attribute their defeats to data centers. Their opponents have been considerably less reluctant to make the connection.
Utah produced the clearest examples. State Senate President J. Stuart Adams
lost his Republican primary in June
to Stephanie Hollist after becoming closely associated with the proposed Stratos data center project in Box Elder County.
Two Box Elder County commissioners, Lee Perry and Boyd Bingham, also
lost their Republican primaries
after voting to advance the project.
The proposed Stratos project has drawn opposition over potential water and environmental impacts. The
commissioners voted
to allow the state’s Military Installation Development Authority to
create the Stratos project area
, giving the state authority to override county zoning and land-use regulations.
Hollist made opposition to Stratos a central campaign issue.
Perry was unusually direct about the political consequences after his defeat.
“Do I think that the data center vote cost me the election? Yes I do,” Perry told
The Salt Lake Tribune
after conceding his primary race.
Adams, who chairs the MIDA board
, also faced pressure over the project and moved late in the campaign to soften his position on its proposed footprint.
The Utah cases provide the clearest evidence in the review that data center politics can reach beyond local zoning fights and threaten senior state officials.
Related:
Praetorian’s Virginia Megasite Could Accommodate Data Center Development
Missouri
Missouri produced another cluster – and one of the most revealing cases. In Festus,
four incumbent city council members
– Jimmy Collier, Brian Wehner, Bobby Venz, and Jim Tinnin – lost their elections after a fight over a
proposed $6 billion data center project
Collier, Venz, and Tinnin voted for the development agreement, while Wehner voted against it. All four lost.
That makes it difficult to characterize the backlash as nothing more than punishment for voting yes. The controversy also involved the city’s development process, transparency and the way the agreement was approved.
In Independence, council members Jared Fears and Bridget McCandless also lost elections amid a fight over a proposed data center and associated tax incentives.
Fears later said the project was a factor in his defeat.
The Missouri cases show that the political exposure can come from the project itself, the approval process or an official’s association with a broader development fight.
Campaign Attacks
The pattern extends beyond Missouri and Utah. In North Carolina, David Batts defeated four-term Edgecombe County Commissioner Donald Boswell after campaigning explicitly against the proposed Kingsboro data center. Batts had warned commissioners that residents would “primary” them over the project.
Related:
AWS Data Center Withdrawal Signals Growing Political, Community Challenges
His campaign signs said: “Vote no for data centers.”
In Virginia, meanwhile, Democrat John McAuliff branded Republican Del. Geary Higgins “Data Center Geary” and made data centers a major attack line in his successful challenge.
Maryland offered a different version of the backlash: officials who had opposed a pause on new data center development still became targets of candidates who argued the county had mishandled growth.
Calvert County commissioners Todd Ireland, Mark Cox Sr. and Earl “Buddy” Hance lost their Republican primaries after challengers criticized their opposition to
a proposed pause
on new data center development and the county’s broader handling of growth.
Frederick County Council President Brad Young also lost his Democratic primary after the council approved a
zoning expansion
that opened more than 2,600 acres to data center development.
Oregon state Sen. Janeen Sollman lost her Democratic primary in a race that included opposition to data center development in the Hillsboro area. Labor and education issues also played major roles, making the data center connection less direct.
Georgia Public Service Commissioner Tim Echols lost his reelection bid in a race dominated by electricity rates and Georgia Power. Data centers were part of the broader debate over who should pay for new generation and grid infrastructure, but the evidence connecting the issue directly to his defeat is weaker.
The cases differ in their evidentiary strength. But together they show a change in political incentives: candidates now see data centers as shorthand for broader complaints about power costs, tax policy, land use and local control.
Industry Response
Mike Casey, president of Tigercomm, an energy tech PR firm, said the industry has underestimated the need to campaign for projects.
“Most tech companies weren’t built to campaign for what they need to build,” Casey told
Data Center Knowledge
. “But winning a community’s permission to build in its midst is the opposite. It’s one county at a time, it’s heavily retail, and it’s person-driven.”
Casey said developers accustomed to rapid permitting are now operating in a “high-friction permitting environment” and are trying to build community-engagement operations after encountering widespread opposition.
“Too many developers are trying to bulldoze projects through instead of skillfully campaigning for them,” he said.
The result, he said, is “a community relations problem metastasizing into a widespread political crisis.”
The Data Center Coalition’s response has focused more on explaining the industry’s economic contribution.
Dan Diorio, the coalition’s executive vice president of state policy and government affairs, said in an email to
Data Center Knowledge
that the industry understands the need for “continued efforts to better explain the role of data centers to the public through community engagement and stakeholder education.”
Diorio cited a PwC report estimating that the industry supported 5.5 million jobs, contributed $927 billion to US GDP, and generated $204 billion in federal, state and local taxes in 2024.
He also said data centers are committed to paying for the energy they consume and being responsible partners in the communities where they operate.
Jeff Thramann, founder and CEO of LT350, a company developing distributed data center infrastructure, argues that communication alone will not resolve the backlash.
“I think fundamental change is required because the impact of huge data centers on a single community is real,” Thramann said.
His prescription is to distribute computing capacity across smaller facilities rather than concentrate hundreds of megawatts at individual sites.
“If 300 MWs of capacity is needed in one location, the impact on that geography compared to spreading 1 MW across 300 grid circuits is incredibly different,” he said.
Thramann said the public distinguishes between a massive centralized campus and smaller computing facilities that have little visible effect on a community.
“A data center can range from an enormous, centralized facility to a closet in an office,” he said. “The public does not care about the closet because it changes nothing in a community, but they do care about the giant facility that changes an entire community.”
State Policy
Data centers are also appearing in paid campaign advertising well beyond the local governments that approve projects.
Campaigns in Ohio, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin, Texas and Michigan have attacked candidates or elected officials over data center development, electricity costs, tax incentives or ties to developers.
Those races are separate from the 18 completed losses. They show that campaigns increasingly view data centers as a viable attack vector, but they do not establish an electoral penalty.
State leaders are also adjusting policy as concerns about power costs, permitting, incentives, and local opposition intensify.
Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, once a strong promoter of data center investment, is pushing to slow new projects and prevent their costs from being shifted to other customers. He said in August that data center companies had “basically dug their own grave” by failing to win community support.
Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro has added environmental and transparency requirements for data center development, while Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine has paused new data center tax-exemption requests.
The moves do not necessarily amount to opposition to data center development. They impose different conditions on its expansion – around electricity, water, permitting, transparency and incentives.
The Political Cost
The 18 races do not prove that data centers caused 18 defeats. They show that data center development has become a political vulnerability that candidates can exploit.
In the strongest cases, officials took documented actions on projects, challengers made those actions campaign issues, and the incumbents lost. In weaker cases, data centers became one issue in broader fights over electricity, taxes, development and local control.
The political bargain around data centers is changing. Developers still offer investment, jobs, and tax revenue, but communities are increasingly asking who pays for the electricity, who bears the effects on water and land, whether tax incentives are justified and how much say residents have before a project is approved.
Those questions are now following data center projects into elections.
And once an opponent can turn a permitting fight into a campaign issue, the project has acquired a political cost that can outlast the public hearing.

title: Italy plans 320 MW BESS next to Terna substation - Energy Storage
content: The municipality of Chiari in the northern Italian province of Brescia is set to host one of the largest BESS projects planned in Italy. The 320 MW facility will not be built in the town center or inside the Terna electrical substation in the Santellone area, but directly adjacent to it, on privately owned land that has been intermittently cultivated for years and was recently affected by the substation’s expansion to the south, Chiari Mayor Gabriele Zotti told pv magazine Italia . The project will occupy agricultural land, although in an area that is already heavily developed for electricity infrastructure, Zotti said. Opposition councilor Marco Salogni said the existing infrastructure burden around the Terna substation in the rural Santellone area requires compensation measures, including replanting and the creation of green buffer strips. Zotti said the municipality is already negotiating with the project company, Milan-based Carpi Srl, over road improvements and, in particular, compensation measures related to the impact of climate change on the area. These would focus primarily on increasing water loads, which are putting underground infrastructure and underpasses at risk, he said. Salogni said his motion on the Chiari BESS is not intended to block the project but to improve conditions for the local community. Zotti agreed, while highlighting two aspects of the project. First, the Italian Ministry of Environment and Energy Security (Mase) has designated the BESS as a project of national strategic importance, meaning the municipality’s role is not to assess or approve it but to facilitate its construction while securing local benefits rather than simply bearing its impacts. Second, while the project will benefit Chiari, it is also important for the wider Bergamo-Mantua transmission corridor, giving the municipality a role in supporting neighboring communities, he said. The Chiari BESS is not the only storage project under development in Brescia province. According to Terna data, projects are also planned in Brescia itself, with 710 MW, Flero, with 450 MW, Lonato del Garda, with 190 MW, Nave, with 200 MW, Torbole Casaglia, with 310 MW, and Travagliato, with 200 MW. title: Metlen scales BESS across UK, Italy, Greece and Central and Eastern Europe - Energy Storage
content: Metlen has signed a balance-of-plant contract with UK developer Pulse Clean Energy for the 129 MW/362 MWh Penn BESS project in the West Midlands, England – the largest battery storage project the company has undertaken in the United Kingdom to date. The scope includes grid-connection works, with energization targeted for the end of 2027. Metlen says it has now delivered or is working on approximately 30 storage units across the United Kingdom, representing nearly 2 GWh of capacity. In Italy, the Greek energy group secured €18 million ($20.9 million) in long-term financing for a 25 MW/75 MWh BESS in Apulia, in the province of Brindisi, now fully operational. The project benefits from a seven-year physical tolling agreement with Dolomiti Energia Group, which Metlen describes as one of the first deals of its kind in the Italian storage market. In Greece, Metlen’s 330 MW/790 MWh standalone BESS in Thessaly – the largest such project planned to date in the country and one of the largest in Europe, according to the companies – has been integrated into the national transmission system. The project is a joint venture with Karatzis Group. Separately, Metlen completed the 48 MW/96 MWh Aenaos project in Polygyros, Halkidiki, implemented under Greece’s National Recovery and Resilience Plan with funding from the EU’s NextGenerationEU instrument. Metlen and Greek utility PPC agreed in March to form an equally owned joint venture targeting up to 1.5 GW/3 GWh of two-hour, liquid-cooled lithium-iron-phosphate storage in Romania, Bulgaria and Italy. Project sites, investment figures, and a country-by-country capacity split have not been disclosed. title: BYD Q2 profit jumps 30% as record exports offset weak China sales
content:
Fred Lambert
| Aug 28 2026 - 7:52 am PT
BYD posted its first quarterly profit increase in more than a year, with second-quarter net profit rising 29.8% to 8.2 billion yuan ($1.22 billion) as a record surge in exports offset a weak Chinese market.
The rebound ends four straight quarters of profit declines and reverses the 55.4% collapse BYD reported just three months earlier.
The quarter turned, but the first half is still down
Despite the Q2 recovery, BYD’s first-half results remain lower year-over-year. Revenue for the six months through June fell 7.13% to 344.82 billion yuan ($50.9 billion), and net profit attributable to shareholders dropped 20.54% to 12.33 billion yuan, according to the company’s stock exchange filing.
BYD blamed the revenue decline on weakness in its new energy vehicle (NEV) business, compounded by foreign-exchange losses tied to currency swings as it expands abroad.
Automotive and related products generated 275.34 billion yuan in the first half, down 8.98% and accounting for 79.85% of group revenue. The electronics division rose 0.96% to 69.41 billion yuan.
Exports are doing the heavy lifting
BYD sold 1,808,511 NEVs in the first half, down 15.72% from a year earlier. But the drop was almost entirely a domestic problem — and it narrowed sharply as the year went on.
Second-quarter sales fell just 3.24% to 1,108,048 units, a dramatic improvement from the 30.01% plunge in the first quarter.
The reason is overseas demand. BYD exported roughly 792,000 vehicles in the first half, up 67.8% year-over-year and equal to about 44% of its total sales. In the second quarter alone, overseas sales hit 471,091 units, up 82.46% and nearly 47% higher than the previous quarter.
That international push is also lifting profitability. First-half gross profit slipped 2.81% to 64.99 billion yuan, but gross margin rose to 18.85% from 18.01% a year earlier — a sign that higher-value export sales are more lucrative than the price-war volume BYD is fighting for at home.
Sales of BYD’s premium brands — Denza, Fang Cheng Bao, and Yangwang — climbed 61% and now make up 12.8% of its passenger-vehicle sales.
The China price war is the backdrop
BYD’s domestic struggles reflect the brutal price competition that has gripped China’s auto market, where Beijing has started pressuring automakers to end the “involution” of endless price cuts that have crushed margins across the industry.
BYD kept spending through the downturn. First-half R&D investment reached about 28.9 billion yuan — roughly 2.3 times its net profit for the period — bringing cumulative R&D spending above 270 billion yuan.
Operating cash flow rose 17.3% to 37.34 billion yuan, though the overseas expansion stretched BYD’s inventory turnover to 109 days from 79 a year ago, as more cars sit in transit on long ocean voyages.
Momentum heading into the second half
The recovery appears to be accelerating. July sales rose 21.76% to 419,211 units, the third consecutive month of year-over-year growth. Overseas sales of passenger vehicles and pickups hit a record 179,841 units in July, up 124.3% and about 43% of the month’s total.
BYD has told analysts it is targeting 1.5 million vehicle exports for all of 2026.
How BYD stacks up against Tesla
BYD remains the world’s largest maker of electric vehicles by volume. In the second quarter, it delivered
557,090 fully electric vehicles, well ahead of Tesla
, even before counting its plug-in hybrids.
Tesla, by comparison,
delivered 480,126 vehicles in Q2
, its own rebound quarter, but
reported record revenue alongside a big profit miss
. Both automakers are leaning on markets outside their home turf, and both are being squeezed on margins.
Electrek’s Take
Strip out the international business and this is a rough year for BYD in China. First-half deliveries fell nearly 16%, and profit is still down more than 20% for the half. The price war Beijing is now trying to cool did real damage. What saved the quarter was BYD’s ability to sell cars in Europe, Southeast Asia, and Latin America at higher margins than it can get at home — the same dynamic we’ve watched play out as
BYD outsells Tesla across Europe
and other overseas markets.
That’s a healthier revenue mix, but it comes with new risks. Inventory days jumped to 109 from 79 because cars are spending weeks on ships, tariffs in the EU and elsewhere are a moving target, and BYD is now exposed to the currency swings that already cost it real money this half. The export engine is powerful, but it’s more fragile than the domestic machine BYD built its dominance on.
Still, the trajectory is definitely better. Three straight months of sales growth, a rebuilt margin, and a 1.5-million-unit export target say BYD has found its footing again.
I think it’s fairly clear that BYD will come out on top here. Competition is fierce in China, and the automakers that will survive are those that already have a strong international presence. The dust from the price war in China will eventually settle, and BYD is likely best positioned to resume growth in the market.
Meanwhile, it’s still incredible to me that BYD brought in more profit than Tesla last quarter, and yet its market cap is roughly one-tenth of Tesla’s. Beyond the TSLA cult believing Musk, it’s hard to understand why, as I find BYD’s product roadmap way more interesting than Tesla’s. It is also catching up with advanced driver assist systems, and its battery business is a decade ahead of Tesla’s.

title: Ontario airport set to spend $5.5 million on electric ground support equipment
content:
Commercial EVs
aviation
Jo Borrás
| Aug 28 2026 - 4:41 am PT
California’s Ontario International Airport (ONT) has been awarded a $~4.15 million grant from the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to expand its zero emission infrastructure and add more electric ground support equipment (GSE).
With the short distances driven at limited speeds under extreme loads
, ground handling and support equipment (GHE/GSE) at airports present a nearly ideal use case for battery-electric vehicles. That’s a good thing, too.
As demand for on-road fossil fuels drops
, airports and airlines –
historically responsible for about 4% Earth’s global warming
– are becoming a bigger and bigger slice of a rapidly shrinking pie when it comes to the fossil fuel emissions generated by the aviation and air travel industries as a whole,
making investment in this sector extra impactful
“This latest investment by the FAA is a tremendous vote of confidence in the work we are doing to build a more sustainable Ontario International Airport,” explains Atif Elkadi, chief executive officer of the Ontario International Airport Authority. “Three VALE grants in three years represents meaningful progress, and this latest award will allow us and our airline partners to continue reducing emissions while investing in the infrastructure ONT will need for the future.”
The Federal Voluntary Airport Low Emissions (VALE) grant program helps airports meet air-quality goals by funding eligible projects that reduce GHG emissions. ONT’s latest award will reduce the need for aircraft and ground equipment to burn fuel while parked at the terminal, supporting cleaner and more efficient airport operations – and, after Ontario’s 25% cost match, the $4,147,752 will bring total spending on electric GSE at Terminals 2 and 4 to $5.53 million.

Autonomous baggage handler; via OshKosh.
Reduced operating costs, fossil fuel use, and air pollution are their own rewards, of course – the fact that GHE like
refueling trucks
baggage handlers
airplane tugs

I can only hope that more airports accelerate their adoption of cleaner GSE/GHE

title: Private equity bribed Trump $1M, then got a $900M payday from taxpayers
content:
Offshore wind power
department of the interior
Jameson Dow
| Aug 28 2026 - 7:00 am PT
Photo by Roy Luck on
The largest benefactor of the Interior Department’s most recent
illegal wind buyout
is an Australian-American billionaire whose private equity firm will receive $900 million in exchange for a stake in a methane gas terminal in Louisiana. The near-billion-dollar buyout comes after the same billionaire gave a $1 million bribe to the originator of the deal.
At issue is the recent deal by the Department of the Interior with RWE, a German energy company that had been set to build several wind farms off the US coast.
Interior illegally gave $1.22 billion to RWE to get them to stop building these projects, and RWE will instead put $900 million of that money into purchasing a stake in a methane gas terminal in Louisiana and $300 million into building dirty methane gas turbines for data centers, which are making electricity both more expensive and dirtier.
It’s part of a pattern of wasteful spending by the Interior Department, which has so far
spent around $4 billion of taxpayer money
on canceling wind projects in order to starve America of energy and raise electricity prices.
This money has been spent illegally – not only is it coming out of a government fund that can’t be used for this purpose, but the government cannot haphazardly cancel energy projects on the outer continental shelf.
But it turns out the RWE deal is even more nefarious than we previously thought, as it
has now been reported
that the $900 million will go to buying out a portion of the stake owned by Stonepeak, a private equity fund owned by Australian-American billionaire Michael Dorrell. The project is considered riskier than others, and Stonepeak seems to be looking to reduce its financial exposure.
Dorrell owns property near Mar-A-Lago and is a member of Mr. Trump’s private club. He has bragged publicly about meeting the former reality TV host.
Adding to the corruption, it turns out that Dorrell isn’t just one of Mr. Trump’s neighbors, but he also gave a $1 million bribe to Mr. Trump in order to attend the
rally, headlined by a speaker who gave two unambiguous Nazi salutes
, which Trump held as part of his inauguration (to an office he
cannot legally hold
It seems that this relatively small bribe has produced pretty massive results, as with
other bribes
given to the same corrupt individual, both from US and
foreign sources
(though at least one of those bribes
didn’t go so well
Political bribery has been known to be an efficient way for corporations to make money, particularly so since the
US “Supreme” Court
opined in
Citizens United v FEC
that bribery should be legal.
Various analyses have suggested that the average return on investment from political bribes (sometimes called “lobbying”) is anywhere between
104,000%
But Mr. Trump has been
more brazen in accepting and acting on direct bribes
than most. And here is just the latest example: a transaction where he receives $1 million, and illegally gives that person $900 million of your money, with the (desired) side effect of
raising your electricity bills
restricting your energy supply
However, the bribes may not work out in the long term. States
have already sued
threatened further lawsuits
over these wind buyout plans, and Democrats in Congress are stating their intention not to allow these wasteful, illegal deals to go through (incidentally,
click here to register to vote
in this November’s midterms). Jared Huffman of California’s 2nd district was particularly clear, telling energy companies that “you better tell your shareholders that we are coming for that money.”

title: Qronge X1 Spark L Review: Does a $1,299 Sur-Ron Light Bee alternative cut the right corners?
content:
If you are late to the pre-teen suburban e-moto scene, we’ve been wading through the exploding market of low-cost Sur-Ron competitors over the past months. While we can all debate the safety and legality issues these bikes bring, the reality is that they are incredibly popular and useful for those who can get around their neighborhoods and back roads and are comfortable hitting speeds up to and above 40mph. Enter the low cost $1299 Qronge X1 Spark L.
Qronge has spent the last couple of years building a reputation the way most budget e-bike brands do: undercut an established category by a factor of two or three and hope the compromises don’t show up until long after the warranty window closes. The X1 Spark L is the company’s bid at the “mini electric dirt bike” segment that Sur-Ron created and Talaria, Segway, and a dozen Amazon-native brands have since piled into. However, at $1,299, it’s positioned directly against bikes that cost 3-4x as much — so the real question isn’t whether it’s fun in a parking lot. It’s whether it survives actual trail use, and whether the spec sheet is telling the truth.
For us in the last month, it has largely been a pleasant surprise.
The X1 Spark L runs the same drivetrain as the smaller X1 Spark M (and HeyBike Villan/Yozma IN 10Pro): a 4,500W peak mid-drive motor claimed to produce 283 Nm of torque, fed by a 60V 28.8Ah (1,728Wh) battery. The L steps up with 17″/14″ wheels instead of the M’s 14″/12″ setup, a full-twist throttle, and a heavier-duty 420H chain — a sensible upgrade given how much torque a budget drivetrain is being asked to absorb. Qronge claims a 50 mph top speed and up to 60 miles of range. Both of those are incredibly “optimistic,” as Electrek readers know by now, and you should expect to hit 40+mph and maaaaybe 30-mile range in real-world usage with a 200-lb rider. Qronge notes that their 60 mile claim is at just 12.5 mph and you’ll see HALF that range – 30 miles – at 22mph (!!) and just 21 miles of range at full throttle. I think this is actually being brutally honest though I don’t know if I’ve ever seen an e-Moto driver stop at 12mph.
Where it’s genuinely competitive
The torque and hill-climbing numbers aren’t just marketing. Multiple independent testers noted the same thing and I can confirm — steep, loose inclines that stall underpowered budget bikes didn’t slow this one down, and the motor itself is physically larger than the one in the Sur-Ron Light Bee X it’s obviously benchmarked against. For a bike costing roughly a third of the Sur-Ron, that’s a legitimate point in its favor, not a marketing talking point…if size is the most important factor.
The 420H heavy-duty chain is a small spec choice, but it’s the kind of thing that tells you whether an engineering team is thinking past launch day. A 4,500W motor putting torque through a standard 420 chain is a wear-item failure waiting to happen; Qronge apparently anticipated that point of failure.
Corners were cut to get to $1299
The 2A charger is the typical corner-cutting move, saving $50 or so over a quicker 4-6A option. We’ll allow it on this e-moto because you can always upgrade it yourself or maybe 30 miles/day is plenty for your riding needs. But expect longer charge times on the Qronge than the top shelf e-motos.
The seat is not comfortable, and I’d taken to putting a towel under my keister for longer rides. For people like my teen without back issues, it wasn’t even a consideration so your mileage will vary here.
Fit and finish are par for a $1299 e-moto. It took a hammer to get one of the pegs in. Some of the screws didn’t feel threaded properly, and parts like the rear shock took a while to assemble. However, the bike eventually came together nicely and those extra minutes of assembly are just a forgotten memory now.
The biggest problem, and one I think deserves a significant pause, is that the brake levers here are very cost-cutter. The bottom line is that they do work fine but the limited travel and ability to use one finger are severely limited. We didn’t have any outages and the hydraulics worked fine for the month of testing, but this is one corner I don’t like to cut.

Motor & Battery

|---|---|
| Motor type | Mid-drive |
| Peak power | 4,500W |

| Battery | 60V 28.8Ah (1,728Wh), removable |

Chassis & Drivetrain

|---|---|

Warranty / Support
1-year warranty, 15-day return window, free shipping, partial factory assembly required.
Electrek’s take:
The Qronge X1 Spark L looks like a legitimate budget alternative to the Sur-Ron-style mini dirt bike category — if you go in accepting that “budget” means some inconsistent components, limited brakes and a seat you’ll probably replace if you are an adult, and if you mentally discount the range claim by roughly a half before you ever throw a leg over it.
Strangely, after all was said and done, this bike actually performed quite well and is still one of the our favorites in the budget stable. The bigger 14/17 wheels take it above the Tuttio/Yozma/Heybike 14/12 class where it is priced at so if the budget doesn’t reach close to $2000, I say go for it. It is also a fairly good-looking bike, and I can recommend it as long as the caveats above aren’t dealbreakers.
