title: TotalEnergies, TES-led e-methane project in US enters FEED
content:
A consortium led by French energy group TotalEnergies SE (EPA:TTE) and green energy firm TES has launched front-end engineering and design (FEED) work for the Live Oak electric natural gas (e-NG) project in Northeast Nebraska, which aims to supply e-methane to customers in Japan.
US engineering company KBR and Spain's Tecnicas Reunidas will conduct parallel FEED studies for the project, after which one of the concepts will be selected for execution.
Located in Norfolk, Nebraska, Live Oak will produce e-NG, or e-methane, by combining renewable hydrogen produced through electrolysis with CO2 captured from bioethanol plants through methanation. The facility is expected to be equipped with 250 MW of electrolysis capacity and to have an output of 75,000 tonnes of e-NG annually.
Live Oak is targeting completion of FEED and the start of execution in 2027. Commercial operations can potentially start in 2030.
The consortium, in which TotalEnergies and TES each hold a 33.35% stake, also includes Osaka Gas, Toho Gas and ITOCHU, which jointly
own the remaining 33.3%
.
Osaka Gas and Toho Gas are set to serve as the project's primary off-takers. The e-NG will be exported to Japan using existing US natural gas and LNG infrastructure.

title: Trianel Borkum I enters German balancing market with 70 MW
content:
German municipal utilities network Trianel has prequalified 70 MW of capacity from Trianel Borkum I offshore wind farm to provide negative secondary balancing reserve for the local energy market, opening up a new source of revenue for the North Sea asset.
The Trianel Borkum I has been providing the grid-balancing service since July 2026, while the marketing of the capacity started on July 22.
Under the service, the wind farm can automatically reduce its power output within five minutes at the request of the transmission system operator. The participation in the balancing market was made possible by a specially developed remote control infrastructure that transmits requests from grid operators to the wind farm in real time and automatically implements the required adjustments.
Borkum I, which has been operating for more than a decade, has generated over 6.59 billion kWh of electricity since its commissioning.

title: Trump bans some foreign electric equipment in US energy grid
content:
US President Donald Trump on Thursday issued an emergency executive order that restricts the use of certain foreign-made transformers and other critical energy equipment in electric grid projects over national security concerns.
The order bans any acquisition, importation, transfer, or installation of any foreign-produced bulk-power system electric hardware, including transformers, inverters, battery energy storage systems, power generation turbines, substation voltage regulations, circuit breakers, control systems and other electrical equipment. The use of those products in the bulk power system creates vulnerabilities for national security and opens the door for malicious cyber activities, which represents “unusual and extraordinary foreign threat.”
The order could result in publishing a white list of pre-qualified equipment and vendors and establishing procedures to license prohibited transactions.
“The rapid growth of advanced manufacturing, data centers, artificial intelligence, and defense production has increased the Nation’s dependence on abundant, reliable electricity and magnified the consequences of a successful attack or supply disruption on the bulk-power system,” Trump said.
The Department of Energy (DOE) has 120 days to publish formal rules implementing the policy. In the meantime, government authorities are directed to identify and recommend ways to identify, monitor or replace bulk-power system electric equipment which has already been installed.
According to the latest International Energy Agency (IEA) statistics, China accounts for 85% of the world’s solar and 80% of the lithium-ion battery supply chain production capacity. The shares for photovoltaic (PV) wafers and anode materials are 95% and 97%, respectively.
The new directive comes amid several cyberattacks on US water systems, in which Iran-linked hackers are reportedly involved.

title: UK onshore wind farm pipeline tops 50 GW, RenewableUK says
content:
The UK’s onshore wind farm pipeline of projects at any stage of development has reached 50,134 MW, growing by more than 3 GW in the past year as planning activity reached record levels, according to new data from industry group RenewableUK.
The country's pipeline of onshore wind farms, ranging from early-stage projects to operational assets, has increased by 6.5% on a yearly basis, or by 3,076 MW, from 47,058 MW.
Planning submissions across the UK hit a record 5,043 MW in 2025, exceeding the previous peak of 3,440 MW set in 2013 by 47%, RenewableUK said in its latest EnergyPulse Onshore Wind report.
The increase came as England saw a renewal in new project proposals following the lifting of restrictions on onshore wind development in July 2024. In 2025, the first full calendar year after the change, some 233 MW of projects were submitted into the planning system, exceeding the 188 MW submitted during the previous nine years combined.
Scotland tops the chart, accounting for 75% of the UK's current onshore wind portfolio, followed by Wales with 12%, England with 8% and Northern Ireland with 5%.
The proportion of onshore wind capacity being cleared by local authorities also reached 64% in 2025, matching the record set in 2020. The approval rate for larger projects determined by the government stood at 77%.

title: Westbridge to sell 225-MW Red Willow solar, BESS project in Canada
content:
Canada's Westbridge Renewable Energy SA (CVE:WEB) said on Friday it had signed a definitive agreement to sell its Red Willow solar-plus-storage project in Alberta, with total proceeds expected to reach CAD 26.725 million (USD 19.2m/EUR 16.6m) if all conditions and milestones are met.
The transaction involves the sale of all shares in Westbridge's wholly owned subsidiary Red Willow Solar Inc, which owns the project in Stettler County No. 6 in central Alberta.
Currently in an advanced stage, the Red Willow project is expected to have up to 225 MWac of solar capacity and a 100-MW battery energy storage system (BESS). The solar farm and BESS have received power plant and substation approvals from the Alberta Utilities Commission, while the project has an interconnection position in the Alberta Electric System Operator process (AESO), Westbridge said.
Under the agreement, the company will receive CAD 10.5 million in cash at closing, together with reimbursement or replacement of a CAD-4.725-million security payment to the AESO.
A further CAD 4.5 million will be payable when the BESS reaches commercial operation, while Westbridge will receive CAD 25,000 per MWdc when the solar farm reaches commercial operation. The latter payment is currently estimated at about CAD 7 million.
The transaction is subject to customary closing conditions, including regulatory approvals and other conditions precedent. No finder's fees are payable and the transaction is at arm's length, Westbridge said.
The buyer of Red Willow was not disclosed.

title: Amex GBT: Exploring Supply Chain Impact on the Rental Market
content:
Amex GBT: Exploring Supply Chain Impact on the Rental Market
Prioritise Us
on Google
Amex GBT explores the state of the car rentals market amid ongoing geopolitical shifts. Credit: Unsplash
The car rental market is undergoing transformation, driven by geopolitical disruption, the growing demand of supply chain operations and electrification
American Express Global Business Travel (Amex GBT) has launched its Ground Monitor report, exploring how the
car rental market
is set to be transformed throughout 2026-27.
Various factors are contributing to a shift in the market, including the increasing uptake of electrification, as well as heightened logistics needs.
Amex GBT explores the current trends alongside global shifts, working to create more resilience within operations.
This recall activity is forcing operators to maintain larger fleets than necessary, adding operational costs that may translate to higher rental prices.
Joshua Collier, Global Business Consulting, Amex GBT
Influences on the market
The last few years have seen increasing instability and fluctuating prices across every market place. Though Amex GBT does anticipate car prices to grow somewhat throughout the next year, it estimates the prices will remain stable.
Factors driving these increases can be seen across the world, with geopolitical influences having disrupted trade significantly in recent years. Ongoing trade tensions, volatility in the Middle East, the
electrification transition
and global inflation are all impacting how operations run.
The four main influences of car prices are:
Supply and demand
- Amex GBT reports a better balance between supply and demand, which means car rental rates should be stable. As deliveries have been consistently keeping pace with demand around the world, there is a downward pressure on rental prices.
Geopolitical issues
- Though conflict in the Middle East rose prices immediately for air transport, the impact on auto supply chains is coming at a delay. Aluminium supply is being disrupted and car tires are increasing in price. As more cars become 'smart cars',
shortages
in semiconductor chips are a growing concern, caused – in part – due to reduced production of helium.
Smarter cars
- The increase in smart cars is making driver safer and more efficient, they are also more expensive. Fixing the vehicles requires specialist technicians, which increases the cost of service. According to Amex GBT, smarter cars increase the global recall list, which makes supply of them less reliable, translating into the need for rental providers to have larger inventory buffer.
Lower resale values
- For car rental companies, selling off cars acts as an important revenue stream. However, the used car sector across Europe and the US is seeing declining pricing for electric vehicles and internal combustion engine vehicles. This means less opportunity for used car sales, but also more upwards pressure on rental rates.
"The car rental industry has overcome supply shortages caused by semiconductor chip constraints," Joshua Collier, Global Business Consulting, Amex GBT says to Supply Chain Digital.
Joshua Collier, Global Business Consulting, Amex GBT
"While cost pressures from inflation, insurance, labour, maintenance and vehicle expenses persist, normalised fleet supply is expected to keep price increases modest."
Key facts
Amex GBT expects rates in the US to increase between 1.5% and 2%
In Brazil, EV growth in rental fleet in 2025 was up 124.5% from the year before
In France, Amex GBT forecasts a 0.5% rate increase
Regional shifts
The Amex GBT report explores regional differences regarding the rental market, looking at North America, Latin America, Europe and Asia-Pacific.
Following minimal GDP growth and improved supply rates, Amex GBT predicts modest increases to car rental rates across Canada and the US. A cause for concern surrounds city surcharges, which are becoming more common in the region.
In Latin America, the rental sector is undergoing a steady growth, due to an increase in demand regarding both leisure and corporate operations. EVs in particular are seeing a growth – in the space of four years, Brazil's rental fleet grew from 2,545 vehicles to 33,562.
Across Europe, Amex GBT is predicting a varied increase, with flat to moderate growth. In the Netherlands, a high rate is anticipated due to rising motor vehicle taxes. Fleet scarcity is resulting in modest rate rises in Germany, with lower rates in the UK due to strong competition.
Amex GBT expects Australia to see some of the largest rental rate increases. In remote mining locations, competition is limited which can translate to higher price increases.
Joshua adds: "As supply stabilises, we are monitoring a range of dynamics that could determine whether rates hold steady or rise in business travel. Used car market
volatility is weakening
– used car prices are forcing rental companies to adjust fleet book values downward, creating cost pressures that could push rates up. Another influence is manufacturer fleet recalls growing. This recall activity is forcing operators to maintain larger fleets than necessary, adding operational costs that may translate to higher rental prices."
Electric Vehicles are impacting cost for rental companies. Credit: Getty Images
Meeting demands
Amid the ongoing electrification transition, businesses are expected to
add more sustainability
into their fleets. This means more sustainable fuels and more EVs. However, this is a major cost to companies, especially those which are newer or smaller.
Though using sustainable fuel or EVs is more cost-efficient in the long-term, the initial cost of purchasing can be a major hit to companies. As a result, many supply chain businesses use rental companies to meet new regulations and standards.
Renting instead of purchasing allows for the quick integration of sustainable options at a significantly lower cost. This means they can meet consumer expectations and meet the guidelines from reporting standards.
This has had its own issues, of course, as business owners around the world move towards rentals. Auto supply chains have mostly recovered following various shocks in recent years, but volatility is something owners need to be aware of.
"When it comes to car rental companies, today they operate more as asset management companies, prioritising residual value optimisation and cost control over actual fleet size," Joshua explains.
"In turn, that ensures that car rental companies are in greater control of their fleets and are less reliant on the manufacturer than previously. Whilst there would be some short-term insulation in the event of vehicle shortages, ultimately access to fleet supply is the number one factor that influences prices in the car rental market."
Amex GBT also suggests that business owners should work with a single rental provider for
fleet management
and car rentals, as it helps drive cohesion and reliability. Moreover, there needs to be collaboration between colleagues across the organisation to ensure visibility across HR, procurement, operations, legal and finance.

title: Court Limits Pentagon Use of Supply Chain Risk Label
content:
Court Limits Pentagon Use of Supply Chain Risk Label
Prioritise Us
on Google
A US judge has ruled that Anthropic's supply chain risk designation be removed (Image source: Getty Images/Mariakray)
Judge Rita Lin ruled the Pentagon's supply chain risk designation against Anthropic unlawful, a first-of-its-kind use of the FASCSA tool
Anthropic a "supply chain risk" earlier this year, a designation that had, until now, been reserved almost exclusively for companies linked to foreign adversaries.
US District Judge Rita Lin, ruling on 27 August 2026 in the Northern District of California, ordered the designation removed. She added that the Department of Defense's actions “constituted unlawful retaliation in violation of the First Amendment” and that Anthropic “was denied the pre-deprivation process required under the Fifth Amendment”.
The ruling matters beyond the specifics of one company's dispute with the Pentagon. It tests the boundaries of a legal tool that determines which vendors an entire chain of government contractors is permitted to work with.
What the supply chain risk label actually does
The designation stems from the Federal Acquisition Supply Chain Security Act of 2018 (FASCSA), which established the Federal Acquisition Security Council to assess
national security risk
in the federal technology supply chain and recommend exclusion or removal orders against specific vendors.
In the past, FASCSA orders have targeted companies with ties to nations designated as adversarial. The first public order issued under the Act, in September 2025, excluded
cybersecurity
firm Acronis AG and its affiliates from Intelligence Community contracts. Anthropic's case marks a significant departure: it is the first time the tool has been used against a US-founded company over a policy dispute rather than a foreign-ownership concern.
Key facts: the Pentagon-Anthropic dispute
The Department of Defense sought to use Anthropic's Claude model for “all lawful purposes”, including sensitive military and intelligence applications.
Anthropic maintained guardrails preventing its models being used in fully autonomous lethal weapons or mass surveillance of Americans.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth designated Anthropic a supply chain risk in February 2026, barring the Pentagon and its contractors from using its products.
Anthropic filed suit in March 2026, arguing the designation was retaliation for its public position on AI safety.
A second, related lawsuit brought by Anthropic remains before a Washington, DC court.
Why the judge ruled against the Pentagon
Judge Lin found the government's stated justification did not hold up to scrutiny, ruling that the measures imposed on Anthropic were “illegal and baseless”. She noted that the Pentagon continued pursuing work with Anthropic even after issuing the designation, undermining its own claim of distrust.
“The empty invocation of national security is not a blank check to punish and retaliate against government critics.”
Judge Rita Lin, US District Judge, Northern District of California
Announcing the original designation in February, Hegseth said “America's warfighters will never be held hostage by the ideological whims of Big Tech”, framing the move as a defence of military autonomy over vendor choice. The Department of Justice is expected to challenge the ruling.
An Anthropic spokesperson welcomed the decision, saying the company remains focused on working with the government to ensure the
benefits of AI reach
“so all Americans”.
Anthropic welcomed the decision, saying it remains focused on working with the government. Credit: Anthropic
Why this matters beyond one company
For federal contractors and their suppliers, a
supply chain risk designation
is not a minor procurement flag. It can bar an entire tier of contractors, not just the named company, from using a vendor's products. As a result, it is one of the most consequential tools available to federal agencies for reshaping a supply chain overnight.
The ruling does not challenge the Pentagon's right to choose its vendors freely, something Judge Lin explicitly affirmed. What it curtails is the use of a national security mechanism as leverage in a commercial or policy disagreement, a distinction that matters to any technology vendor operating inside federal supply chains, particularly as AI procurement across defence and intelligence agencies continues to expand.
Key company in focus: Anthropic
Anthropic is an AI safety and research company headquartered in San Francisco, California, and the developer of the Claude family of AI models. Dario Amodei serves as Co-Founder and Chief Executive Officer. The company has publicly maintained safety guardrails restricting its models from use in autonomous weapons systems and mass surveillance applications.

title: Trade and Tariffs: Inside the US-Canada Relationship Dispute
content:
Trade and Tariffs: Inside the US-Canada Relationship Dispute
Prioritise Us
on Google
Trade relationships between US and Canada face new levels of volatility | Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and US President Donald Trump. Credit: Wikimedia Commons
Following an attempt at a trade deal, the US and Canada's relationship is on unstable grounds, with threats and implementation of tariffs going both ways
Amid claims of an almost-achieved trade agreement, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has claimed that the proposed deal was uneven, with the US asking too much and giving too little back.
The deal was in place to reduce tariffs, which have shaken trade in recent years. Now, however, tensions have increased and trade between the two nations is at a volatile standing.
With counter offers and tariffs threats at a high, businesses across the US and Canada are left in a vulnerable position.
Preferential access to any major market is now a political variable, not a structural guarantee.
Scott Lehmann, GVP at Sphera
Trade disputes
Following months of back and forth upon US President Donald Trump's re-election, the trade relationship between the two nations may have reached a breaking point. Weeks of urgent talks came to a head, with results neither leader had desired.
Though Trump had briefly declared that the countries had reached a deal, Carney recalled negotiations on August 22, citing unfair trade agreements. According to Ottawa, the US attempted to make last-minute changes to the agreement, but the US disputes that and states the nation had attempted to turn away from earlier commitments.
The deal would have cut US tariffs on Canadian cars and light-duty trucks from 25% to 15%, and tariffs on steel and aluminium from 50% to 25%. In response, Canada was going to reduce tariffs on items and reduce import administration for dairy products.
Now, however, the countries are facing further disputes, with tariff threats at another high.
"The breakdown of
US-Canada trade
talks is the clearest example of how the world order that governed global trade for thirty years is ending," explains Scott Lehmann, Group Vice President at Sphera.
Scott Lehmann, Group Vice President at Sphera
"Trade has become power and the system is being rewired around leverage, resilience, industrial depth and strategic control. We have a front row seat to the unfolding of a harder, more selective, more political form of re-globalisation. The logic of great power competition, control resources, control markets, control supply chains, never quite disappeared; the vocabulary of globalisation and free trade simply obscured it for thirty years."
Policy and counter-offers
On July 20, the US invoked Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 in order to implement
50% tariffs
on Canadian goods. Demands from Washington impacted Canadian trade policy autonomy and
critical mineral
access. In response, Canada has imposed counter-tariffs, which are effective from September 8.
These measures will mirror the US actions on a dollar-for-dollar basis, targeting more than 700 product categories from the US. This will include everyday consumer items such as toilet paper, clothing, seafood and cheese.
In a press conference, Canada’s Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne explained: “Canada's counter tariffs are designed primarily to provide protection for Canadian industry impacted by US tariffs and allow them to compete against US products in the Canadian market. It's all about fairness. It's all about level playing field. It's all about supporting Canadian workers and Canadian businesses."
François-Philippe Champagne, Finance Minister of Canada. Credit: Parliament of Canada
Canada exported approximately US$451bn worth of goods in 2025. Now, the US has
imposed tariffs
on Canadian exports such as hockey equipment, whiskey, textiles and auto parts, making up 4% of Canada's exports to the US.
These extra costs will be felt by the consumers and the companies – particularly the smaller business owners.
On the US side, Scott states that the impact will be mostly felt by parts suppliers and producers. He says, "Parts suppliers on the US side will absorb the worst of the cost.
Steel producers
have had over a year of Section 232 exposure to begin adjusting, and automakers have the balance sheets and lobbying operations to absorb short-term cost increases while pursuing exemptions. Parts suppliers have neither. They operate on thin margins, cannot pass costs upward to OEMs or downward to raw material suppliers without losing the contract, and a 50% stacked tariff likely eliminates their margins."
For these organisations, the impact may not be felt immediately. In Canada, however, the damage will be felt sooner and will be more widespread. Its export economy is reliant on the US, as ocean freight costs make trade to European and Asian buyers less cost-effective. Market diversification takes many years to securely put in place, meaning the market will see a major hit once these tariffs start taking place.
Unstable trade relationships
have been a constant in the last year, impacting job security, product cost and trade efficiency. This relationship breakdown is the newest in a long line, but the volatility may end before the new costs come to fruition.
"Preferential access to any major market is now a political variable, not a structural guarantee," Scott warns.
"The Canada situation will resolve. But not before it claims companies, jobs and supply chain relationships that took decades to build and cannot be reconstructed by the time the politics move on.”

title: Nickel exposure at CATL plant in Hungary - electrive.com
content:
The occupational safety authority in CATL's battery plant in Debrecen, Hungary, has temporarily suspended work in three areas when nine employees were found to have experienced elevated nickel exposure. The incident affects CATL amid the already delayed ramp-up of its cell production.
Module production (pictured) has already begun at CATL in Debrecen, but cell manufacturing has not yet started.
Image: CATL
Authorities stopped work in some areas of CATL’s plant in Debrecen, Hungary, after CATL reported that nine employees had been exposed to elevated levels of nickel. A subsequent occupational safety inspection by authorities in Hajdú-Bihar County found that workers had not been adequately provided with protective equipment.
According to Hungarian media, local authorities have prohibited work in three areas of the cell manufacturing building until the identified deficiencies are rectified. The affected areas include systems for laser cutting cathode and anode foils, winding electrode foils, and cell drying. Reports also indicate that a procedure to impose a fine is underway.
However, the suspension of work does not amount to a complete production stop at the site. While cell manufacturing in Debrecen has not yet commenced as the plant is still being developed, CATL is already producing battery modules. In May, the Chinese battery manufacturer commissioned a new
module assembly line with an annual capacity of 5 GWh
on its premises. The cells required for this continue to be sourced from other CATL plants.
CATL awaits full approval for cell production
Alongside the occupational safety measures, approvals for cell production have also hit some hurdles. The two processes are separate. The authority denied the usage permit for the second expansion stage not because of nickel exposure, but due to a deficiency in formal proceedings. A permit was initially rejected on 19 August when a completed building was not correctly represented in a site plan. However, during the first expansion stage, the authority granted the usage permit on 25 August after missing documents were submitted.
The incident comes at a challenging time for CATL as it ramps up production. The cell factory was initially designed for an annual capacity of 40 GWh. While the company says the plant has been completed, cell production is behind schedule. As the end of last year, CATL had projected the start of
series production for March or April 2026
The delays have already impacted Mercedes-Benz. The batteries for the new electric van VLE were originally supposed to come from Debrecen but are now being supplied from China. CATL is covering the additional costs incurred. BMW has not been affected so far, as the car manufacturer is not due to receive cells from the nearby CATL plant until
For CATL, the priority now is to resolve both the outstanding approval issues and the identified occupational safety deficiencies. It remains unclear whether the work ban in the three affected areas will further delay the start of cell production. In the long term, CATL plans to expand the production capacity in Debrecen to up to 100 GWh per year.

title: $950 million in annual savings to be achieved with new OpenAI deal
content: An Atlanta-based company has signed a new contract with OpenAI. With this, Georgia Power will now serve OpenAI’s new project in Effingham County. The latest deal arks the latest step in the company’s proactive strategy to ensure Georgia’s growth benefits the customers it serves. With the projects announced to date and projected future growth in the state, Georgia Power customers are expected to see savings of at least $15 per month beginning in 2029 for the typical residential customer using 1,000 kilowatt-hours per month, an increase from the company’s December 2025 commitment of $102 per year to $180 per year.1,000 MW of flexible demand response“We know every dollar counts, and we know that in many parts of the country growth is pushing electric rates up. That is not happening in Georgia,” said Kim Greene, chairman, president and CEO of Georgia Power. “In December, we committed to $102 a year in savings for the typical family beginning in 2029. Today, that number is expected to be $180. We appreciate the continued diligence of the Commission and its staff in helping us deliver these savings for customers, and ensuring the right protections are in place for the millions of Georgians we are privileged to serve.”The company’s contract with OpenAI was filed with the Georgia Public Service Commission (PSC) in July and includes 3,200 megawatts (MW) of new demand. Under that agreement, OpenAI will pay the full cost of the infrastructure needed to serve it and has committed up to 1,000 MW of flexible demand response, which enables Georgia Power to reduce energy delivered to the facility during periods of high demand and invest in fewer new generation resources to serve future growth, according to a press release. When the first signs of projected extraordinary growth appeared in the state, Georgia Power began developing a framework with the Georgia PSC designed to turn that projected growth into lower costs and higher reliability for customers. The recent announcement also follows the prior freeze on base rates approved by the Georgia PSC in July 2025, as well as the plan approved in May 2026 to lower overall rates, as per the release.Large-load customers like data centers, manufacturers choosing GeorgiaThe company also highlighted that with new residents moving to the state and large-load customers like data centers and manufacturers choosing Georgia, Georgia Power and the Georgia PSC took early action to put protections for customers in place by introducing new Georgia PSC Rules and Regulations. In addition, the company made a broader commitment to customers in the Georgia Power Customer Protection Pledge which reaffirms the company’s commitment to serving the interests, the communities, and the priorities of its 2.8 million customers.“Data centers are paying more so families and small businesses can pay less, and our goal with every contract we sign under this framework is to deliver value for them,” added Greene. “Our customers depend on us for reliable and affordable energy every day, and that is the focus behind every decision we make.”

title: 80-year nuclear model reveals what drives coolant pipe ruptures
content: Seoul National University of Science and Technology researchers have developed a probabilistic method to estimate how likely nuclear power plant coolant pipes are to rupture, potentially giving engineers a clearer picture of which failure scenarios deserve the most attention.The team used probabilistic fracture mechanics to examine two piping systems at a reference Korean nuclear power plant. Unlike approaches that rely on fixed assumptions, the method accounts for uncertainty in material behavior, degradation, operating conditions, and inspection effectiveness.The researchers focused on a type of accident in which a primary coolant pipe breaks and causes a loss of coolant. Such failures are an important safety consideration because the primary coolant system helps maintain the reactor’s operating conditions.The analysis could help engineers distinguish extremely unlikely pipe failures from scenarios that are more credible. That could support decisions on reactor design, inspection schedules and maintenance, particularly as nuclear plants operate for longer periods.Modeling cracks across decadesThe researchers used the eXtremely Low Probability of Rupture (xLPR) code to model the behavior of two leak-before-break-approved piping systems: a steam-generator coolant, or SC, piping system and a surge nozzle.They simulated 80 years of plant operation, assuming stress corrosion cracking (SCC) was the only degradation mechanism. The team then varied several factors to see how they affected predicted rupture frequency.These included weld residual stress (WRS), crack growth rate (CGR), weld overlay (WOL) repairs, and inspection performance.The results showed that these variables do not affect rupture predictions equally. WRS emerged as the most influential factor. Using the 95th-percentile WRS profile led to a considerable reduction in predicted rupture frequency for the SC piping compared with the base case.Crack growth rate also had a significant effect on the results. Meanwhile, the surge nozzle showed no rupture across the scenarios examined, while the weld-overlay analysis produced no rupture for either piping system.Inspections produced one of the clearest effects. Periodic inspections reduced the predicted rupture frequency by several orders of magnitude, showing how maintenance and monitoring can significantly influence calculated nuclear-piping risk.Probabilities can sharpen safety decisionsThe researchers say probabilistic analysis can provide information that deterministic approaches may miss. Instead of treating individual parameters as fixed values, the framework evaluates how uncertainty in those parameters changes the estimated likelihood of failure.“Probabilistic fracture mechanics makes it possible to estimate rupture frequency while accounting for the stochastic nature of material behavior, degradation over time, loading conditions, and even effectiveness of inspections,” said Nam-Su Huh, a professor at the School of Mechanical Systems Engineering at Seoul National University of Science and Technology.The approach could be particularly relevant to aging nuclear plants, where degradation can accumulate over decades. It could also help operators determine where inspection and maintenance resources are likely to have the greatest safety impact.“A probabilistic framework can help engineers identify which factors govern the predicted failure behavior, providing a reliable technical basis for plant design and safety evaluations,” Huh said. “In the long term, this research could contribute to risk-informed approaches to maintain the safety of both aging plants and new plants.”The study does not predict that the analyzed pipes will fail. Instead, it provides a way to quantify how different assumptions and degradation factors can change calculated rupture probabilities, potentially giving engineers a more detailed basis for nuclear safety decisions.The study is set to be published in Engineering Failure Analysis.

title: China builds lithium metal battery with over 600 Wh/kg energy density
content: Chinese researchers have developed a high-stability lithium metal pouch cell with an energy density exceeding 600 Wh/kg, potentially addressing the limited flight endurance of drones and electric vertical take-off and landing aircraft.The battery was created by a joint team from Tianmushan Lab and Tsinghua University using a new electrolyte additive designed to protect both electrodes. The research targets stability, cycle life, and safety problems that have restricted the commercial use of high-energy lithium metal batteries.Battery reaches 602.5 Wh/kgCommercial lithium-ion batteries typically use graphite anodes and are approaching a theoretical energy density limit of about 350 Wh/kg. That ceiling makes it increasingly difficult for conventional batteries to meet the endurance requirements of emerging electric aircraft.Lithium metal offers a higher-capacity alternative, but it introduces significant technical challenges. Electrolyte decomposition can occur under high-voltage operating conditions, while needle-like lithium dendrites can grow on the anode.These dendrites reduce battery stability and can create safety risks. Researchers have consequently struggled to achieve high energy density without sacrificing cycle life or safe operation.The Chinese team tested its electrolyte design in 10Ah pouch cells equipped with high-nickel ternary cathodes. These cells achieved an energy density of 550.7 Wh/kg and retained 80 percent of their original capacity after 180 cycles.When the researchers paired the lithium metal anode with a lithium-rich manganese-based cathode, the reversible specific energy climbed to 602.5 Wh/kg. According to the reported results, this represents an improvement of more than 50% compared with mainstream power batteries currently available.New additive protects both electrodesThe advance relies on what the researchers describe as an additive-strong coordination solvation structure. This approach uses a new electrolyte additive to control the reactions taking place at the battery’s electrodes.On the cathode, the additive forms a thin and dense protective film. This layer helps reduce damage to the cathode material during repeated high-voltage charging and discharging.The additive also creates a stable interface layer on the lithium metal anode. That interface suppresses lithium dendrite formation, improves the efficiency of lithium-ion transport, and reduces the associated safety risks.By protecting both sides of the cell, the electrolyte design attempts to balance properties that have been difficult to achieve simultaneously in lithium metal batteries: high energy density, cycling stability, and safer operation.Longer flights remain a future goalThe research could eventually support China’s growing low-altitude economy, where drones and eVTOL aircraft are being developed for a range of commercial applications. Their broader adoption, however, remains constrained by the amount of energy batteries can store without adding excessive weight.A battery with energy density at the 600 Wh/kg level could carry substantially more energy for the same battery mass than existing commercial cells.That could help electric aircraft remain airborne longer, although the study did not provide specific flight-time estimates.The technology is also not yet ready for commercial deployment. The researchers said it remains at the laboratory research stage and will require further technical development before it can be manufactured at scale.The research was published in Nature Communications journal.

title: Chinese automaker targets faster EV charging with new 1.5 MW chargers
content: Geely is working on a new 1,000-volt electrical system for its electric vehicles, aiming to make charging times more like those of traditional cars. The company has built charging stations that can deliver up to 1.5 megawatts. In a recent test, a Lynk & Co 01 charged from 10 to 80 percent in just 5 minutes and 32 seconds.These results show how fast Geely’s EV technology is improving. The company is now developing higher-voltage systems that could let future models charge even more quickly.Geely moves beyond 800 voltsGeely has increasingly adopted 800-volt technology across its current EV lineup. The architecture extends across the vehicle’s battery, electric motors, power electronics, onboard charger, and wiring.The company is now developing a 1,000-volt system and drive units that work at higher voltages. Geely has not yet shared detailed specs for this new technology, such as the maximum charging power future vehicles will support.Its current charging performance already offers a glimpse of what the next generation could achieve. The Lynk & Co 01 recently charged from 10 to 80 percent in 5 minutes and 32 seconds. Reaching 97 percent from a 10 percent starting point took 8 minutes and 42 seconds.01 reaches 1,100 kW peakSome reports have described the Lynk & Co 01 as using a 900-volt system. However, its 95-kWh battery reportedly has a nominal voltage of 772.8 volts, placing it within the 800-volt category.In tests, the car briefly hit a peak charging power of 1,100 kW at a Zeekr fast charger. At a BYD Flash Charging Station, it reached 430 kW.The 1,100-kW figure represents peak output rather than power maintained throughout the session. Charging performance depends heavily on the battery’s charging curve, temperature, and thermal management.1.5 MW chargers are already deployedIn March, Geely said it had set up over 2,100 Zeekr charging points that can deliver up to 1,500 kW. Current EVs cannot use all that power yet, so there is a gap between the chargers and the cars.The planned 1,000-volt architecture could help close this gap. But higher voltage by itself will not ensure 1.5 MW charging. The battery and cooling system also need to be built to handle the extra heat and power.BYD and CATL raise the stakesGeely is joining a market where BYD already has similar technology. BYD’s Super e-Platform runs at 1,000 volts and is used in models like the Han L EV and Tang L EV. This system can support charging above 1,000 kW, and the Han L EV can reportedly add about 400 kilometers (249 miles) of CLTC range in five minutes.BYD’s Megawatt Flash Charger can deliver up to 1,360 kW, while CATL’s second-generation Shenxing battery is targeting charging power of up to 1.3 MW.Geely is also working on solid-state batteries, with testing planned for 2027. The top version could offer up to 500 Wh/kg of energy density and a range of over 1,000 kilometers (621 miles), but mass production is still some time off.

title: Diamond-cooled microchips boost power density 3.3x for radar systems
content: Northrop Grumman has secured a $7 million DARPA contract to develop diamond-enhanced microchips that could handle far more power without overheating. The work forms Phase 2 of DARPA’s Technologies for Heat Removal in Electronics at the Device Scale program, known as THREADS. Researchers want to solve a growing problem inside advanced military electronics: heat.Modern radio-frequency chips generate enormous amounts of heat in increasingly compact spaces. Engineers often limit their performance to prevent damage or premature failure. Northrop Grumman believes diamond could change that equation.Heat limits chip performanceThe aerospace and defense firm plans to integrate diamond directly into advanced semiconductor devices. The material would pull heat away from microscopic hotspots inside high-power RF circuits.Diamond offers exceptionally high thermal conductivity. According to Northrop Grumman, it can conduct heat about five times faster than copper. That capability could allow chips to operate at higher power levels without reaching damaging temperatures.The technology targets systems where power and size remain critical constraints. Potential applications include military communications, radar and satellite links.Ben Heying, director of microelectronics at Northrop Grumman’s Space Park Foundry, said temperature has long restricted semiconductor performance. “Embedding diamond directly into chips works like a turbocharged cooling system,” Heying said. “It keeps the chips cool so we can crank up the power without risk of burnout.” Northrop Grumman will now try to push the technology significantly further under DARPA’s second THREADS phase.Diamond channels carry heatEngineers at the company’s Microelectronics Center have developed methods for placing microscopic diamond structures within semiconductor devices.Northrop Grumman partnered with Stanford University on the approach. Their process grows diamond on the backside of a device and within microscopic channels.Those channels provide a direct path for heat to escape areas where temperatures can rapidly rise. The company has already conducted high-power tests involving diamond-based semiconductor technology. It says those tests supported the material’s potential for advanced electronics.Gallium nitride remains a major material for high-power and RF applications today. Yet even GaN devices face thermal limits as engineers demand greater output from smaller hardware.Better cooling could help change that tradeoff. During THREADS Phase 1, Northrop Grumman increased power density by 3.3 times. Power density measures how much electrical power engineers can pack into a given area.Power density faces another jumpPhase 2 now aims to increase power density by more than three times again. If successful, the effort could produce substantially more powerful RF transmitters without requiring proportionally larger electronics.That matters for defense systems where every additional watt creates cooling and packaging challenges. Smaller, more capable microchips could also support future military satellites and communications systems. High-power electronics must often operate for long periods under demanding conditions.Northrop Grumman has researched diamond-based thermal technology since 2019. The THREADS program now gives the work a larger pathway toward practical semiconductor manufacturing.The company also says its open-access foundry model could make the technology available across the broader U.S. microelectronics industry. That could prove important beyond a single defense program.Northrop Grumman‘s diamond approach places that cooling solution directly inside the semiconductor. The next phase will determine how far that idea can push military electronics beyond today’s thermal limits.

title: Electric flyer to connect downtown Chicago to America’s busiest airfield
content: A new plan has been introduced in the United States to redefine the airport transportation experience in Chicago with O’Hare Flyer, the first airport express train in the US. O’Hare Flyer, a fully electric train, will provide a 15-minute ride from Chicago’s downtown to O’Hare Airport’s Terminal 2 on a dedicated track with a reliable schedule of whisper-quiet train departures every 15 minutes. Clean trains with comfortable seatsThe company highlighted that O’Hare Flyer will provide concierge-level service on clean trains with comfortable seats and luggage racks in every car. The train will run on continuous rail and recharge at its Downtown station near the Old Post Office and at its Terminal 2 O’Hare station. “This is an important first for Chicago and for the country. O’Hare Flyer will build on Chicago’s heritage as America’s rail capital and center of innovation,” said O’Hare Flyer Founder and Chief Engineering Officer Mark Walbrun.“By combining three existing but underused freight rights-of-way into a dedicated express rail service, we will create the best airport transportation experience in America – and one of the best in the world.”O’Hare Flyer is a private endeavor. The project is not seeking government subsidies or funding that could otherwise go to regional transit agencies such as the CTA or Metra. With an objective to launch the project within the next five years, the O’Hare Flyer team is now meeting with public officials, business, finance, government, and community groups and will be expanding outreach throughout the region in the months ahead, according to a press release.Best airport transportation experience in America“This is an important first for Chicago and for the country. O’Hare Flyer will build on Chicago’s heritage as America’s rail capital and center of innovation,” said O’Hare Flyer Founder and Chief Engineering Officer Mark Walbrun. “By combining three existing but underused freight rights-of-way into a dedicated express rail service, we will create the best airport transportation experience in America – and one of the best in the world.”The company also pointed out that O’Hare Flyer will run on freight rail right-of-way owned by three class one railroads: CSX, Canadian National (CN) and Union Pacific (UP). The O’Hare Flyer has reached agreement on terms, memorialized in a Letter of Intent (LOI) with CSX and is moving forward with the other carriers as well. “O’Hare Flyer will be a job creation engine and an investment in working families and communities across Greater Chicago,” said Mike Macellaio, President of the Chicago and Cook County Building and Construction Trades Council. “Our MOU is an important first step toward a Project Labor Agreement that will help ensure this landmark project is built by Greater Chicago’s highly skilled unionized construction workforce while expanding opportunities for local workers and delivering lasting economic benefits throughout the region.”Over the last three years, with the O’Hare Flyer project in exploratory development, the project team has built a platform of best-in-class partners and service providers, with most based in Chicago. These partners include top engineering, law, architecture, urban planning, design, marketing and public relations firms. Two of the Big Four accounting and consulting firms are also supporting the project, as per the release.“For decades, Chicago’s economic and political leaders have dreamt about a fast connection between O’Hare and Downtown because it is economic development rocket fuel,” said O’Hare Flyer co-founder Kristi Lafleur. “This quiet, pollution-free electric train will attract visitors and more businesses to downtown and the region. It is also important and noteworthy that it will be led by and for Chicagoans.”

title: High-risk radioactive source material removed from key facility
content: Officials linked to United States’ Defense Threat Reduction Agency (DTRA) successfully removed a high-risk radioactive material from a key facility. The team worked with the National Nuclear Security Administration (NNSA) and removed a cobalt-60 source in Guatemala, strengthening U.S. and global radiological security.  While cobalt-60 is used in medical devices to treat cancer, the highly radioactive source could be stolen and used to create a “dirty bomb.”Radioactive material’s removal is a massive win“Our mission is simple: protect American citizens, secure our borders, and ensure our adversaries never get their hands on materials that could harm our country,” said Matthew Napoli, Deputy Administrator for NNSA’s Office of Defense Nuclear Nonproliferation. “This successful removal is a massive win for homeland security and demonstrates our positive relationship with the Guatemalan government. NNSA will do whatever it takes to defend America and keep our communities safe.”In May, a team from NNSA’s Los Alamos National Laboratory worked with a facility in Guatemala to remove part of a disused U.S.-origin medical radiation device – a teletherapy machine – containing cobalt-60 and transport it to secured storage in the United States. Guatemalan representatives from the National Centre of Radioactive Wastes and the Ministry of Energy and Mines provided expert transportation, logistical, and physical security support throughout the removal process, according to a press release.NNSA securely packaged radioactive cobalt-60 componentWorking together, NNSA securely packaged the cobalt-60 component, and DTRA provided secure transportation of the source back to the United States.  “The successful repatriation of the cobalt-60 source is a product of vital U.S. Government interagency cooperation,” said Robert Bridges, DTRA Program Manager of Nuclear Transportation & Disposition. “We are proud to work with NNSA to take meaningful action in their mission to eliminate radiological risk and keep America safe.”NNSA works with partner nations around the world to reduce nuclear and radiological risk. The Trump Administration’s 2026 Counterterrorism Strategy  underscores that preventing terrorists from acquiring chemical, biological, radiological, or nuclear weapons is a critical national security responsibility of the U.S. Government.One of the major concerns is the possibility that such material could be stolen and used in a radiological dispersal device, commonly known as a “dirty bomb.” Unlike a nuclear weapon, a dirty bomb does not produce a nuclear explosion. Instead, it uses conventional explosives or another mechanism to spread radioactive contamination, potentially causing casualties, disruption and widespread public concern.For this reason, international efforts to remove unnecessary high-activity radioactive sources are an important part of preventing radiological terrorism. NNSA’s Office of Radiological Security works both to eliminate such risks and to strengthen security around radioactive materials that continue to be needed.The operation represented more than a technical removal of radioactive material. It demonstrated how international cooperation, specialized scientific expertise and secure transportation capabilities can be combined to reduce a potential security threat.

title: Marine microbe engineered in US makes rocks absorb CO2 faster
content: Scientists have genetically engineered a widespread marine bacterium to accelerate rock weathering, a natural process that removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and helps regulate Earth’s climate.The team from Harvard University’s Wyss Institute, Harvard Medical School, and the Stanford Doerr School of Sustainability modified Alteromonas macleodii to increase the weathering of olivine in seawater. Tested in custom bioreactors, the bacterium accelerated the process by 2.6-fold and increased atmospheric CO2 removal. Bacteria remove rust from mineral surfacesRock weathering begins when silicate minerals such as olivine dissolve after exposure to water, air, and biological activity. The process releases magnesium, iron, and silicate while converting atmospheric CO2 dissolved in water into bicarbonate.However, the released iron oxidizes when exposed to the atmosphere and forms rust over the mineral surface. This coating slows further dissolution and limits the rate at which the rock can capture carbon.Some bacteria naturally produce siderophores, molecules that bind to oxidized iron and make it soluble. By removing this iron, the microbes effectively strip rust from the mineral surface and allow weathering to continue faster.The researchers found that natural bacteria stopped producing siderophores once they obtained enough iron for growth. They therefore engineered A. macleodii to continue producing the molecules regardless of surrounding iron levels.“To enable enhanced weathering at scale, we engineered A. macleodii to always produce siderophores. We essentially decoupled siderophore production from environmental iron levels,” said first author Neil Dalvie.Pilot reactors capture carbon from airAfter initial experiments showed promise, the researchers built pilot-scale bioreactors containing several kilograms of green olivine sand submerged in raw seawater collected from Boston Harbor.Seawater and bacteria continuously flowed over the mineral, allowing the team to measure weathering under steady-state conditions. The system eventually absorbed 0.5 grams of atmospheric CO2 per day.The engineered microbes increased olivine weathering by 2.6 times compared with the control conditions. According to the researchers, the experiment provided proof that synthetic biology could accelerate a geological process that normally unfolds over extremely long periods.“Our study embraces the concept of biologically inspired engineering and how synthetic biology can be applied to enhance normal climate-regulating processes, which ultimately could have a positive impact on our planet,” said Pamela Silver, a founding core faculty member at the Wyss Institute.Larger basins could process seawaterThe team also completed a life-cycle analysis covering carbon captured and emitted across the biological, geological, and chemical components of the system. The assessment helped identify which operating parameters would be important for achieving net carbon removal at an industrial scale.Further research is needed to locate economically viable sources of silicate minerals and other feedstocks. Scientists are also studying whether valuable metals could be recovered from the minerals while carbon is sequestered.One proposed deployment would involve growing the engineered bacteria in large basins similar to those used at sewage treatment facilities. Untreated seawater would be pumped through the basins before alkaline water containing the captured carbon is released into the ocean.“We believe this easily applicable, risk-free environmental engineering strategy could be implemented at many places with real-world decarbonization outcomes,” Silver said.

title: Micro-reactors set to yield 300,000 tons of fuel from methane waste
content: Emvolon, an MIT spinout developing technology to turn methane-rich waste gas into liquid fuels, has signed two commercial agreements with commodities trader Freepoint Commodities to scale production, targeting up to 300,000 metric tons annually as projects are deployed globally.Under a seven-year commodity purchase agreement, Freepoint will become the primary buyer of biomethanol and other liquid fuels produced at Emvolon’s projects. The fuel will enter Freepoint’s existing physical distribution network, giving Emvolon an established route to market as production expands.The second agreement gives Freepoint rights to co-invest in Emvolon’s project portfolio through equity and debt. The arrangement is designed to provide capital alongside technology deployment, particularly for projects using waste gas from landfills, dairy farms and industrial sites.Emvolon, founded in 2021, is developing systems that convert methane-rich waste gases into fuels and chemicals at the location where the waste is generated.Waste gas becomes fuelThe company’s approach uses modular micro-reactors built around mass-produced automotive engines. These systems are designed to convert waste gas directly into liquid fuels without relying on new pipeline or grid infrastructure.That could allow fuel production at sites where methane would otherwise be flared, released or left unused. Emvolon says its model can be applied to different feedstocks and locations, reducing the need for bespoke engineering for each project.“Energy security and supply chain resilience and sustainability dictate that we produce essential liquid fuels locally using domestic waste resources that are currently flared or lost,” said Emmanuel Kasseris, Ph.D., Co-Founder and CEO of Emvolon. “This dual commercial and capital agreement with Freepoint systematically solves the core bottleneck in decentralized fuel manufacturing by securing our buyer and anchoring our project financing platform. We are building our first commercial system now and will put that foundation to work across North America and key international growth regions.”The companies see methanol as a significant market for the technology. Methanol is used in shipping, heavy transport and chemical production, while newer pathways are also being developed to use methanol in sustainable aviation fuel production.Emvolon says low-carbon biomethanol that meets RED-II requirements can command a premium of more than $1,000 per metric ton. Its strategy is to produce the commodity close to waste sources, potentially cutting infrastructure requirements and transportation needs.Capital backs modular rolloutFreepoint’s investment rights could also help Emvolon move individual projects from technology deployment toward long-term financing. Rather than simply licensing its technology, Emvolon plans to package feedstock access, fuel production, financing and product sales into a single project model.The company has already demonstrated part of this approach through a joint venture with Montauk Renewables, which provides access to waste-gas resources.“Freepoint is focused on building resilient commodity supply chains and identifying proprietary technologies capable of scaling rapidly to meet physical supply deficits,” said Mark Lay, Managing Director at Freepoint. “Emvolon’s modular deployment model offers a practical solution to localized fuel production. Our dual commercial and capital commitment reflects our commitment to renewable chemicals and fuels.”The model is intended to support projects across landfill, agricultural and industrial waste streams in North America and other regions. If deployment scales as planned, the 300,000-metric-ton annual target would give the partnership a sizeable position in the emerging market for waste-derived fuels.

title: Non-flammable sodium battery tech clears critical accelerator milestones
content: The long-term future of energy storage hinges on solving one persistent, highly dangerous problem: fire risk.Conventional lithium-ion batteries power modern energy grids, but carry a known risk of thermal runaway. It is like a domino effect of overheating that causes catastrophic blazes. Hyundai Motor Group wants to eliminate that hazard entirely inside its manufacturing plants.The automaker just completed an extensive battery validation program with US-based UNIGRID Inc. through its ZER01NE Accelerator initiative. UNIGRID’s sodium chromium oxide (NCO) cell chemistry passed extreme safety testing with zero fire and zero thermal propagation. The technology is intended to deliver non-flammable, ultra-safe Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) for grid energy needs.“UNIGRID’s impressive validation performance demonstrates that their advanced sodium-ion chemistry is well positioned to meet the high safety and performance criteria of our upcoming energy initiatives,” said Jongguk Bae, Senior Manager at the Group’s Green Factory Development Team.Successful validationSodium is cheap, abundant, and chemically similar to lithium. But most of the attempts to scale sodium-ion cells stumbled over short lifespans and poor heat tolerance.UNIGRID’s proprietary NCO formulation will likely be able to break that pattern. During testing, the company’s 210Ah cells ran continuously at 100 percent depth of discharge with minimal capacity loss. Interestingly, the batteries performed across a harsh temperature spectrum of -20°C to 60°C. Heat didn’t trigger runaway and cold didn’t freeze performance. “Validating our chemistry under the Group’s rigorous standards confirms that our NCO technology solves the dual challenges of safety and longevity required to successfully deploy sodium-ion to solve emerging grid energy needs,” said Darren H. S. Tan, CEO & Co-Founder of UNIGRID.Safer choice over lithium As NCO chemistry operates safely across a wide temperature range without risk of thermal runaway, BESS installations can run fully passively. It will remove the the need for heavy HVAC systems, liquid cooling loops, or parasitic power loads to regulate temperatures. Apart from the safety hazard, lithium-ion depends on expensive, supply-constrained materials like lithium, cobalt, and nickel. These challenges often leave large-scale deployments vulnerable to price and geopolitical issues. On the other hand, the sodium advantage lies in its abundance and resilience. Sodium is thousands of times more abundant than lithium, and far cheaper to extract, which could help protect companies from supply-chain disruptions. As per the UNIGRID website, the NCO chemistry is engineered to reach up to 30,000 cycles at 80 percent capacity retention. This equates to roughly a 25-year operational lifespan (compared to standard LFP batteries, which degrade after 3,000–4,000 cycles). Hyundai is taking notice of these promising results and actively putting the technology to work. Aligned with its overarching “Green Factory” initiative, the automotive titan is shifting from evaluation to execution by partnering with domestic Korean integration specialists to engineer complete, commercial-scale NCO-based BESS. Once integrated, Hyundai Motor Group will deploy these specialized platforms across its global manufacturing plants as core distributed energy resources. It will eventually insulate the firm’s high-tech facilities from grid outages and establish a non-flammable benchmark for clean industrial power.

title: Raytheon expands radar plant with $50M investment in Mississippi
content: Raytheon has completed a $50 million expansion of its manufacturing facility in Forest, Mississippi, adding 17,000 square feet of space to increase production of electronic warfare and radar systems.The expansion is expected to create 100 high-skill jobs by 2028 and brings the facility’s total manufacturing space to 445,000 square feet. The new space will support production, testing and integration of Next Generation Jammer Mid-Band (NGJ-MB) pods for the US Navy and Australian government, along with other airborne radar programs.The NGJ-MB is an electronic warfare system designed to help aircraft disrupt or degrade enemy radar and communications. Increasing manufacturing capacity for the system could help Raytheon meet demand from the US and allied militaries.More room for electronic warfareThe Forest facility has become a major manufacturing site for Raytheon’s defense systems. The latest expansion follows three projects over the past decade that together represented $280 million in capital investment.Those projects included a 20,000-square-foot addition in 2013 and a 50,000-square-foot radar production and testing facility completed in 2020.The new expansion is aimed at more than simply increasing floor space. It is intended to provide additional capacity for the production and integration of complex defense electronics, where manufacturing and testing requirements can be extensive.“Completing this expansion underscores our long-term commitment to Forest and the state of Mississippi,” said Barbara Borgonovi, president of Naval Power at Raytheon. “Together with state and local partners, we’re building the workforce, infrastructure and capabilities needed to boost production in support of critical national defense programs.”The investment comes as militaries are placing greater emphasis on electronic warfare, airborne sensing and the ability to operate in environments where communications and radar systems may be contested.Scaling systems for allied forcesRaytheon’s Forest operation has supported the company for 40 years and is now one of Mississippi’s largest defense manufacturing plants.The facility’s expanded capacity will be used for systems serving both US and allied forces. The NGJ-MB pods are being produced for the US Navy and Australia, giving the manufacturing expansion an international role.Electronic warfare systems such as NGJ-MB are carried by aircraft and use advanced electronics to interfere with or counter hostile electromagnetic systems. Radar programs, meanwhile, provide the sensing capabilities needed to detect and track objects in the air.The combination means the expanded facility will support two closely connected areas of modern warfare: finding threats and operating when an adversary is trying to prevent that detection or communication.The project is also expected to expand the skilled workforce at the site. Raytheon plans to add 100 high-skill positions by 2028, extending the manufacturing site’s role beyond its current 445,000 square feet.“Rebuilding the American Arsenal creates more opportunities and more jobs right here at home. Today, our partners at Raytheon are expanding their manufacturing capacity and bringing 100 new jobs to Forest, Mississippi. These are critical jobs modernizing our military and supporting our troops – work Mississippi families can be proud of.”The expansion reflects a broader effort to increase domestic manufacturing capacity for defense technologies while supporting production for US allies. For Raytheon, the additional space provides room to scale radar and electronic warfare systems as demand grows.

title: Tiny fuel particles could power next-gen reactors on Earth, space
content: Antares Nuclear, a US company developing compact nuclear reactors for defense and space applications, has signed a multi-year agreement with Standard Nuclear to secure up to eight metric tons of TRISO fuel through 2035.The fuel will be used to power Antares’ microreactors, which are designed to provide reliable electricity in places where conventional power sources are difficult to deploy. The company is targeting applications ranging from US military installations to remote infrastructure and space missions.The agreement gives Antares a long-term supply of specialized nuclear fuel as it moves from reactor demonstrations toward planned deployments. Standard Nuclear will manufacture and deliver the TRISO fuel under the binding agreement.The two companies have been working together since 2025 on fuel specifications, manufacturability and production planning. The new deal formalizes that work and gives Antares greater certainty over fuel availability as it scales its reactor program.Tiny fuel for demanding missionsTRISO, or tristructural isotropic particle fuel, consists of small fuel particles enclosed in multiple protective layers. The design is intended to retain radioactive material under extreme conditions and is being developed for several advanced nuclear reactor applications.For Antares, securing fuel is an important part of getting its microreactors from testing to deployment. The company says its Mark-0 microreactor achieved initial criticality in 2026 under the US Department of Energy’s Reactor Pilot Program.Antares is targeting electricity production from an advanced reactor in 2027, with initial production deployments to US military installations planned for 2028.“Antares exists to deliver nuclear power exactly where and when it is needed most, whether supporting stateside military installations, enabling persistent space operations, or powering mission-critical infrastructure far from the grid,” said Jordan Bramble, CEO and Co-founder of Antares. “Securing a long-term, industrial-scale supply of TRISO fuel from Standard Nuclear is a foundational step in moving our microreactors from demonstration to deployments.”The agreement also illustrates a challenge facing advanced nuclear developers. Building a reactor is only part of the task. Developers also need reliable supplies of specialized fuel, manufacturing capacity and supporting infrastructure before reactors can be deployed at scale.Building the advanced fuel pipelineStandard Nuclear says it is currently the only US company with industrial-scale TRISO fuel fabrication facilities. The company is working to expand its production capacity through additional facilities as demand for advanced nuclear fuel grows.“Antares is building reactors for some of the most demanding environments on earth and in space, and Standard Nuclear is proud to support Antares for their strategic energy applications,” said Kurt Terrani, CEO of Standard Nuclear. “We are working to scale our TRISO production capacity across identical facilities and continue to adhere to our customers’ needs.”The companies’ agreement is therefore more than a fuel purchase. It connects a microreactor developer with a domestic fuel manufacturer at a time when the US is trying to build a larger advanced nuclear supply chain.Antares was founded in 2023 and says it has raised more than $600 million. Its compact reactors are being developed for applications where grid power or conventional generators may not provide the required combination of reliability, mobility and resilience.The fuel agreement does not guarantee that Antares’ planned reactor deployments will meet their target dates. However, it addresses one of the practical requirements for moving its technology toward commercial and government customers.

title: Tiny open-source robot duck can walk and learn from its mistakes
content: Hugging Face has unveiled the Microduck, a small open-source robot designed to make physical AI more accessible to developers and researchers.Developed with French robotics company Pollen Robotics, the duck-shaped robot is priced at $399 and is expected to begin shipping before Christmas. The Microduck can be programmed and trained by developers, with its software, simulation tools and reinforcement-learning stack made available for experimentation and further development.The launch adds another low-cost hardware platform to Hugging Face’s growing robotics efforts, as the company seeks to bring open-source AI beyond software and into physical machines. Tiny robot learnsMicroduck is a compact bipedal robot designed to give researchers, developers and students an accessible platform for experimenting with physical AI, reinforcement learning and robot control.Standing 25 centimeters (about 9.8 inches) tall and weighing less than 800 grams (1.8 pounds), Microduck packs 15 motors, a camera, a small depth sensor and two inertial measurement units (IMUs). Its articulated beak can also pick up objects, allowing the robot to combine locomotion with simple manipulation tasks. The robot can walk, sit, crouch and recover from many common falls. It can also roller-skate, demonstrating the range of movement behaviors that can be developed on the platform.Unlike conventional desktop robots that focus primarily on human-robot interaction, Microduck has been designed around physical action. Pollen Robotics says the platform is intended to let developers explore how robots learn movements, test behaviors in simulation and then transfer those behaviors to physical hardware.This makes reinforcement learning a central part of the system. Robots can learn by repeatedly attempting actions, failing and adjusting their behavior. On larger robots, this process can be expensive and potentially dangerous. Microduck’s small size and low weight make experimentation easier to conduct on a desk, in a classroom or in a home environment. The robot is also designed to recover from many falls, reducing the need for users to reset it manually after every failed experiment.Robot training simplifiedMicroduck comes with pre-trained behaviors so users can begin experimenting without first building their own control systems. It can be controlled with a gamepad, follow a laser dot, perform different movements and respond to its surroundings.However, the pre-installed behaviors are only intended as a starting point. Pollen Robotics is positioning Microduck as an open development platform, with software covering robot control, simulation, reinforcement learning and sim-to-real deployment. The company’s open-source Microduck repository provides the software development kit and robot software. In contrast, a separate Microduck RL repository contains tools for reinforcement learning and transferring learned behaviors from simulation to the physical robot.The sim-to-real capability is particularly important for robotics research. Training behaviors directly on physical machines can require significant time and hardware access. Simulation lets developers test and refine behaviors digitally before deploying them on a real robot, although reliably transferring those behaviors between simulated and physical environments remains a major challenge in robotics.Pollen Robotics also sees Microduck as a platform for multi-robot experiments. Multiple robots can be used to explore behaviors such as racing, football, and interaction between machines, potentially allowing developers to investigate multi-agent robotics without requiring expensive full-sized robots. The company says the broader goal is to make physical AI development more accessible. By combining inexpensive hardware with open-source software, simulation and reinforcement-learning tools, Microduck is intended to provide a practical way to experiment with how AI systems can learn physical skills.Microduck is currently available for pre-order for $399 before taxes and shipping. It comes in Cream, Graphite, Lavender, and Sky color options, with first deliveries targeted before Christmas 2026 in North America, Europe, and the UK.
